text: The periodic table was first organized by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, who arranged the 63 known elements by atomic weight and left gaps for elements yet to be discovered. His predictions for gallium, scandium, and germanium proved remarkably accurate when those elements were later found.

Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, making up approximately 75% of all normal matter by mass. It is also the lightest element, with an atomic number of 1 and a standard atomic weight of about 1.008.

Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, with a density of 22.59 g/cm³ — nearly twice as dense as lead. Its name comes from the Greek word 'osme,' meaning smell, because of the pungent odor of its volatile tetroxide.

Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the periodic table, with a Pauling electronegativity of 3.98. This extreme electronegativity makes it the most powerful oxidizing agent among all elements.

Water is one of only a few substances that expands when it freezes, because hydrogen bonding forces water molecules into a hexagonal lattice that is less dense than liquid water. This property is why ice floats, which is critical for aquatic life in cold climates.

Carbon forms more compounds than any other element, with over 10 million known organic compounds catalogued. This versatility arises from carbon's ability to form stable single, double, and triple bonds with itself and with many other elements.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2023 was awarded to Moungi G. Bawendi, Louis E. Brus, and Alexei I. Ekimov for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots, semiconductor nanocrystals whose properties depend on their size. These nanoscale crystals are now used in displays, lighting, and medical imaging.

Marie Curie remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 for research on radiation and Chemistry in 1911 for the discovery of polonium and radium. She was also the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon (allotropes), yet they have radically different properties. In diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in a tetrahedral lattice, making it the hardest natural material, while graphite has planar layers held together by weak van der Waals forces, making it soft and electrically conductive.

Avogadro's number (6.022 × 10²³) defines the number of particles in one mole of a substance, a concept essential to stoichiometry. It was named after Amedeo Avogadro, who in 1811 proposed that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

The Haber-Bosch process, developed by Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch in the early 20th century, synthesizes ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen at high temperature and pressure with an iron catalyst. It is estimated to sustain the food production needed for about half of Earth's current population.

Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) is the most widely produced industrial chemical in the world, with annual global production exceeding 200 million metric tons. It is used in fertilizer manufacture, petroleum refining, wastewater processing, and the synthesis of many other chemicals.

Benzene (C₆H₆) has a unique ring structure where the six π electrons are delocalized over all six carbon atoms, conferring extra stability known as aromaticity. August Kekulé famously described dreaming of a snake biting its own tail, which inspired him to propose the cyclic structure in 1865.

Chirality in chemistry refers to molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other, called enantiomers. The drug thalidomide is a famous example where one enantiomer treated morning sickness while the other caused severe birth defects.

Nylon, the first synthetic polymer, was developed by Wallace Carothers at DuPont and introduced commercially in 1938. It is a polyamide formed by condensation polymerization of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid, and was initially marketed as a replacement for silk in women's stockings.

The pH scale measures acidity and basicity on a logarithmic scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is basic. A one-unit change in pH represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

Electrochemistry underpins lithium-ion batteries, which power most modern portable electronics and electric vehicles. During discharge, lithium ions migrate from the anode through the electrolyte to the cathode, and the process reverses during charging.

Enzymes are biological catalysts — almost all of which are proteins — that accelerate chemical reactions in living cells by factors of up to 10¹⁷. They lower the activation energy of reactions without being consumed, and are exquisitely specific to their substrates.

DNA is a polymer made of four nucleotide monomers — adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine — linked by phosphodiester bonds. The double-helix structure was elucidated by Watson, Crick, Franklin, and Wilkins in 1953, earning Watson, Crick, and Wilkins the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

TNT (trinitrotoluene) is a yellow solid explosive whose rapid decomposition releases a large amount of gas and heat very quickly. It was first synthesized in 1863 by Julius Wilbrand and became widely used as a military explosive because it is stable enough to be safely handled and transported.

The Maillard reaction is a chemical reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars that gives browned food its distinctive flavour. It occurs above about 140–165 °C and is responsible for the complex aroma and color of roasted coffee, bread crust, seared meat, and many other cooked foods.

Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a two-dimensional hexagonal lattice, first isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov using Scotch tape. It is the thinnest known material and is stronger than steel, yet lightweight and highly electrically conductive.

PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), sold under the brand name Teflon, is a fluoropolymer so chemically inert that almost no substance sticks to it or reacts with it. It was accidentally discovered by Roy Plunkett at DuPont in 1938 when a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene gas polymerized overnight.

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) was first synthesized in a pure and stable form by Felix Hoffmann at Bayer in 1897. It works by irreversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, which reduces the production of prostaglandins responsible for pain, fever, and inflammation.

The discovery of penicillin by Alexander Fleming in 1928 launched the antibiotic era. The molecule contains a β-lactam ring that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis by irreversibly binding to penicillin-binding proteins, making it lethal to many Gram-positive bacteria.

Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plants that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis. Its molecular structure features a porphyrin ring with a central magnesium ion, and it selectively absorbs red and blue light while reflecting green wavelengths — giving leaves their characteristic color.

Linus Pauling, winner of the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and the 1962 Nobel Peace Prize, developed the concept of electronegativity and the resonance theory of chemical bonding. He is the only person to have won two unshared Nobel Prizes.

Ozone (O₃) is an allotrope of oxygen consisting of three oxygen atoms bound in a bent molecular geometry. In the upper atmosphere it forms the ozone layer that absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation, while at ground level it is a harmful air pollutant.

Soap works through its amphiphilic molecular structure: one end (the hydrophilic head) is attracted to water, while the other end (the hydrophobic tail) is attracted to grease and oils. When soap is agitated in water, it forms micelles that trap oil droplets and allow them to be rinsed away.

The element mercury (Hg) is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature and standard pressure, the other being bromine. Mercury's unusual liquid state at room temperature arises from relativistic effects that contract its 6s electron orbital, weakening metallic bonding.

Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using light energy. The overall equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, making it the primary source of oxygen and organic matter in Earth's biosphere.

Green chemistry, coined by Paul Anastas and John Warner in the 1990s, defines 12 principles that guide the design of chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances. It aims to make chemistry more sustainable at the molecular level.

Fermentation is an anaerobic metabolic process in which yeasts or bacteria convert sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The reaction, C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, has been exploited for thousands of years in breadmaking, brewing, and winemaking.

Gold is one of the least reactive metals and does not oxidize in air or react with most acids, which is why it has been prized since antiquity for coins and jewelry. It can only be dissolved in aqua regia, a mixture of concentrated nitric and hydrochloric acids in a 1:3 ratio.

Kevlar, a para-aramid synthetic fiber invented by Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont in 1965, has a tensile strength about five times that of steel on an equal-weight basis. Its rigid polymer chains are held together by hydrogen bonds that align in parallel sheets, making it ideal for bulletproof vests and cut-resistant gloves.

Limonene is a chiral molecule found in citrus peel: the (R)-enantiomer smells like oranges, while the (S)-enantiomer smells like turpentine. This dramatic olfactory difference illustrates how the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms can profoundly affect biological interactions.

The catalytic converter in automobiles uses platinum, palladium, and rhodium catalysts to convert toxic exhaust gases. Carbon monoxide is oxidized to CO₂, hydrocarbons are burned to CO₂ and water, and nitrogen oxides are reduced to harmless N₂.

Insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose, was the first protein to have its complete amino acid sequence determined, achieved by Frederick Sanger in 1955 — work that earned him the 1958 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Sanger later won a second Nobel in 1980 for DNA sequencing methods.

Salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) is an ionic compound whose crystal structure consists of alternating sodium and chloride ions in a face-centered cubic lattice. This ionic bonding gives salt its high melting point of 801 °C and its ability to conduct electricity when dissolved in water.

Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a thermoplastic polyester used in plastic bottles and clothing fibers. It is made by the condensation polymerization of terephthalic acid with ethylene glycol, and it is one of the most widely recycled plastics, given the resin code #1.

Nitrogen makes up approximately 78% of Earth's atmosphere but is nearly inert in its molecular form (N₂) because the two nitrogen atoms are held together by a very strong triple bond with a dissociation energy of 945 kJ/mol. Breaking this bond is the key challenge in nitrogen fixation.

Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀), nicknamed 'buckyball,' is a spherical carbon allotrope discovered in 1985 by Robert Curl, Harold Kroto, and Richard Smalley, who were awarded the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Its 60 carbon atoms are arranged in 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons resembling a soccer ball.

Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) is a purine alkaloid that acts as a central nervous system stimulant by competitively inhibiting adenosine receptors, thereby reducing the feeling of drowsiness. It is the world's most widely consumed psychoactive drug, naturally found in coffee, tea, and cacao.

Thermite is a pyrotechnic composition of aluminum powder and iron oxide (rust) that, once ignited, undergoes an exothermic oxidation-reduction reaction reaching temperatures of around 2500 °C. The reaction produces molten iron and aluminum oxide slag, and is used in welding and incendiary devices.

Capsaicin, the active compound in chili peppers, produces its burning sensation by binding to the TRPV1 receptor on sensory neurons, which normally responds to temperatures above 43 °C. This tricks the nervous system into perceiving heat even when the tongue is at normal body temperature.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2022 was awarded to Carolyn Bertozzi, Morten Meldal, and K. Barry Sharpless for click chemistry and bioorthogonal chemistry. Click chemistry enables rapid and highly selective reactions between molecules, revolutionizing drug development and the labelling of biological molecules.

Perfumes are composed of three layers of notes: top notes (first impression, lasting ~15 minutes, e.g., citrus), heart notes (the core character, lasting hours, e.g., floral or spicy), and base notes (the long-lasting foundation, e.g., musk and woody ambers). This structure reflects the different volatilities of the aroma compounds.

Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust and forms the basis of semiconductor electronics. Its ability to act as either a conductor or insulator depending on doping makes it the ideal material for transistors, microchips, and solar cells.

The alloy nitinol, composed of nickel and titanium in roughly equal atomic proportions, is a shape-memory alloy that can be deformed at low temperature and then returns to its original shape upon heating. It is used in medical stents, orthodontic wires, and aerospace actuators.

Antoine Lavoisier, often called the 'father of modern chemistry,' established the law of conservation of mass in the late 18th century, demonstrating that in a chemical reaction matter is neither created nor destroyed. He also named oxygen and hydrogen and helped reform chemical nomenclature.

Superconductors are materials that exhibit zero electrical resistance and expel magnetic fields (the Meissner effect) below a critical temperature. The 2023 controversy surrounding LK-99 highlighted global scientific interest in room-temperature superconductors, which could revolutionize energy transmission.

Acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is the main component of vinegar beyond water, typically at 5–8% concentration. It is classified as a weak acid because it only partially dissociates in water, and it is produced industrially by the carbonylation of methanol (the Monsanto process).

Zinc is essential for over 300 enzymes in the human body and plays structural roles in proteins such as zinc-finger transcription factors. Zinc deficiency affects an estimated 2 billion people worldwide and impairs immune function, growth, and neurological development.

Prussian blue, one of the first synthetically produced pigments (early 18th century), is an iron cyanide compound with the formula Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃. Its deep blue color is due to charge transfer between Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions across cyanide bridges, and it is used medically as an antidote to thallium and cesium poisoning.

The 2001 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to William Knowles, Ryoji Noyori, and K. Barry Sharpless for their work on chirally catalysed hydrogenation and oxidation reactions. These asymmetric catalysts can selectively produce one enantiomer of a chiral molecule, which is vital in pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Vanillin, the primary aromatic compound in vanilla, is now predominantly synthesized from lignin or guaiacol rather than extracted from vanilla beans, since natural extraction is extremely expensive. Approximately 85% of all vanillin used in food and fragrance is synthetic.

Phosphorus exists in several allotropes: white phosphorus is a waxy, highly reactive solid that ignites spontaneously in air; red phosphorus is more stable and used in matchsticks; and black phosphorus is the most stable form, with a layered structure similar to graphite.

Zeolites are microporous aluminosilicate minerals with a rigid, cage-like crystal structure that can selectively adsorb molecules based on size and shape — a property called molecular sieving. They are used as catalysts in petroleum cracking, water softeners in laundry detergents, and in the separation of gases.

Hemoglobin is a metalloprotein in red blood cells that contains four heme groups, each with an iron(II) ion at the center. Each iron atom can reversibly bind one oxygen molecule, allowing hemoglobin to transport oxygen from the lungs to tissues throughout the body.

Aerogel is a synthetic ultra-lightweight material derived from a gel in which the liquid component has been replaced with gas, yielding a material that is over 99% air by volume. Made primarily from silica, it has extremely low thermal conductivity and is used as insulation in NASA spacecraft and high-performance winter garments.

The Grignard reaction, discovered by Victor Grignard who received the Nobel Prize in 1912, involves organomagnesium halide reagents that act as nucleophiles to form new carbon-carbon bonds with carbonyl compounds. It remains one of the most versatile and widely used reactions in organic synthesis.

Titanium dioxide (TiO₂) is used as a white pigment in paints, sunscreens, and food coloring (E171) because of its very high refractive index and bright whiteness. It also exhibits photocatalytic activity under UV light, enabling self-cleaning surfaces and the degradation of pollutants.

Indigo is one of the oldest dyes in the world, having been used since ancient Egypt to dye textiles blue. The synthetic route was developed by Adolf von Baeyer in 1880, and synthetic indigo now dyes the vast majority of the world's blue jeans through a process of vatting, dyeing, and oxidation.

Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical structures made of rolled graphene sheets, exhibiting remarkable mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties. A single-walled carbon nanotube can be either metallic or semiconducting depending on its chirality — the direction in which the graphene sheet is rolled.

Activated charcoal has an extremely large surface area — up to 3000 m² per gram — due to its highly porous structure. This vast surface enables it to adsorb a wide range of toxins and is used in emergency medicine to treat certain types of poisoning.

The Born-Haber cycle is a thermodynamic cycle used to calculate the lattice energy of ionic compounds — the energy required to completely separate an ionic solid into its component ions in the gas phase. It applies Hess's law to a series of hypothetical steps including ionization, electron affinity, and sublimation.

Helium is the second most abundant element in the universe but extremely rare on Earth, as it is light enough to escape Earth's gravity. Most commercial helium is extracted from natural gas wells in the United States and Qatar, where it accumulates from the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium.

The concept of oxidation states (or oxidation numbers) provides a framework for tracking electron transfer in redox reactions. Manganese is notable for displaying the widest range of oxidation states of any element, from −3 to +7, making its compounds important in oxidizing agents like permanganate.

Polylactic acid (PLA) is a biodegradable polymer derived from renewable resources like corn starch or sugarcane. Made by ring-opening polymerization of lactide, it is used for 3D printing filaments, biodegradable packaging, and sutures, offering a more sustainable alternative to petroleum-based plastics.

Bioluminescence is the production and emission of light by living organisms through chemical reactions involving luciferin and the enzyme luciferase. The reaction oxidizes luciferin to produce an excited-state product that releases energy as light, a process used in fireflies, deep-sea fish, and many marine bacteria.

Coordination chemistry studies metal ions surrounded by ligands (Lewis bases) that donate electron pairs. Alfred Werner received the 1913 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his theory explaining the bonding and geometry of coordination compounds, including the octahedral geometry of cobalt complexes.

Ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃) is a white crystalline salt widely used as a nitrogen-rich fertilizer. Under confinement and with sufficient heat, it can explosively decompose to produce nitrogen gas, oxygen, and water vapor, as demonstrated catastrophically in the 2020 Beirut port explosion.

Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is a neurotransmitter and monoamine synthesized from the amino acid tryptophan. About 90% of the body's serotonin is found in the gut, where it regulates intestinal movements; it also plays a key role in mood, sleep, and appetite when acting in the brain.

The Diels-Alder reaction is a cycloaddition between a conjugated diene and a dienophile to form a six-membered ring. Otto Diels and Kurt Alder received the 1950 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its discovery; it remains a cornerstone of organic synthesis for constructing complex polycyclic molecules, including steroids and terpenes.

Gallium is a soft, silvery metal with an unusually low melting point of 29.76 °C — it will melt in the palm of your hand. Despite its low melting point, gallium has a very high boiling point of 2400 °C, giving it one of the widest liquid ranges of any element.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 was awarded to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna for developing the CRISPR-Cas9 method of genome editing, a molecular tool that acts like chemical scissors to cut DNA at precise locations. It has transformed medicine, agriculture, and fundamental biological research.

Radium, discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, was historically added to consumer products such as watch dials and health tonics because of its luminescent and energetic properties. After workers who painted watch dials with radium paint developed severe bone cancers, the dangers of radioactivity became undeniable.

Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with at least 10.5% chromium by mass, which forms a thin, adherent chromium oxide layer on the surface that protects against corrosion. Different grades may also contain nickel, molybdenum, and other elements to enhance specific properties.

Citric acid, found abundantly in citrus fruits, is a triprotic weak acid used widely as a food additive (E330) for its sour taste and preservative properties. In biochemistry, it is the first intermediate in the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle), the central metabolic pathway that oxidizes acetyl-CoA to CO₂.

Cholesterol is a waxy lipid molecule that is essential for animal cell membrane structure and the synthesis of steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. Despite its bad reputation, cholesterol is not inherently harmful; it is transport proteins (LDL and HDL) and lifestyle factors that determine cardiovascular risk.

The Periodic Table now officially contains 118 confirmed elements, with the four newest — nihonium (113), moscovium (115), tennessine (117), and oganesson (118) — being named in 2016. All elements beyond uranium (atomic number 92) are synthetic, produced in nuclear reactors or particle accelerators.

Hydrogen bonds are not true chemical bonds but rather relatively strong intermolecular forces between a hydrogen atom bonded to a very electronegative atom (N, O, or F) and a lone pair on another electronegative atom nearby. They are responsible for the high boiling point of water, the structure of proteins, and the base pairing in DNA.

Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide (CO₂), which sublimes directly from solid to gas at −78.5 °C at atmospheric pressure without passing through a liquid phase. Because CO₂ has no liquid phase at atmospheric pressure, it skips melting entirely — a property exploited in fog machines, food preservation, and industrial cleaning.

The Wittig reaction, developed by Georg Wittig, converts carbonyl compounds into alkenes using phosphorus ylides. Wittig shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this discovery, which is particularly valuable in organic synthesis because the double bond forms at a predictable location.

The noble gases (group 18) were long thought to be completely inert because of their full valence electron shells. Neil Bartlett disproved this in 1962 by synthesizing xenon hexafluoroplatinate, the first noble gas compound, showing that the heavier noble gases can form chemical bonds under certain conditions.

Lactase is the enzyme that breaks down lactose (milk sugar) into glucose and galactose in the small intestine. Most humans lose the ability to produce sufficient lactase after childhood — a condition called lactase nonpersistence — which leads to lactose intolerance affecting roughly 65% of the global population.

Lithium is the lightest metal and the least dense solid element, with a density of just 0.534 g/cm³. It is so reactive that it must be stored under oil, and its compounds are used in mood-stabilizing medications for bipolar disorder, as well as in rechargeable batteries and heat-resistant glass.

Pheromones are chemical signals secreted externally by animals to trigger specific behavioral or physiological responses in other members of the same species. Bombykol, the sex pheromone of the silkworm moth (Bombyx mori), was the first pheromone to be chemically characterized in 1959 by Adolf Butenandt, requiring the processing of half a million moths.

Electroplating is an electrochemical process in which a metal is deposited on a surface to improve its corrosion resistance, wear resistance, or appearance. In gold plating, the object acts as the cathode, a gold anode dissolves into the electrolyte solution, and gold ions are reduced and deposited onto the object.

Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) is a process used to produce high-quality solid materials by decomposing gaseous precursors on a heated substrate. It is the dominant technique for depositing thin films of silicon, silicon dioxide, and many other materials in microelectronics manufacturing.

The Hückel rule states that monocyclic, planar, fully conjugated molecules with 4n+2 π electrons (where n is a non-negative integer) are aromatic and therefore unusually stable. For benzene, n=1 giving 6 π electrons; for naphthalene, n=2 giving 10 π electrons.

Musk molecules in perfumery are macrocyclic compounds or polycyclic aromatics that provide soft, warm, long-lasting base notes. Natural musk was originally obtained from the gland of the Himalayan musk deer, but due to conservation concerns, all modern perfume musks are now synthetic.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any pure element at 3422 °C, which is why it was used as the filament in incandescent light bulbs. It also has the highest boiling point and one of the highest tensile strengths among metals, making it essential in high-temperature applications such as rocket nozzles and electrical contacts.

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, making up about one-third of total protein content. Its triple-helix structure — three polypeptide chains wound around each other — is stabilized by the regular occurrence of glycine at every third residue and by hydroxyproline cross-links that require vitamin C (ascorbic acid) to form.

The synthesis of urea by Friedrich Wöhler in 1828 from ammonium cyanate was a landmark moment that disproved vitalism — the belief that organic compounds could only be made by living organisms. This single experiment established that organic and inorganic chemistry obey the same laws.

The element curium (Cm, atomic number 96) was named after Marie and Pierre Curie, honoring their pioneering contributions to radioactivity research. Synthesized in 1944 by Glenn Seaborg's team at the University of California, it is an intensely radioactive actinide used as a power source in spacecraft.

Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda, NaHCO₃) reacts with acids to produce CO₂ gas, which causes baked goods to rise. When combined with an acid like cream of tartar or vinegar, it undergoes the reaction: NaHCO₃ + H⁺ → Na⁺ + H₂O + CO₂, creating bubbles that expand during baking.

Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant metal known — it does not react with any acid or base at any temperature up to around 2000 °C. Along with osmium, it is one of the rarest naturally occurring stable elements on Earth, primarily found in meteorites and deep-mantle rocks.

The nucleophilic substitution reaction (SN2) proceeds by a single-step mechanism where a nucleophile attacks a carbon atom on the face opposite the leaving group, inverting the stereochemistry of the carbon center. This 'Walden inversion' is one of the best-understood mechanisms in organic chemistry.

Photochromic lenses in eyeglasses darken in sunlight due to a reversible photochemical reaction involving silver chloride or organic dye molecules. UV light causes these molecules to change structure and absorb visible light; in the absence of UV, they revert to their transparent form.

Polycarbonate (PC) is a tough, transparent engineering thermoplastic made by the reaction of bisphenol A with phosgene. Its high impact resistance and optical clarity make it the material of choice for safety goggles, bulletproof glass, CDs, and DVDs.

Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive noble gas produced by the decay of radium in uranium-bearing rocks and soils. It seeps into buildings through foundations and, being eight times denser than air, can accumulate to dangerous levels in basements, making it the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking in the US.

The concept of hybridization in chemical bonding explains how atomic orbitals mix to form new hybrid orbitals with specific geometries. Carbon in methane is sp³ hybridized (tetrahedral), in ethylene it is sp² hybridized (trigonal planar), and in acetylene it is sp hybridized (linear).

Plutonium (Pu) was the first element to be produced in weighable quantities artificially, synthesized by Glenn Seaborg and his team in 1940. It has 94 protons and is best known as the fissile material in nuclear weapons, but it also powers spacecraft via radioisotope thermoelectric generators.

Acetylene (ethyne, C₂H₂) is the simplest alkyne and one of the hottest-burning hydrocarbon fuels. When combusted in an oxyacetylene torch, it produces a flame exceeding 3500 °C — hot enough to cut through steel — making it invaluable in metal welding and cutting.

The Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle), discovered by Hans Krebs in 1937, is a series of eight enzyme-catalyzed reactions in the mitochondrial matrix that oxidize acetyl-CoA to CO₂ and generate NADH and FADH₂. Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this fundamental discovery.

Phenolphthalein is a pH indicator that is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions but turns bright pink in basic solutions above pH 8.2. It was first synthesized in 1871 by Adolf von Baeyer and is widely used in acid-base titrations in educational and industrial laboratories.

The Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction is a classic example of a non-equilibrium chemical oscillator in which the concentrations of reactants cycle periodically, producing striking color changes and spatial patterns. It demonstrates that chemical systems can exhibit sustained rhythmic behavior far from equilibrium.

Dysprosium is a rare earth element with the highest magnetic moment per atom of any element. It is a critical component of the permanent magnets (NdFeB magnets with dysprosium additions) used in wind turbines and electric vehicle motors, making it strategically important for the clean energy transition.

Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is produced by the fermentation of sugars by yeasts and is the intoxicating component of alcoholic beverages. It is metabolized in the liver first to acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase and then to acetic acid by aldehyde dehydrogenase, and acetaldehyde is responsible for many hangover symptoms.

Fluorescence occurs when a molecule absorbs high-energy (short-wavelength) photons and re-emits lower-energy (longer-wavelength) photons almost instantaneously. Green fluorescent protein (GFP), isolated from jellyfish, has become an indispensable tool in cell biology for tagging proteins; its developers received the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Soap bubbles are thin films of water sandwiched between two layers of soap molecules. The characteristic iridescent colors arise from thin-film interference: light reflected from the outer and inner surfaces of the bubble interferes constructively or destructively depending on the film's thickness and the wavelength of light.

Potassium nitrate (saltpeter, KNO₃) is an oxidizing agent that has been used in gunpowder for over a millennium. Black powder is a mixture of approximately 75% potassium nitrate, 15% charcoal, and 10% sulfur by weight; when ignited, the rapid oxidation of carbon and sulfur by nitrate generates a large volume of hot gas.

Retrosynthetic analysis, a strategy developed by E.J. Corey and recognized with the 1990 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, involves working backwards from a target molecule to identify simpler precursors through a series of logical disconnections. This approach transformed the systematic planning of complex organic syntheses.

The element cesium (Cs) has the lowest ionization energy of all stable elements at 375.7 kJ/mol, making it the most electropositive metal. Because it readily releases its outermost electron, cesium is used in photoelectric cells, atomic clocks (which define the SI second), and as a catalyst in various reactions.

Morphine is an opium alkaloid isolated from the poppy plant that acts on μ-opioid receptors in the central nervous system to produce analgesia, euphoria, and respiratory depression. It was first isolated in 1804 by Friedrich Sertürner and named after Morpheus, the Greek god of dreams.

Le Chatelier's principle states that if a chemical equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, temperature, or pressure, the system will shift in the direction that counteracts the disturbance and re-establishes equilibrium. This principle is applied industrially to optimize yields of products such as ammonia and methanol.

Carmine (cochineal red) is a vivid natural red dye derived from dried female cochineal insects. Its primary component is carminic acid, which forms an aluminium lake pigment giving the brilliant crimson color used in food (E120), cosmetics, and textiles. Approximately 70,000 insects are required to produce one pound of dye.

Buckypaper, composed of a thin film of carbon nanotubes, is about 500 times stronger than steel by weight and conducts electricity as well as copper. Potential applications include lightweight armor, next-generation electronics, and membranes for water filtration and medical devices.

Oxidative phosphorylation is the process by which mitochondria synthesize ATP using energy derived from the electron transport chain. Electrons flow from NADH and FADH₂ through a series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane, driving proton pumps that create a gradient used by ATP synthase to make ATP.

Luminol is a chemical that exhibits chemiluminescence when oxidized — producing a blue glow without producing heat. Forensic investigators use luminol to detect trace amounts of blood at crime scenes, as the iron in hemoglobin catalyzes the luminol oxidation reaction even when blood has been cleaned away.

Rhenium (Re) is one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust and has the third-highest melting point of any element (3186 °C). It is alloyed with nickel to make single-crystal superalloy turbine blades in jet engines, which must withstand extreme temperatures and mechanical stress during operation.

Acetone (propanone, CH₃COCH₃) is the simplest ketone and an important industrial solvent produced in quantities of millions of tons per year. The human body also produces acetone endogenously during ketosis — the metabolic state induced by fasting or low-carbohydrate diets — which accounts for the characteristic fruity breath of people on ketogenic diets.

The Solvay process, developed by Ernest Solvay in the 1860s, is the dominant industrial method for producing sodium carbonate (soda ash, Na₂CO₃) from brine and limestone via ammonia intermediates. Soda ash is essential in glassmaking, detergents, and paper production.

Copper is one of the earliest metals used by humans, with evidence of its use dating back more than 10,000 years. Its excellent electrical conductivity — second only to silver among pure metals at room temperature — makes it the material of choice for electrical wiring globally.

Sodium vapor street lamps produce their characteristic yellow-orange light through the emission spectrum of sodium atoms. When electrons in sodium are excited by electrical discharge and then fall back to lower energy states, they emit photons at two wavelengths very close together at 589.0 and 589.6 nm — the sodium D-lines.

Myrcene is a monoterpene that gives hops their distinctive piney, herby aroma, making it one of the most important flavor compounds in beer. It is also found in cannabis, lemongrass, and mango, and is a key building block for the synthesis of many other terpene flavor and fragrance molecules.

Xenon difluoride (XeF₂) is one of the rare compounds of a noble gas, taking the form of a white crystalline solid. It is a powerful fluorinating agent used in semiconductor manufacturing to etch silicon and is notable because its existence disproved the long-held belief that noble gases could not form stable compounds.

The Menshutkin reaction is a nucleophilic substitution in which a tertiary amine reacts with an alkyl halide to form a quaternary ammonium salt. This reaction is the basis for synthesizing many surfactants, ion-exchange resins, and pharmaceutical intermediates.

Anthocyanins are water-soluble plant pigments that produce red, purple, and blue colors in fruits, vegetables, and flowers such as blueberries, red cabbage, and purple roses. Their color is pH-dependent: red in acidic conditions and blue/green in basic conditions, which is why red cabbage juice makes an excellent natural pH indicator.

The Heck reaction, developed by Richard Heck, enables the palladium-catalyzed coupling of an aryl halide with an alkene to form a substituted alkene with new carbon-carbon bonds. Heck shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Ei-ichi Negishi and Akira Suzuki for palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions.

Methane (CH₄) is the simplest hydrocarbon and the primary component of natural gas. As a greenhouse gas, it is 28 times more potent than CO₂ over a 100-year period, and global warming from methane emissions — from livestock, wetlands, and fossil fuel operations — is a major concern in climate science.

Palladium, platinum, and rhodium are precious metals collectively known as platinum-group metals (PGMs), prized for their exceptional catalytic activity. South Africa holds approximately 91% of the world's known platinum reserves, making PGM supply vulnerable to geopolitical risk.

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the universal energy currency of living cells. When one of its phosphoanhydride bonds is hydrolyzed to yield ADP and inorganic phosphate, about 30.5 kJ/mol of free energy is released under standard conditions, powering muscle contraction, ion pumping, and biosynthesis.

Cinnabar (mercury(II) sulfide, HgS) is a vivid red mineral historically prized as the pigment vermillion. Ancient Romans imported cinnabar from mines in Spain to use in wall paintings and cosmetics, unaware of the toxicity of mercury compounds — the miners and artisans who worked with it suffered severe health consequences.

Supramolecular chemistry, recognized with the 1987 Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to Donald Cram, Jean-Marie Lehn, and Charles Pedersen, studies non-covalent interactions between molecules — including hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic effects, and van der Waals forces — to build functional molecular assemblies.

Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) is the primary mineral component of limestone, chalk, marble, seashells, and coral. When heated strongly (calcination), it decomposes to calcium oxide (quicklime) and CO₂, a process that is one of the largest industrial sources of carbon dioxide emissions globally.

Oud (agarwood) is one of the world's most expensive perfume ingredients, derived from the resinous heartwood that forms in Aquilaria trees in response to fungal infection. Its complex chemical profile includes sesquiterpenoids and chromone derivatives, and it can fetch up to $30,000 per kilogram for the highest grades.

The saponification reaction involves the hydrolysis of an ester (fat or oil) with a strong base such as sodium hydroxide to produce glycerol and fatty acid salts (soap). The process has been known for at least 2,800 years and remains the basis of commercial soap manufacturing today.

Scandium, although classified as a rare earth element, is actually more abundant in Earth's crust than lead or tin; it is 'rare' only because it does not occur in concentrated mineral deposits. Alloyed in small amounts with aluminum, it significantly increases strength and weld quality, making scandium-aluminum alloys prized in aerospace and sporting equipment.

Sublimation is the phase transition directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid phase, occurring when the vapor pressure of the solid exceeds atmospheric pressure before the melting point is reached. Iodine crystals sublime readily at room temperature, producing a purple vapor — a vivid demonstration used in fingerprint detection.

Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1909) proved that the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space. When alpha particles were fired at a thin gold foil, most passed straight through, but a small fraction bounced back — an observation Rutherford described as 'like firing artillery at tissue paper and having the shells bounce back.'

Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is a silicon-based organic polymer most commonly encountered as silicone, prized for its biocompatibility, thermal stability, and flexibility. It is used in breast implants, contact lens materials, lubricants, food-safe cooking molds, and as an anti-foaming agent (E900) in food products.

Astatine (At) is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, with an estimated total natural occurrence of only about 28 grams worldwide at any given time. It is a halogen but also exhibits metallic properties and is highly radioactive, with its most stable isotope (At-210) having a half-life of only 8.1 hours.

Biodiesel is produced by the transesterification of triglycerides (vegetable oils or animal fats) with methanol in the presence of an alkali catalyst, yielding fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) and glycerol as a byproduct. It can be used directly in diesel engines or blended with petroleum diesel to reduce particulate and CO₂ emissions.

Haemocyanin is a copper-containing metalloprotein found in the blood of many mollusks and crustaceans that serves the same oxygen-transport function as haemoglobin in vertebrates. Because it contains copper rather than iron, haemocyanin-rich blood appears blue when oxygenated — which is why octopus and horseshoe crab blood is blue.

The aldol reaction is a key carbon-carbon bond-forming reaction in organic chemistry where an enolate ion attacks a carbonyl group to form a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound (an aldol). It is used in the biosynthesis of sugars (via aldolase enzymes) and in industrial syntheses of fine chemicals and pharmaceuticals.

Magnesium is a biologically essential element that acts as a cofactor for over 300 enzymes, including those involved in ATP synthesis, DNA replication, and protein synthesis. In plants, magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule, making it indispensable for photosynthesis.

The smell of rain on dry earth, called petrichor, is mainly produced by geosmin, a bicyclic alcohol synthesized by soil-dwelling Streptomyces bacteria. Humans can detect geosmin at concentrations as low as 5 parts per trillion — one of the lowest odor thresholds known — which may reflect an evolutionary advantage in locating water.

The Ziegler-Natta catalyst, discovered by Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta (Nobel Prize 1963), enabled the stereospecific polymerization of olefins such as propylene to produce isotactic polypropylene — a material with uniform tacticity and therefore useful mechanical properties. It transformed the plastics industry.

Epoxy resins are thermosetting polymers formed by the reaction of an epoxide resin with an amine or anhydride hardener. Once cured, they form a highly crosslinked network that is extremely strong, chemically resistant, and adhesive — making them essential in aerospace composites, coatings, and electronics encapsulation.

Ibuprofen (2-(4-isobutylphenyl)propionic acid) is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes. The original synthesis by Stewart Adams at Boots UK in the 1960s required 11 steps; a later green chemistry synthesis by the BHC Company reduced this to just 3 steps and won the Presidential Green Chemistry Challenge Award.

Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at standard room temperature and pressure (the other being mercury). It is a reddish-brown liquid with a pungent, toxic odor, and most commercially produced bromine is used in flame retardants, fumigants, and water purification chemicals.

Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), invented in 1981 by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer (Nobel Prize in Physics, 1986), images surfaces at the atomic scale by measuring the quantum tunneling current between a sharp metallic tip and the surface as the tip scans across it. It allowed chemists to image and manipulate individual atoms for the first time.

Glycerol (glycerin, C₃H₈O₃) is a sweet, viscous triol that is a byproduct of biodiesel production and soap manufacture. It is widely used as a moisturizer in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals, a sweetener in food, and a solvent in pharmaceutical preparations because of its hygroscopic nature and low toxicity.

Lanthanides (rare earth elements, atomic numbers 57–71) are used in powerful neodymium magnets, phosphors in LED lighting, and contrast agents in MRI scans. Despite being called 'rare,' most lanthanides are relatively abundant in Earth's crust — they are 'rare' because they rarely occur in concentrated mineral deposits.

Synthetic rubber was developed during World War II when natural rubber supplies from Southeast Asia were cut off. Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), a copolymer of styrene and 1,3-butadiene, became the dominant synthetic rubber and today accounts for about 50% of all rubber production used in tires.

Taxol (paclitaxel), first isolated from the Pacific yew tree (Taxus brevifolia) in 1967, is one of the most important anticancer drugs ever discovered. It works by stabilizing microtubule polymers and preventing cell division. Total synthesis of taxol was achieved in 1994 by the Holton and Nicolaou groups in a landmark achievement of complex natural product chemistry.

Rose oil (attar of roses) requires approximately 3.5 tons of rose petals to produce just 1 kg of essential oil, making it one of the costliest natural fragrance materials. Its aroma character comes primarily from β-damascenone, citronellol, and geraniol — molecules formed by the enzymatic degradation of carotenoids and fatty acids in the petals.

Polystyrene foam (Styrofoam) is approximately 95% air trapped in a matrix of polystyrene polymer. It was accidentally discovered in 1941 by Dow Chemical researcher Ray McIntire while attempting to find a flexible electrical insulator. Its excellent thermal insulating properties and light weight made it ubiquitous in food packaging and construction.

The nuclear binding energy per nucleon is greatest for iron-56, making iron the most thermodynamically stable nucleus. This is why stellar nucleosynthesis of elements heavier than iron requires energy input (endothermic) and only occurs in supernova explosions, while fusion of lighter elements releases energy.

Terpenes are a large class of natural organic compounds built from repeating five-carbon isoprene units. They include the flavors and fragrances of plants (limonene in lemons, pinene in pine trees, menthol in mint), the rubber polymer polyisoprene, and biological molecules such as cholesterol, steroid hormones, and fat-soluble vitamins.

Napalm is a thickened flammable liquid developed during World War II, originally made from aluminum naphthenate and aluminum palmitate mixed with gasoline. Modern napalm-B uses polystyrene as the thickener, creating a gel that burns at around 800–1200 °C and adheres to surfaces, making it a highly destructive incendiary weapon.

The Pauling electronegativity scale assigns values from 0.7 (francium) to 3.98 (fluorine) based on bond dissociation energies. When the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms exceeds approximately 1.7, the bond is considered predominantly ionic; below this value it is predominantly covalent.

Polypropylene (PP) is one of the most widely produced commodity plastics, made by Ziegler-Natta catalyzed polymerization of propylene. Its chemical resistance, heat tolerance, and light weight make it the material of choice for food containers, automotive parts, textiles (fleece), and medical devices.

Cinnamaldehyde is the compound responsible for the characteristic aroma and flavor of cinnamon, making up 55–90% of cinnamon bark essential oil. It has a reactive α,β-unsaturated aldehyde structure that gives it antimicrobial properties, which is why cinnamon has been used as a food preservative for millennia.

Carbon-14 radiocarbon dating, developed by Willard Libby (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1960), exploits the fact that living organisms continuously incorporate atmospheric ¹⁴C; after death, the ¹⁴C decays with a half-life of 5730 years. By measuring the ratio of ¹⁴C to ¹²C, the age of organic material up to about 50,000 years old can be determined.

Methylene blue is a phenothiazine dye with the remarkable property of cycling between a blue oxidized form and a colorless reduced form (leucomethylene blue). It is used as a redox indicator, an antidote for methemoglobinemia, a stain in histology, and most recently as a photosensitizer in photodynamic therapy for certain cancers.

Oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) is a solution of SO₃ dissolved in concentrated H₂SO₄. It is more reactive than ordinary sulfuric acid and is used industrially for sulfonation reactions in the manufacture of dyes, detergents, and explosives such as nitroglycerine.

Nitrous oxide (N₂O, 'laughing gas') was the first anesthetic agent used in dentistry and surgery, introduced by Horace Wells in the 1840s. As a greenhouse gas, it is approximately 265 times more potent than CO₂ over a 100-year period and depletes stratospheric ozone, making agricultural emissions of N₂O a significant environmental concern.

Enzyme kinetics is described by the Michaelis-Menten equation, which relates the reaction rate to substrate concentration, with two key parameters: Km (Michaelis constant, the substrate concentration at half maximum velocity) and Vmax (the maximum rate). This model, derived by Michaelis and Menten in 1913, underpins drug design and metabolic engineering.

Silver iodide (AgI) has been used since the 1940s in cloud seeding — dispersing it into clouds causes water droplets to freeze around AgI crystal nuclei, promoting precipitation. It works because AgI has a crystal structure nearly identical to ice, tricking water molecules into forming ice crystals.

The Dewar flask (vacuum flask), invented by James Dewar in 1892 and commercialized as the Thermos, uses a double-walled container with a vacuum between the walls to minimize heat transfer by conduction and convection. Its development was intertwined with Dewar's work on liquefied gases, allowing him to store liquid hydrogen.

Sulforaphane, found in cruciferous vegetables like broccoli, is formed when the enzyme myrosinase acts on glucoraphanin upon cell damage (such as chewing). It activates the Nrf2 transcription factor, upregulating antioxidant and detoxification enzymes, and is actively researched for cancer-prevention properties.

RDX (Research Department Explosive, cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine) is a powerful military explosive with a detonation velocity of about 8750 m/s. Introduced during World War II, it remains in widespread military use as a component of plastic explosives such as C-4, which contains approximately 91% RDX.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is an analytical technique used to separate, identify, and quantify compounds in complex mixtures by passing a liquid sample under high pressure through a column packed with a stationary phase. It is the workhorse analytical method in pharmaceutical quality control, food safety testing, and environmental monitoring.

Terpene indole alkaloids include strychnine, quinine, vincristine, and morphine — some of the most pharmacologically important natural products. Their structural complexity spurred some of the greatest achievements in total synthesis, including R.B. Woodward's synthesis of strychnine in 1954, widely considered one of the greatest accomplishments in organic chemistry.

Potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) is a strong oxidizing agent with a distinctive deep purple color due to charge-transfer absorption of light. In aqueous solution it is reduced to colorless Mn²⁺ in acidic conditions or to brown MnO₂ in neutral/basic conditions, a color change exploited in volumetric analysis and water purification.

Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner, and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission in 1938 by bombarding uranium with neutrons and finding barium in the products. Hahn received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone; Meitner, who was Jewish and had fled Nazi Germany, was controversially excluded despite her theoretical interpretation of the results.

Squalene is a triterpene hydrocarbon found in shark liver oil and olive oil, and it serves as a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of all steroid hormones, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins in humans. It has also become important as an adjuvant in influenza vaccines, enhancing the immune response.

Metallic hydrogen, in which hydrogen behaves as an electrical conductor rather than an insulator, is predicted to exist at pressures exceeding 400 GPa. It is theorized to be present in the cores of gas giants like Jupiter and could theoretically be a room-temperature superconductor, though sustained production under laboratory conditions remains a major challenge.

The first organic synthesis of a natural product was quinine from cinchona bark by William Henry Perkin's mentor August Wilhelm von Hofmann — though Perkin accidentally synthesized mauveine (the first synthetic dye) in 1856 while attempting the synthesis of quinine. This chance discovery launched the synthetic dye industry.

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), once widely used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants, were found to catalytically destroy stratospheric ozone — a single chlorine atom can destroy more than 100,000 ozone molecules. The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs globally and stands as one of the most successful international environmental agreements.

The Gibb's free energy equation (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS) determines whether a chemical reaction is spontaneous: if ΔG < 0 the reaction proceeds spontaneously at constant temperature and pressure. It elegantly combines enthalpy (heat) and entropy (disorder), showing that some endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if they produce sufficient entropy.

The Swern oxidation converts primary and secondary alcohols to aldehydes and ketones under mild conditions using oxalyl chloride and DMSO at low temperature. Its mild conditions and compatibility with acid- and base-sensitive functional groups make it widely used in pharmaceutical synthesis.

Sarin is an extremely toxic organophosphate nerve agent that irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine at nerve synapses. Even tiny doses (approximately 1.7 mg/kg by skin contact) can be lethal, causing excessive nerve stimulation, muscle paralysis, and death by respiratory failure.

Nanoparticle drug delivery systems encapsulate therapeutic molecules in particles typically 10–200 nm in diameter, allowing drugs to be targeted to specific tissues (e.g., tumors), improving solubility, extending half-life, and reducing side effects. The mRNA COVID-19 vaccines used lipid nanoparticles to deliver genetic material into human cells.

Copernicium (Cn, element 112) was synthesized in 1996 at GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Germany by bombarding lead-208 with zinc-70 ions. Named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, it is predicted to behave more like a noble gas than a metal due to relativistic effects on its electron configuration.

Hydrothermal synthesis uses hot pressurized aqueous solutions above 100 °C to grow crystals that cannot easily be made at room temperature and pressure. It is the primary industrial method for producing synthetic quartz crystals (used in electronics), zeolites, and gemstones such as synthetic emeralds.

Boron nitride (BN) exists in several structural forms analogous to carbon allotropes: hexagonal BN (h-BN) resembles graphite and is used as a lubricant, while cubic BN (c-BN) is the second hardest known material after diamond and is used in cutting tools. A boron nitride nanotube analog of a carbon nanotube is also known.

Amylase is a digestive enzyme found in saliva and pancreatic juice that hydrolyzes the glycosidic bonds in starch to yield maltose and glucose. This is why holding a starchy cracker in the mouth begins to taste sweet — salivary amylase converts starch to sugars before the food even reaches the stomach.

The concept of aromaticity was extended beyond benzene to include polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) such as naphthalene, pyrene, and coronene. PAHs form during incomplete combustion of organic matter and are of significant health concern as carcinogens found in cigarette smoke, grilled meat, and vehicle exhaust.

Esters are compounds formed by the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol in an equilibrium reaction catalyzed by acid. They are responsible for the fruity aromas and flavors in nature: ethyl acetate gives nail polish remover its smell, isoamyl acetate gives banana candy its flavor, and pentyl butyrate gives pineapple its aroma.

The sol-gel process converts metal alkoxide solutions (sols) into solid oxide networks (gels) through hydrolysis and condensation reactions, without the high temperatures needed for conventional glass melting. It enables the synthesis of glasses, ceramics, and thin oxide films with precise composition at room temperature and is used to make anti-reflective coatings on optical lenses.

Gadolinium (Gd) has exceptional neutron-absorbing properties and the highest magnetic moment of any stable element. Its chelated complexes (e.g., gadopentetate dimeglumine) are the most widely used MRI contrast agents, shortening relaxation times and improving the contrast between different tissues in magnetic resonance imaging.

Polylysine is a food preservative (ε-polylysine, E1105) produced by bacterial fermentation that is widely used in Japan and increasingly globally. It kills bacteria by binding to their negatively charged cell membranes and disrupting them, and is effective against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, molds, and yeasts.

Osmium tetroxide (OsO₄) is used in electron microscopy to stain biological specimens and in organic synthesis to dihydroxylate alkenes with high stereoselectivity. Despite its utility, it is extremely toxic as its vapors attack mucous membranes and corneas; even sub-microgram doses can cause permanent blindness.

Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are crystalline porous polymers built entirely from lightweight elements (C, H, N, O) linked by strong covalent bonds. Their highly ordered porous structures with tunable pore sizes and enormous surface areas (up to 4000 m²/g) make them promising for gas storage, catalysis, and drug delivery.

Dopamine is a catecholamine neurotransmitter that plays a central role in the brain's reward and pleasure pathways. Chemically, it is 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine, synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine, and its concentration is modulated by many drugs of abuse, including cocaine (which blocks its reuptake) and amphetamines (which increase its release).

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024 was awarded to David Baker for computational protein design and to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction using AI (AlphaFold). AlphaFold2 predicted structures for virtually all known proteins with accuracy rivaling experimental methods, solving a 50-year-old grand challenge in biochemistry.

Nylon 6,6, the first fully synthetic fiber, was invented by Wallace Carothers at DuPont in 1935 by condensation polymerization of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid. It was the world's first purely synthetic textile fiber and debuted commercially in women's stockings at the 1939 New York World's Fair.

Kevlar, a para-aramid synthetic fiber developed by Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont in 1965, has a tensile strength five times greater than steel on an equal-weight basis. Its rigidity arises from hydrogen bonds and aromatic stacking between rigid, parallel polymer chains, making it essential in ballistic-resistant vests and helmets.

Host-guest chemistry, a cornerstone of supramolecular chemistry, involves molecules that recognize and bind specific guest species inside a cavity. Crown ethers, discovered by Charles Pedersen in 1967, selectively bind alkali metal cations whose size matches the ether ring cavity — a concept he shared the 1987 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for pioneering.

Photosynthetic reaction centers are among the most efficient photochemical systems known, converting absorbed photon energy into charge-separated states with near-unity quantum efficiency. The primary photochemical act — electron transfer across the membrane — occurs in roughly 3 picoseconds, faster than any competing deactivation pathway.

Technetium-99m is the most widely used medical radioisotope, employed in more than 30 million diagnostic procedures per year worldwide. It emits only a 140 keV gamma ray with a 6-hour half-life — long enough for imaging but short enough to minimize patient radiation dose — and is produced on-site at hospitals from molybdenum-99 generators.

Astrochemistry has identified more than 270 molecular species in the interstellar medium, including complex organics like glycolaldehyde (a sugar) and ethyl formate (which gives raspberries their flavor). Molecules form on cold dust grain surfaces or through gas-phase ion-molecule reactions in the extreme cold and vacuum of space.

Density functional theory (DFT), developed by Walter Kohn (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1998), is the most widely used method in computational chemistry for calculating molecular electronic structure. Rather than solving for many-electron wavefunctions directly, DFT expresses all ground-state properties as functionals of the electron density, dramatically reducing computational cost.

Perovskite solar cells, named for their ABX₃ crystal structure, have seen their power conversion efficiency rise from 3.8% in 2009 to over 26% by 2024 — one of the fastest efficiency improvements in photovoltaic history. The most studied perovskites use methylammonium lead halides and are promising low-cost alternatives to silicon-based cells.

The Langmuir adsorption isotherm, derived by Irving Langmuir (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1932), describes how gas molecules adsorb onto a solid surface by assuming a monolayer of adsorption sites with uniform energy and no adsorbate–adsorbate interactions. It remains the foundational model in surface chemistry and heterogeneous catalysis.

Colloids are mixtures in which one substance is dispersed as particles 1–1000 nm in size throughout another substance. Mayonnaise (oil droplets in water), milk (fat globules), and fog (water droplets in air) are everyday colloids; the Tyndall effect — scattering of light by colloidal particles — explains why a beam of sunlight is visible in dusty air.

Ink chemistry relies on dyes or pigments suspended in a carrier fluid. Modern inkjet inks use water-based solutions of dyes (for photo-quality) or polymer-encapsulated pigments (for longevity); thermal inkjet printers vaporize ink in a resistor-heated chamber, ejecting droplets of ~10 picoliters with each pulse.

The lithium-ion battery, commercialized by Sony in 1991, operates by shuttling lithium ions through an electrolyte between a graphite anode and a lithium metal oxide cathode. John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, and Akira Yoshino were awarded the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its development, which enabled the wireless electronics revolution.

Proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells generate electricity by combining hydrogen fuel with oxygen from air, producing only water as a byproduct. Platinum nanoparticles catalyze the oxygen reduction reaction at the cathode, and the perfluorosulfonic acid membrane (Nafion) selectively conducts protons while blocking electrons, driving the external circuit.

Ozone (O₃) in the stratosphere absorbs most of the sun's UV-B and UV-C radiation, protecting life on Earth. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), once widely used as refrigerants, release chlorine radicals in the stratosphere that catalytically destroy ozone; one chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules before being deactivated.

Vanillin is the primary aromatic compound in vanilla beans, responsible for their characteristic scent and flavor. Over 85% of vanilla flavor used globally is synthetic vanillin made from guaiacol or lignin (a wood byproduct), since the demand far exceeds what natural vanilla orchid cultivation can supply.

Silicone (polysiloxane) polymers consist of a backbone of alternating silicon and oxygen atoms rather than carbon. Their thermal stability, water repellency, and biocompatibility make them ubiquitous in medical implants, waterproof sealants, non-stick cookware coatings, and personal care products such as shampoo conditioners.

Molecular machines — molecules capable of mechanical movement in response to external stimuli — were recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to Jean-Pierre Sauvage, Fraser Stoddart, and Ben Feringa. Examples include rotaxanes (molecular axles and wheels), catenanes (interlocked rings), and light-driven molecular motors that rotate at millions of RPM.

Graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, was isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov using Scotch tape. With a Young's modulus of ~1 TPa, it is the stiffest known material, yet also the most flexible; it conducts electricity better than copper and heat better than diamond.

The Maillard reaction, named after Louis-Camille Maillard who first described it in 1912, is a non-enzymatic browning reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars that produces hundreds of flavor and color compounds. It is responsible for the aromas and golden-brown colors of bread crust, roasted coffee, seared steak, and chocolate.

Isotope ratio mass spectrometry (IRMS) measures the ratios of stable isotopes (e.g., ¹³C/¹²C, ¹⁸O/¹⁶O) in samples with extreme precision. It is used in food authenticity testing to detect adulteration of olive oil or orange juice, in forensics to trace the geographic origin of drugs, and in climate science to analyze ancient ice cores.

Titanium dioxide (TiO₂) is the world's most widely used white pigment, found in about 90% of all white paints, and also used in sunscreen, food coloring (E171), and paper. In its anatase form it is also a photocatalyst: UV light excites electrons to generate reactive oxygen species that can degrade pollutants and kill bacteria on self-cleaning surfaces.

Solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers form spontaneously on lithium battery anodes when the electrolyte is reduced at low voltage. This nanometer-thick film passivates the anode and prevents further electrolyte decomposition, but its composition and stability are critical determinants of battery cycle life, safety, and charging speed.

Disperse dyes are non-ionic dyes used to color hydrophobic synthetic fibers like polyester. Because polyester lacks reactive groups, disperse dyes must physically penetrate the swollen polymer matrix at high temperature and pressure, lodging in amorphous regions by van der Waals forces — a purely physical rather than chemical bonding process.

Forensic toxicology uses liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) as the gold standard for detecting and quantifying drugs and poisons in biological samples. The technique can detect trace amounts at nanogram-per-milliliter levels in blood or urine, distinguishing hundreds of compounds in a single run.

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as superoxide radical (O₂•⁻), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and hydroxyl radical (•OH) are produced in cells as byproducts of mitochondrial respiration. While essential for cell signaling at low levels, excess ROS cause oxidative stress that damages DNA, proteins, and lipids, contributing to aging and diseases like cancer.

Cyclodextrins are cyclic oligosaccharides with a cone-shaped cavity that can host hydrophobic guest molecules in their interior, making hydrophobic substances water-soluble. They are used in pharmaceuticals to improve drug solubility and bioavailability, in food to mask bitter tastes, and in cosmetics to encapsulate fragrances for controlled release.

Indigo, one of the oldest known dyes, has been used to color textiles for at least 6,000 years. The synthetic route discovered by Adolf von Baeyer in 1870 — for which he received the 1905 Nobel Prize — eventually made synthetic indigo so cheap that it collapsed natural indigo farming worldwide. Modern denim blue jeans are dyed exclusively with synthetic indigo.

Aerosol chemistry in the atmosphere involves gas-phase molecules condensing onto particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) or reacting on droplet surfaces. Secondary organic aerosol (SOA) forms when volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from vegetation or combustion are oxidized by hydroxyl radicals and ozone, contributing to smog and climate forcing.

Solid-state NMR spectroscopy probes the chemical environment of nuclei in crystalline or amorphous solids, bypassing the requirement for solution-phase samples. It is indispensable for characterizing polymorphs of pharmaceutical compounds, zeolite frameworks, and battery electrode materials where structure dictates function.

Zeolites are microporous aluminosilicate minerals with highly regular pore structures of molecular dimensions (0.3–1.5 nm). Their shape-selective cavities allow them to act as molecular sieves, separating molecules by size, and as solid acid catalysts. Zeolite ZSM-5, used in fluid catalytic cracking, converts crude oil fractions into gasoline and is one of the most important industrial catalysts ever developed.

Emulsion polymerization is used to make latex paints, synthetic rubber, and adhesives. Monomer droplets suspended in water by surfactant micelles are polymerized by water-soluble radical initiators, producing polymer particles 50–500 nm in diameter; this technique allows high molecular weight polymers to be made at high rates without viscosity becoming unmanageable.

Linalool is a naturally occurring terpene alcohol found in lavender, rose, jasmine, and over 200 other plants. It is one of the most widely used fragrance compounds in the world, added to approximately 60–80% of all perfumed household products; it also exhibits significant calming, anxiolytic effects, explaining the therapeutic reputation of lavender aromatherapy.

The Geiger-Müller tube is a gas-filled radiation detector in which ionizing radiation (alpha, beta, or gamma) produces ion pairs in the fill gas, triggering an avalanche discharge that generates a measurable electrical pulse. Invented in 1908 and refined through 1928, it remains the most common portable radiation detector in radiochemistry and nuclear safety.

Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are crystalline porous materials consisting of metal ion nodes connected by organic ligand linkers. MOF-210, a record-holder, has an internal surface area of 6,240 m²/g — greater than a football field in a single gram — making MOFs promising for hydrogen storage, carbon capture, and drug delivery.

The Staudinger reaction (1919) was the first unambiguous demonstration that polymers are large covalent molecules and not colloidal aggregates of small molecules, as previously believed. Hermann Staudinger coined the term 'macromolecule' and received the 1953 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for founding polymer science.

Fluorescent whitening agents (FWAs) are compounds added to laundry detergents and paper that absorb invisible UV light and re-emit it as visible blue-white light, making fabrics appear brighter and whiter than would be possible from reflection alone. They are also known as optical brighteners.

Actinium-225, a radioactive alpha-emitter with a 10-day half-life, is at the forefront of targeted alpha therapy for cancer. When attached to a cancer-targeting antibody, it delivers a series of short-range, highly ionizing alpha particles directly into tumor cells while sparing surrounding healthy tissue — a concept called radioimmunotherapy.

The Ziegler-Natta catalyst, discovered in the 1950s by Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta (1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), is a titanium chloride / organoaluminium catalyst that enables stereoregular polymerization of propylene into isotactic polypropylene. This discovery made mass-produced commodity plastics possible.

Photodynamic therapy (PDT) uses a photosensitizer drug that, upon activation by specific wavelengths of light, generates singlet oxygen — a highly reactive form that kills cancer cells. Porphyrin-derived photosensitizers like porfimer sodium are approved for treating esophageal and lung cancers, and research continues on next-generation photosensitizers.

Alizarin, derived from the madder plant root, was one of the most commercially important red dyes in history, used to color textiles including British Army 'redcoats.' The first synthetic dye to be made from coal tar (1868), its production by Baeyer and Caro caused the collapse of the natural madder trade almost overnight.

Plasma polymerization deposits thin polymer films on surfaces by exposing a monomer vapor to a plasma discharge, causing non-equilibrium radical reactions that deposit a highly crosslinked, pinhole-free film. It is used to create anti-fouling coatings on medical devices, oleophobic coatings on electronics, and barrier layers on food packaging.

Isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene) is the biogenic building block of natural rubber (polyisoprene) and all terpenes. Emitted by trees in large quantities — globally about 600 million tons per year — isoprene is the single most abundant non-methane volatile organic compound in Earth's atmosphere and significantly influences tropospheric ozone chemistry.

Mucoadhesive polymers such as carbopol and chitosan adhere to mucosal surfaces by interpenetrating with mucin glycoproteins via hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions. They are used in drug delivery systems for nasal, buccal, and ocular routes to extend drug contact time and improve bioavailability of poorly absorbed molecules.

Flow chemistry (continuous flow synthesis) pumps reactants through narrow reaction tubes or microreactors rather than batch flasks, enabling rapid mixing, precise temperature control, and safe handling of hazardous intermediates. It has become indispensable in pharmaceutical manufacturing for producing unstable reactive intermediates like organolithium species at scale.

The Fries rearrangement is an acid-catalyzed migration of an acyl group from an aryl ester to the ortho or para position of the phenol ring. Photo-Fries rearrangement is the photochemical version, occurring under UV irradiation without acid catalyst, and is exploited in photoresist chemistry and the preparation of UV-absorbing compounds for sunscreens.

Perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), sometimes called 'forever chemicals,' are synthetic compounds where hydrogen atoms on carbon chains are entirely replaced by fluorine. The C–F bond is among the strongest in organic chemistry, making PFAS resistant to metabolic and environmental degradation; they are detected in the blood of virtually all humans and animals worldwide.

Hydrogen storage in solid materials is a major challenge for hydrogen fuel cell vehicles. Metal hydrides (e.g., LaNi₅H₆), high-surface-area MOFs, and porous carbon materials can adsorb or absorb hydrogen, but achieving the US DOE targets of ≥6.5 wt% hydrogen at near-ambient conditions simultaneously remains an unsolved materials chemistry challenge.

Reactive nitrogen species (RNS) such as nitric oxide (NO) and peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) play dual roles in biology: at low concentrations NO is a key vasodilator and signaling molecule (its discovery earned the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology), while at high concentrations RNS contribute to inflammation, nitrosative stress, and neurodegeneration.

Capillary electrophoresis (CE) separates charged molecules through a narrow capillary filled with a buffer solution under a high electric field; molecules migrate at speeds determined by their charge-to-size ratio. It is used in forensics for DNA profiling, in pharmaceuticals for chiral separation, and in clinical chemistry for hemoglobin variant analysis.

Amorphous solid dispersions (ASDs) are pharmaceutical formulations in which a poorly water-soluble drug is dispersed at the molecular level within a hydrophilic polymer matrix. By converting the drug from its crystalline to its amorphous (higher energy) form, ASDs can improve aqueous solubility 10–1000-fold, enabling drugs that were previously un-developable to reach patients.

Squalene is a triterpene hydrocarbon (C₃₀H₅₀) found in shark liver oil and human sebum that serves as a key biosynthetic precursor to cholesterol and all steroid hormones. In astrochemistry, squalene-like isoprenoid structures have been proposed as products of Fischer-Tropsch-type reactions in carbonaceous meteorites.

Reductive amination is a versatile one-pot reaction that converts carbonyl compounds (aldehydes or ketones) and amines into secondary or tertiary amines via an imine (Schiff base) intermediate that is then reduced. It is one of the most frequently used transformations in medicinal chemistry for constructing the amine-containing frameworks found in most drug molecules.

The interstellar molecule H₃⁺ (trihydrogen cation) is the most abundant polyatomic ion in the universe and plays a central role in interstellar chemistry by protonating other molecules and initiating reaction cascades. It forms when cosmic rays ionize H₂ and the resulting H₂⁺ reacts rapidly with another H₂ molecule.

Reactive dyes form covalent bonds between the dye molecule and cellulose fiber (cotton) through nucleophilic substitution or addition, giving wash-fast, bright colors. They typically contain a triazine or vinyl sulfone reactive group; the reaction requires alkaline conditions to deprotonate cellulose hydroxyl groups, which then attack the electrophilic dye.
