Salting-out is the phenomenon by which adding a salt to a protein solution promotes protein precipitation, because the salt ions compete with the protein for water molecules, reducing its hydration shell and causing aggregation. Ammonium sulfate is classically used in biochemistry to fractionate proteins by their differential precipitation.

The Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) technique measures distances between fluorescent labels at the nanometer scale; energy is transferred non-radiatively from a donor fluorophore to an acceptor when the two are within about 1–10 nm, with efficiency varying as 1/r⁶. FRET is used in biochemistry to track protein folding, receptor binding, and intracellular signaling in real time.

Conductive polymers such as polyacetylene, polyaniline, and polythiophene are organic polymers that can conduct electricity through delocalized π-electrons along the conjugated backbone. Alan Heeger, Alan MacDiarmid, and Hideki Shirakawa shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery that doped polyacetylene could be as conductive as metals.

Alkyd resins, the most widely used coating resins in the world, are polyesters modified with fatty acid chains derived from drying oils like linseed oil. They crosslink by autoxidation — oxygen from the air initiates free-radical polymerization of unsaturated fatty acid chains — forming the hard, tough film of household oil-based paints.

Positron emission tomography (PET) uses short-lived positron-emitting radioisotopes (commonly ¹⁸F with a 110-minute half-life) attached to biologically active molecules. When the positron annihilates with an electron it emits two 511 keV gamma rays at 180° to each other, which detectors convert into a three-dimensional functional image of metabolic activity.

The Hall-Héroult process (1886) enabled affordable aluminum production for the first time by dissolving aluminum oxide in molten cryolite and applying a strong electrical current to electrolyze molten aluminum from the oxide. Before this, aluminum was more expensive than gold; today, aluminum smelters consume about 3.5% of global electricity.

In photocatalysis, titanium dioxide and other semiconductor photocatalysts can split water into hydrogen and oxygen using only sunlight in a process called artificial photosynthesis. Despite decades of research, achieving the required quantum efficiency (>10%) for economically viable solar hydrogen production from water-splitting remains an unsolved challenge.

Pyrotechnics exploit carefully formulated exothermic redox reactions to produce heat, light, gas, and sound. Metal salts produce vivid fireworks colors: strontium gives red, barium gives green, copper gives blue, sodium gives yellow, and magnesium and aluminum give brilliant white — each color arising from the specific electronic transitions of atoms excited by the flame.

The sodium-sulfur (NaS) battery operates at ~300°C and uses liquid sodium as the anode and liquid sulfur as the cathode separated by a solid beta-alumina electrolyte. It achieves very high energy density (~760 Wh/kg for active material) and is deployed in large-scale grid energy storage, particularly in Japan, for load leveling from wind and solar power.

Dynamic covalent chemistry uses covalent bonds that can reversibly form and break under equilibrium conditions, allowing molecular systems to self-correct toward their thermodynamic minimum. Imine bonds (formed by amines and aldehydes), disulfide bonds, and Diels-Alder adducts are common examples used to make self-healing materials and dynamic covalent frameworks.

Cosmic dust particles, collected from the stratosphere or from Antarctic ice cores, contain presolar grains — tiny minerals (SiC, graphite, diamond) that predate the formation of our solar system. Isotopic analysis reveals they were forged in red giant stars and supernovae, providing direct samples of stellar nucleosynthesis products.

Terpene-based flame retardants are emerging as sustainable alternatives to halogenated flame retardants, which persist in the environment and have endocrine-disrupting effects. Monoterpene-derived phosphate esters and furans can provide effective fire resistance in polymers with a lower toxicological and environmental burden.

The Fenton reaction generates highly reactive hydroxyl radicals from hydrogen peroxide and ferrous iron: Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂ → Fe³⁺ + •OH + OH⁻. Discovered by Henry John Horstman Fenton in 1894, it is used in wastewater treatment to degrade persistent organic pollutants and in forensic blood stain detection alongside luminol.

Sunscreen UV filters work through two mechanisms: organic UV absorbers (such as avobenzone and octinoxate) absorb UV photons and dissipate the energy as heat via photoisomerization; inorganic mineral filters (zinc oxide and titanium dioxide) scatter and absorb UV radiation. Broad-spectrum formulations combine both UVA and UVB protection agents.

Chirality in drug molecules is critically important because enantiomers can have vastly different biological effects. Thalidomide is the most notorious example: the R-enantiomer had therapeutic sedative effects while the S-enantiomer caused severe birth defects; tragically, even pure R-thalidomide racemizes in the body. This disaster accelerated FDA requirements for chiral drug development.

Emulsion stability in cosmetics and food products is maintained by emulsifiers — amphiphilic molecules with hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions — that adsorb at the oil-water interface and lower interfacial tension. Lecithin (from egg yolk) stabilizes mayonnaise, while synthetic emulsifiers like Tween 80 and Span 60 are engineered for precise HLB (hydrophilic-lipophilic balance) values.

Thermochromic pigments change color reversibly with temperature and are based on either liquid crystals (which reflect different wavelengths at different temperatures) or leuco dyes (which switch between colorless and colored forms). They are used in mood rings, temperature-sensitive food packaging, and color-changing 'Hypercolor' fabrics.

The Bergman cyclization is a thermally or photochemically induced reaction of enediyne natural products (like calicheamicin) to form a 1,4-benzenediyl biradical. This highly reactive diradical abstracts hydrogen atoms from the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA, causing double-strand breaks that kill cancer cells; several enediyne antibiotics are used as anticancer warheads in antibody-drug conjugates.

Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are among the most abundant organic molecules in the universe, detected in interstellar space, carbonaceous meteorites, and the rings of Saturn. Astrochemists propose that PAH photodissociation and reactions with interstellar UV photons may have generated small organic molecules relevant to prebiotic chemistry on early Earth.

Wacker oxidation converts terminal alkenes to methyl ketones using palladium(II) chloride as catalyst and oxygen as the terminal oxidant. Developed industrially in 1959, it is the basis for producing acetaldehyde from ethylene and was one of the first examples of homogeneous organometallic catalysis applied at industrial scale.

Polyurethanes are formed by the reaction of a polyol with a diisocyanate. Depending on the formulation, they can be rigid foams (insulation), flexible foams (mattresses and car seats), elastomers (shoe soles), or coatings (wood finishes). The global polyurethane market exceeds 20 million metric tons per year, making it one of the most versatile polymer systems.

Mucin glycoproteins form the viscoelastic gel lining the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts; their extraordinary lubrication and barrier properties arise from heavily glycosylated domains, where oligosaccharide chains attached to serine and threonine residues constitute up to 80% of the molecule's mass by weight.

The VSEPR (valence shell electron pair repulsion) model predicts molecular geometry by assuming that electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize repulsion. It correctly predicts that water is bent (104.5°), ammonia is pyramidal (107°), and carbon dioxide is linear — all from the number and type of electron pairs without quantum mechanics.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) applies a small AC voltage across a range of frequencies to an electrochemical cell and measures the complex impedance response. It can nondestructively diagnose battery state-of-health, characterize corrosion reactions, and study the kinetics of film formation on electrode surfaces.

Phthalocyanines are synthetic macrocyclic compounds structurally related to natural porphyrins (found in heme and chlorophyll). Their intense blue-green colors arise from strong Q-band absorption near 700 nm. Copper phthalocyanine (pigment blue 15) is the most widely used blue pigment in the world, found in inks, paints, and coatings.

The Birch reduction uses lithium or sodium metal dissolved in liquid ammonia with an alcohol proton source to partially reduce aromatic rings to cyclohexadienyl systems. This unusual reaction, which protonates through radical anion intermediates, is one of the few methods to reduce the thermodynamically very stable aromatic ring and is extensively used in steroid and terpene synthesis.

Limonene is the most commercially important monoterpene, responsible for the citrus scent of lemons and oranges. (R)-(+)-limonene smells of oranges while (S)-(−)-limonene smells more like turpentine — a striking example of how chirality affects odor perception. It is used in cleaners, cosmetics, and as a bio-based solvent to replace petroleum-derived solvents.

Anodizing is an electrochemical process that thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminum by making the metal the anode in an electrolytic cell. The anodized oxide layer is hard, corrosion resistant, and porous; dyes can be adsorbed into the pores before sealing, producing the colored anodized aluminum found on consumer electronics and aircraft.

X-ray crystallography, for which William Bragg and his son Lawrence received the first Nobel Prize related to crystals (1915), determines the three-dimensional structure of crystalline materials by measuring how X-rays are diffracted by planes of atoms. It has solved the structures of table salt (1913), penicillin (1945), the double helix of DNA (1953), and the ribosome (2009 Nobel Prize).

Furan, thiophene, and pyrrole are five-membered aromatic heterocyclic compounds containing oxygen, sulfur, and nitrogen respectively. Their aromaticity, derived from donation of a lone pair into the π-system to satisfy Hückel's 4n+2 rule, makes them exceptionally stable and important building blocks in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and organic semiconductors.

The Meisenheimer complex (Jackson-Meisenheimer complex) is an anionic sigma complex that forms as an intermediate in nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) when a nucleophile attacks an electron-poor aromatic ring. Unlike aliphatic SN2 reactions, SNAr proceeds through this stable, isolable intermediate rather than a concerted transition state.

Laccase enzymes are copper-containing oxidoreductases found in fungi, plants, and some bacteria that oxidize phenolic compounds using O₂ as the electron acceptor, producing only water as a byproduct. They have attracted industrial interest for textile dye decolorization, paper delignification, and bioremediation of persistent aromatic pollutants.

All-solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte of conventional lithium-ion cells with a solid ionic conductor (e.g., Li₆PS₅Cl sulfide electrolyte or Li₇La₃Zr₂O₁₂ garnet oxide). They promise higher energy density, improved safety (no flammable liquid), and compatibility with lithium metal anodes, but manufacturing challenges related to interface resistance have so far prevented mass-market deployment.

Chemical looping combustion (CLC) captures CO₂ from fossil fuel burning with near-zero energy penalty by using metal oxide particles (e.g., iron oxide) to transfer oxygen from air to fuel in separate reactor loops; the fuel is burned in the absence of nitrogen, producing a pure CO₂/H₂O stream that can be easily sequestered without energy-intensive separation.

Inkjet-printed perovskite LEDs (PeLEDs) exploit the solution processability of metal halide perovskites to deposit emissive layers at room temperature without vacuum deposition. Their near-100% quantum yield and tunable emission wavelength across the visible spectrum by halide substitution (Cl for blue, Br for green, I for red) make them promising for next-generation displays.

Capsaicin, the pungent compound in chilli peppers, activates the TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1) ion channel which normally responds to heat above 43°C. This explains why spicy food produces a burning sensation — the brain receives signals identical to those produced by genuinely hot temperatures, and the pain causes endorphin release responsible for the 'chilli high.'

Isotope tracing uses stable or radioactive isotopes (e.g., ¹³C, ²H, ¹⁵N) substituted into specific positions of molecules to track their fate in chemical or biological reactions. In metabolomics, ¹³C-labeled glucose tracers allow researchers to map carbon flux through metabolic pathways in living cells or whole organisms.

The Sabatier reaction converts carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane and water over a nickel catalyst at 300–400°C. Named after Paul Sabatier (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1912), it is the basis of power-to-methane systems that store excess renewable electricity as synthetic natural gas and is also used to remove CO₂ aboard the International Space Station.

Electrowetting on dielectric (EWOD) technology controls the shape and movement of aqueous droplets on a surface by applying an electric field that modifies the contact angle between the droplet and the insulator-coated electrode. It is the key mechanism behind electrowetting-based digital microfluidic lab-on-chip devices and some electronic paper (e-paper) displays.

Click chemistry, recognized with the 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Sharpless, Meldal, and Bertozzi), encompasses highly efficient, modular reactions that join molecular building blocks reliably and without toxic byproducts. The copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition and strain-promoted bioorthogonal reactions allow labeling of biomolecules in living organisms without disrupting biological processes.

Platinum-based chemotherapy drugs — cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin — work by forming covalent crosslinks between guanine bases on adjacent DNA strands or on the same strand, distorting the double helix and triggering apoptosis in rapidly dividing cancer cells. Discovered accidentally by Barnett Rosenberg in 1965 through electrical experiments on bacteria, cisplatin is now on the WHO Essential Medicines List.

Carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy (¹³C NMR) exploits the 1.1% natural abundance of the ¹³C isotope to reveal the number and chemical environment of carbon atoms in organic molecules. Chemical shifts range from 0 ppm (TMS) to over 220 ppm for carbonyl carbons, providing complementary structural information to ¹H NMR for unambiguous molecular structure elucidation.

Amphiphilic block copolymers — chains of two chemically distinct polymer blocks — self-assemble in solution into a rich variety of nanostructures including spherical micelles, vesicles (polymersomes), and wormlike micelles, driven by the hydrophobic effect. Polymersomes have 5–50 nm thick membranes far tougher than lipid bilayers and are studied as drug-delivery vehicles for cancer therapy.

Electrochemical reduction of CO₂ to useful products (CO, formate, ethylene, ethanol) using renewable electricity offers a route to carbon-neutral fuels and chemicals. Copper is uniquely active for producing multi-carbon products by catalyzing C–C bond coupling steps; controlling selectivity among the many possible products remains a central challenge in this field.

Molecular imprinting creates synthetic polymer receptors with shape-complementary cavities for a specific template molecule. When the template is removed from the crosslinked polymer matrix, the remaining cavity selectively rebinds the target, mimicking antibody-antigen specificity. Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) are used as artificial antibodies in biosensors and drug delivery.

The discovery of phosphine (PH₃) in the atmosphere of Venus announced in 2020 generated extraordinary scientific debate because no known abiotic process can produce it at the observed concentrations under Venusian conditions. While the initial detection has been contested, the controversy reignited interest in Venus as a potential target for astrobiology and drove new astrochemical models of gas-phase and cloud chemistry.

Surfactants (surface-active agents) reduce surface tension by adsorbing at liquid-air or liquid-liquid interfaces with their hydrophilic head in the water phase and hydrophobic tail pointing away. Soap, SDS (sodium dodecyl sulfate), and Tween-20 are classic examples; above the critical micelle concentration (CMC), they aggregate into micelles that encapsulate grease and enable its removal.

The Stille coupling is a palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling of organotin reagents with aryl or vinyl halides to form C–C bonds. Though the organotin (stannane) reagents are toxic, Stille coupling tolerates a wide range of functional groups and is extensively used in pharmaceutical synthesis and natural product total synthesis.

Computational protein design uses algorithms to calculate amino acid sequences that should fold into a target three-dimensional structure. David Baker's Rosetta software suite has designed enzymes for reactions not found in nature, de novo proteins with novel folds, and self-assembling protein cages — advances recognized by the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Nitinol (nickel-titanium alloy) is a shape-memory alloy that can be deformed at low temperature and returns to a predetermined shape upon heating, due to a reversible solid-state phase transition between martensite and austenite crystal structures. It is used in orthodontic wires, cardiovascular stents, and actuators in aerospace engineering.

The von Weimarn ratio explains why precipitation conditions determine crystal size: rapid addition of excess precipitant produces small particles (colloidal precipitate) because many nuclei form simultaneously, while slow precipitation from dilute solutions yields large crystals because few nuclei form and grow slowly. This principle guides synthesis of materials with controlled particle sizes.

Acyl carrier protein (ACP) is a small protein that tethers fatty acid chain intermediates as thioester adducts during fatty acid biosynthesis. The phosphopantetheine arm attached to ACP acts as a flexible 'swinging arm' delivering intermediates sequentially to each enzyme in the fatty acid synthase complex — a remarkable example of substrate channeling.

Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) records an infrared spectrum of a sample by measuring the absorption of IR radiation at all frequencies simultaneously using an interferometer, then computing the spectrum using a Fourier transform. It is the standard method for identifying functional groups in organic compounds and for quality control of raw materials in pharmaceutical and polymer manufacturing.

Oleum calaminthae — the essential oil of calamint — contains high levels of pulegone (up to 90%), a monoterpene ketone found also in pennyroyal. Pulegone is a potent hepatotoxin and has caused fatal poisonings when used in high doses as an abortifacient; it is metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes to menthofuran, the actual toxic species.

The contact angle of a liquid droplet on a solid surface quantifies wettability: hydrophilic surfaces have contact angles below 90° (water spreads), hydrophobic surfaces above 90°, and superhydrophobic surfaces (like the lotus leaf) above 150°. Lotus-effect surfaces combine micro/nanoscale surface roughness with waxy chemistry so that water beads up and rolls off, carrying dirt with it.

Hydrogen bonds (X–H···Y, where X and Y are electronegative atoms) are the most important non-covalent interaction in biology and chemistry. With energies of 5–30 kJ/mol (stronger than van der Waals forces but weaker than covalent bonds), they determine the secondary structure of proteins (alpha helices, beta sheets), the base pairing of DNA, and the anomalous properties of water.

Inorganic photochemistry explores light-induced reactions of metal complexes. Ruthenium(II) tris(bipyridyl) — [Ru(bpy)₃]²⁺ — is the most studied photosensitizer: it absorbs visible light, reaches a long-lived excited state (>1 μs), and can both oxidize and reduce substrates, making it a model system for artificial photosynthesis and photocatalytic hydrogen evolution.

Spandex (Lycra, elastane) is a segmented polyurethane-urea copolymer consisting of alternating hard (urethane/urea) and soft (polyether) segments. The soft segments can stretch up to 600% and recover elastically, while the hard segments act as physical crosslinks. Developed by DuPont in 1958, it revolutionized sportswear and underwear manufacturing.

Vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) store energy in two tanks of vanadium sulfate solutions at different oxidation states; energy is released when the solutions flow past a membrane-separated electrochemical cell. Because the active species cannot permanently cross-contaminate (both tanks use vanadium), VRFBs have extraordinarily long cycle lives (>20,000 cycles) ideal for grid storage.

Nitro compounds (R-NO₂) are synthesized by electrophilic aromatic nitration using a nitrating mixture of concentrated sulfuric and nitric acids. The actual electrophile is the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺), formed by protonation of HNO₃; the reaction is industrially important for producing aniline, TNT, and dye intermediates.

Solvothermal synthesis carries out crystallization reactions in sealed autoclaves at temperatures above the solvent's normal boiling point, achieving high pressures that enhance solubility and kinetics of crystal nucleation. Most zeolites, many MOFs, and battery cathode materials like lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO₄) are synthesized solvothermally.

Bisphenol A (BPA) is a monomer used to make polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins. It has attracted widespread regulatory attention as an endocrine disruptor because it mimics estrogen by binding to estrogen receptors; it leaches from food containers and cans into food and drink, particularly when heated. The EU and many countries have banned BPA in baby bottles and food-contact materials.

Ion exchange chromatography separates molecules based on their affinity for a charged stationary phase; cation exchangers retain positively charged species and anion exchangers retain negatively charged ones, with elution achieved by increasing ionic strength or changing pH. It is the primary industrial method for water softening (replacing Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ with Na⁺) and for protein purification at manufacturing scale.

Covalent bonds in Si–O–Si networks are the backbone of silica glass, quartz, and most silicate minerals. Silica glass lacks long-range order because each SiO₄ tetrahedron connects to neighbors at random angles, creating an amorphous network; the addition of network modifiers like Na₂O breaks Si–O–Si bonds, lowers viscosity, and enables glass shaping at lower temperatures.

Quantum dots are semiconductor nanocrystals (2–10 nm) whose electronic properties depend strongly on their size due to quantum confinement of electrons. As the dot shrinks, the bandgap increases and emission blue-shifts; by tuning dot size, emission can be set to any wavelength across the visible and near-infrared spectrum. They are used in QLED TV displays and medical fluorescence imaging.

Transamination is a major metabolic reaction in which an amino group is transferred from an amino acid to an alpha-keto acid, catalyzed by aminotransferases (transaminases) that use pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. These reactions interconnect amino acid catabolism and synthesis with the central carbon metabolism through alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate.

Dry cleaning does not use water but rather organic solvents; historically tetrachloroethylene (perchloroethylene, PERC) dominated the industry. PERC effectively dissolves grease and oils without shrinking or distorting wool and silk, but it is a suspected carcinogen; greener alternatives including liquid CO₂ and hydrocarbon solvents are increasingly adopted.

Photoresist chemistry is central to semiconductor lithography. In positive photoresists, UV exposure converts a photoactive compound (e.g., diazonaphthoquinone) into a carboxylic acid that becomes soluble in developer, while negative photoresists crosslink upon UV exposure and remain after development. Modern extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography at 13.5 nm wavelength uses novel chemically amplified resists to pattern features below 5 nm.

Retrosynthetic analysis, formalized by E.J. Corey (1990 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), is the strategy of breaking a target molecule into simpler precursors by identifying key disconnection points (retrons). Working backwards through a disconnection tree guides chemists toward practical synthetic routes, a methodology now implemented in AI-driven synthesis planning tools.

The osmotic pressure of a colloidal solution is described by the van't Hoff equation: π = iMRT, where i is the van't Hoff factor, M is molar concentration, R is the gas constant, and T is temperature. In blood plasma, the colloidal osmotic pressure (oncotic pressure) exerted by albumin and other proteins (~3.5 kPa) is critical for retaining fluid within blood vessels.

Aerogels are ultralow-density solid materials made by replacing the liquid in a gel with gas through supercritical drying, preserving the porous network. Silica aerogels can be 99.98% air with densities as low as 1 kg/m³ (barely denser than air), extraordinarily low thermal conductivity (0.015 W/m·K), and surface areas exceeding 1000 m²/g. They are used in NASA spacecraft insulation and are now finding applications in windows and apparel.

Perylene diimide (PDI) dyes produce vibrant red colors and are among the most photostable organic pigments known, resistant to UV, solvents, and heat. Their near-unity fluorescence quantum yield and strong electron-accepting ability make them popular in organic photovoltaics, non-fullerene acceptors, and luminescent solar concentrators.

The Buchwald-Hartwig amination is a palladium-catalyzed reaction for forming C–N bonds between aryl halides and primary or secondary amines. It has become one of the most widely used bond-forming reactions in medicinal chemistry, given that nitrogen-containing aromatic heterocycles appear in over half of all approved pharmaceutical drugs.

Atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) is a mass spectrometry interface that ionizes analytes at atmospheric pressure by corona discharge in a heated spray of solvent vapor. It extends the range of LC-MS to relatively non-polar compounds like steroids, lipids, and many pesticides that ionize poorly by the more common electrospray ionization (ESI) technique.

Phospholipid bilayers spontaneously assemble in water because the hydrophobic fatty acid tails cluster away from water while the hydrophilic phosphate heads face the aqueous environment. This self-assembly into vesicles and membranes is driven entirely by the hydrophobic effect — an entropic phenomenon arising from water's restructuring around hydrophobic surfaces.

Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), recognized by the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, images biological macromolecules in their near-native state by rapidly freezing aqueous samples in vitreous ice. Advances in direct electron detectors and computational image processing now allow cryo-EM to routinely resolve protein structures to near-atomic (2–3 Å) resolution.

Reactive sputtering deposits compound thin films by sputtering a metal target in a reactive gas atmosphere (e.g., argon/nitrogen for TiN, argon/oxygen for TiO₂). The energetic metal atoms and ions react with the gas to form the compound film on the substrate. Hard nitride coatings on cutting tools and the iridescent gold color of TiN-coated watch casings are produced this way.

Prussian blue (iron(III) hexacyanoferrate(II)) is one of the first synthetic pigments, made accidentally in Berlin around 1704. Its intense blue color arises from intervalence charge transfer between adjacent Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions. It has medical uses as an antidote for thallium and radioactive cesium poisoning, as it traps these metal cations in its lattice structure.

Tribochemistry studies chemical reactions induced by mechanical forces (friction and wear) at material interfaces. When two surfaces slide against each other, localized flash temperatures, pressure spikes, and mechanically generated radicals trigger reactions that can lubricate, form protective tribofilms, or accelerate wear. Engine lubricant additives like ZDDP work by tribochemically forming a protective zinc phosphate glass film on metal surfaces.

The polarity of a solvent is often expressed as its dielectric constant (relative permittivity); water has ε ≈ 80, ethanol ε ≈ 25, and hexane ε ≈ 2. The rule 'like dissolves like' reflects solubility being driven by solvent–solute interactions; choosing the right solvent polarity is essential in organic synthesis, extraction, and pharmaceutical formulation.

Solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), developed by Robert Bruce Merrifield (1984 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), attaches the first amino acid to an insoluble resin bead and adds subsequent residues one at a time using protected amino acids and coupling reagents. The chain is cleaved from the resin and deprotected to yield the finished peptide. SPPS enables automated production of custom peptide drugs such as insulin analogs and GLP-1 receptor agonists.

Polyfuran and polythiophene are intrinsically conducting polymers whose conductivity can be tuned by doping with oxidizing agents (p-doping) or reducing agents (n-doping). PEDOT:PSS (poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene sulfonate)) is the most commercially successful conducting polymer, used in antistatic coatings, solar cell electrodes, and bioelectronic devices.

Asymmetric organocatalysis uses small chiral organic molecules — rather than metals — to catalyze enantioselective reactions. Benjamin List and David MacMillan received the 2021 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing this field, showing that proline and imidazolidinone catalysts can mediate aldol reactions and Diels-Alder cyclizations with very high enantiomeric excesses.

Excitons are electrically neutral quasiparticles formed in semiconductors when an electron absorbs a photon and leaves behind a positively charged hole; the electron and hole remain bound by Coulombic attraction. Exciton diffusion length is a critical parameter for organic solar cell performance, since the exciton must reach a donor-acceptor interface to generate current before it recombines.

Fischer-Tropsch synthesis converts syngas (CO + H₂) over iron or cobalt catalysts into liquid hydrocarbons ranging from methane to waxes through a chain-growth polymerization mechanism. Developed in Germany in the 1920s and used extensively in WWII and apartheid-era South Africa to produce liquid fuel from coal, it is currently deployed in gas-to-liquids plants converting natural gas or biomass into clean diesel.

Photocatalytic water splitting using semiconductors aims to mimic photosynthesis by using solar energy to drive the thermodynamically uphill splitting of water into H₂ and O₂ (ΔG = +237 kJ/mol). Tanaka's GaN:ZnO photocatalyst and cocatalyst-loaded systems have achieved solar-to-hydrogen efficiencies approaching 2% in powder slurries, though practical targets for viable fuel production require efficiencies >10%.

In supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC), liquid CO₂ above its critical point (31°C, 74 bar) is used as the mobile phase. Its low viscosity and high diffusivity give faster separations than HPLC, and CO₂ is non-toxic and easily removed; SFC is the preferred method in pharmaceutical development for chiral separation of drug enantiomers at both analytical and preparative scales.

Amyloid fibrils are highly ordered protein aggregates in which peptide chains adopt a cross-beta sheet structure with hydrogen bonds running perpendicular to the fibril axis. While pathological amyloid deposits cause diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, some organisms exploit the remarkable mechanical strength of amyloid (comparable to silk) in biological structures like fungal biofilms and barnacle adhesive proteins.

The Ostwald ripening process causes large particles in a colloidal suspension to grow at the expense of smaller ones, driven by the greater solubility of small particles (Gibbs-Thomson effect). It is responsible for ice cream becoming grainy over time (ice crystal coarsening) and is intentionally exploited in nanoparticle synthesis to narrow particle size distributions by controlled aging.

Iron-sulfur clusters ([2Fe-2S], [4Fe-4S]) are ancient cofactors found in proteins across all domains of life, serving as electron carriers, sensors, and catalysts. In nitrogenase, the unique FeMo-cofactor (a [Mo:7Fe:9S:C:homocitrate] cluster) is the active site that reduces dinitrogen to ammonia — one of the most difficult reactions in all of chemistry.

Liquid crystal displays (LCDs) use the electro-optical properties of thermotropic liquid crystals — materials that flow like liquids but have long-range orientational order of the rod-like molecules. An applied electric field rotates the directors of nematic liquid crystals, changing the polarization of transmitted light to create on/off pixels. Fred Reinitzer and Otto Lehmann discovered liquid crystals in 1888.

Nitride ceramic cutting tools — silicon nitride (Si₃N₄), aluminum nitride (AlN), and cubic boron nitride (cBN) — are used for high-speed machining of hardened steel and cast iron because they retain their hardness above 1000°C where tungsten carbide tools soften. Their hardness stems from directional covalent Si–N or B–N bonds that resist dislocation motion.

Capillary condensation is the phenomenon where vapors condense in nanoporous materials at pressures well below the normal saturation vapor pressure, as described by the Kelvin equation: ln(p/p₀) = -2γVₘ/(rRT). It is exploited to measure pore size distributions in mesoporous materials (MOFs, silica, zeolites) by nitrogen adsorption at liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K).

Trifluoromethyl groups (–CF₃) are among the most common substituents in modern drugs, appearing in about 20% of all FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. The high electronegativity of fluorine dramatically increases metabolic stability (C–F bonds resist cytochrome P450 oxidation), enhances membrane permeability, and often improves binding to protein targets by occupying hydrophobic pockets.

Ultrafast laser spectroscopy using femtosecond pulses can capture the motion of atoms during a chemical reaction in real time. Ahmed Zewail (1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry) used femtosecond pump-probe spectroscopy to observe transition states of reactions as they occur, founding the field of femtochemistry and demonstrating that chemical bonds break on time scales of 100–200 femtoseconds.

Polyethylene terephthalate (PET), the plastic used in most water and soft drink bottles, is made by condensation polymerization of terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol. It is the most recycled plastic globally, capable of being processed into new bottles or polyester fiber for fleece garments; yet only about 30% of PET bottles are currently recycled worldwide.

Geochemical carbon isotope fractionation: photosynthetic organisms preferentially fix the lighter ¹²C over ¹³C, so organic carbon in sediments is depleted in ¹³C (δ¹³C ≈ −25‰). The Great Oxygenation Event ~2.4 Ga ago is recorded as a sharp negative ¹³C excursion in ancient carbonate rocks, providing isotopic evidence of massive burial of photosynthetically produced organic matter.

Electrochemical biosensors detect biological analytes through signal transduction at an electrode modified with a biorecognition element (enzyme, antibody, or nucleic acid). The glucose sensor used by diabetics — a thin strip coated with glucose oxidase enzyme — is the world's most widely used biosensor, performing over one billion measurements per day globally.

The Reformatsky reaction uses a zinc enolate generated from an alpha-halo ester to add to an aldehyde or ketone, forming a beta-hydroxy ester. Named after Sergei Reformatsky (1887), it is milder than analogous organolithium or Grignard reactions because zinc is less reactive, making it compatible with sensitive functional groups in complex synthesis.

Hydrogels are three-dimensional crosslinked polymer networks swollen with water that can contain up to 99.9% water by weight while maintaining solid-like mechanical properties. They are used in contact lenses, wound dressings, drug-delivery depots, and tissue engineering scaffolds; stimuli-responsive hydrogels that swell or collapse in response to temperature, pH, or light are used as soft actuators and sensors.

Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (RBS) fires a beam of MeV helium ions at a thin film sample; the energy of ions backscattered by atomic nuclei reveals the mass and depth profile of elements in the film without destruction. It is the gold standard for characterizing thin film composition in semiconductor manufacturing and for determining the stoichiometry of complex oxide films.

Bioluminescent chemistries have evolved independently at least 94 times across the tree of life, with each lineage evolving its own luciferin substrate and luciferase enzyme. The sea pansy Renilla and the firefly Photinus use very different luciferins but both require ATP and oxygen; deep-sea fish and some dinoflagellates use coelenterazine-based systems instead.

Free radical polymerization is initiated by radical species (from peroxides or azo compounds upon heating or UV exposure) that add to alkene monomers and grow long chains rapidly. Though less stereoregular than Ziegler-Natta or living polymerizations, it is the industrial method for making polystyrene, PVC, PMMA (Plexiglas), and many emulsion latexes at scales of millions of tons per year.

Gas hydrates (clathrate hydrates) are ice-like crystalline inclusion compounds in which small gas molecules (methane, CO₂, H₂S) are trapped inside hydrogen-bonded water cages at low temperatures and high pressures. Enormous methane hydrate deposits on continental shelves and in permafrost represent a vast carbon reservoir; their destabilization as oceans warm could release potent greenhouse gas.

Scent diffusion in perfumes is governed by volatility (vapor pressure) of fragrance molecules, which correlates with molecular weight. The classic perfume structure divides notes into three tiers: top notes (small, volatile molecules like citrus terpenes that evaporate within 15 minutes), heart notes (mid-sized molecules like linalool lasting 1–4 hours), and base notes (large, fixative molecules like musks lasting many hours).

Dendritic macromolecules (dendrimers) are perfectly branched, tree-like synthetic polymers with precisely defined molecular weight, size, and surface functionality. Poly(amidoamine) dendrimers (PAMAM) are studied as gene delivery vehicles and drug carriers; their multivalent surface can display many targeting ligands simultaneously, amplifying binding affinity through the 'dendritic effect.'

Mechanochemistry uses mechanical energy — grinding, milling, or compression — to drive chemical reactions without solvents. Ball-milling can achieve reactions that require harsh conditions in solution, including C–C bond formation and the synthesis of pharmaceutical co-crystals; it is a greener alternative to solution-phase synthesis by eliminating toxic solvents and enabling room-temperature reactions.

The Meerwein-Ponndorf-Verley (MPV) reduction is a metal alkoxide-catalyzed transfer hydrogenation in which a carbonyl compound is reduced by a sacrificial alcohol. It is highly chemoselective for carbonyls over alkenes, does not require molecular hydrogen, and can be performed with cheap aluminum alkoxide catalysts — making it attractive for reducing sensitive pharmaceutical intermediates.

Calcium-looping carbon capture cycles CaCO₃/CaO between a calciner (950°C, releases CO₂) and a carbonator (650°C, absorbs CO₂ from flue gas): CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃. The sorbent regenerates automatically, and the concentrated CO₂ stream can be sequestered; several pilot plants have demonstrated the technology for post-combustion capture from cement and power plants.

Cosmetic sunless tanning agents rely on dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a 3-carbon keto-sugar that reacts with amino acids (lysine residues) and proteins in the stratum corneum through the Maillard reaction to produce brown melanoidin pigments. The tan develops over 4–6 hours and lasts about a week as the surface skin cells turn over — it involves no melanin and provides minimal UV protection.

Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy detects species with unpaired electrons — free radicals, transition metal ions, and excited triplet states. It is used in radiochemistry to characterize radiation-damaged materials, in biochemistry to map the structure of metalloenzyme active sites, and in forensics to date burned bone and tooth enamel through radiation-induced radical accumulation.

Pinene is the most abundant biogenic terpene in Earth's atmosphere. Alpha-pinene emitted by conifer forests reacts with atmospheric ozone and OH radicals to form low-volatility products that condense into secondary organic aerosol particles, contributing to the characteristic haze over forested mountains and playing a significant role in cloud formation and climate.

Cryoprotectants prevent ice crystal formation in biological tissues during freezing. Glycerol and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) are colligative cryoprotectants that lower the freezing point; trehalose is a biological cryoprotectant that replaces water molecules in hydrogen bonds with biomolecules, preventing denaturation at low water activity in organisms like the brine shrimp and the resurrection plant.

Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the delivery vehicle for mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. They consist of ionizable lipids (positively charged at low pH to condense negatively charged mRNA, then neutral at physiological pH to reduce toxicity), helper lipids, cholesterol, and PEGylated lipids. LNP formulation technology developed over 30 years was the key enabling chemistry that made the rapid vaccine deployment possible.

Sulfuric acid is the most widely produced industrial chemical in the world, with global production exceeding 250 million tonnes per year. Made by the contact process (oxidizing SO₂ to SO₃ over V₂O₅ catalyst then dissolving in water), it is consumed primarily for phosphate fertilizer production, but also in petroleum refining, battery acid, metal processing, and thousands of other applications.

Phosphors are materials that absorb energy (from UV light, X-rays, or electrons) and re-emit it as visible light through luminescence. Modern white LEDs use a blue InGaN chip coated with a yellow-emitting cerium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Ce:YAG) phosphor; the combination of the blue chip and yellow phosphor emission appears white to the human eye.

The trans fatty acids in partially hydrogenated vegetable oils are formed when the cis double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids undergo partial isomerization during catalytic hydrogenation. Trans fats elevate LDL cholesterol and lower HDL cholesterol more than saturated fats; following recognition of their cardiovascular risk, the FDA banned partially hydrogenated oils from the US food supply in 2018.

The radiosynthesis of PET tracers must be completed within a few half-lives of the radioisotope — often under 30 minutes for ¹⁸F-FDG synthesis. Automated radiosynthesis modules perform ¹⁸F-fluorination, hydrolysis, and purification in shielded 'hot cells' in a single highly automated sequence, producing sterile, pyrogen-free radiotracer doses for immediate injection into patients.

OLED (organic light-emitting diode) displays emit light when current flows through thin layers of organic semiconductors between two electrodes. Phosphorescent OLEDs using iridium(III) complexes as emitters achieve near-100% internal quantum efficiency by harvesting both singlet and triplet excitons; they are used in premium smartphone displays and rollable TV screens.

Ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) uses a metal carbene catalyst (Grubbs catalyst) to open strained cyclic olefins and link them into polymers. The release of ring strain drives the polymerization; ROMP is 'living' — meaning it produces polymers of precisely controlled molecular weight with narrow dispersity — and is used to make specialty elastomers and block copolymers.

Coatings chemistry in automotive paint systems uses a multi-layer structure: a corrosion-resistant electrocoat primer (~20 µm), a stone-chip resistant primer surfacer, a pigmented base coat (2–5 µm, containing metallic flake for sparkle), and a clearcoat (~40 µm) of crosslinked acrylic-melamine resin that provides gloss and UV protection. The clearcoat is designed to self-heal minor scratches through thermal relaxation.

Glycosylation — the enzymatic attachment of sugars to proteins or lipids — is the most common and complex post-translational modification of proteins. Over 50% of all human proteins are glycoproteins. N-linked glycans on antibodies critically determine their immune effector functions; biopharmaceutical manufacturers must control glycosylation patterns precisely during cell culture production.

Photonic crystals are periodic dielectric structures with a lattice spacing comparable to the wavelength of light, creating photonic bandgaps that prevent certain wavelengths from propagating. The structural coloration of opal gemstones, butterfly wings, and some beetles arises from photonic crystal effects rather than pigments; the colors are iridescent and never fade.

Supercritical CO₂ (scCO₂) is used as a green solvent in decaffeination of coffee, extraction of hops for brewing, and dry cleaning. Above its critical temperature (31.1°C) and pressure (73.8 bar), CO₂ has liquid-like density but gas-like diffusivity, making it an excellent solvent for non-polar compounds; selectivity is tuned by varying pressure and temperature.

Prussian blue analogues (PBAs) are a family of MOF-like coordination frameworks that can intercalate a variety of cations (Na⁺, K⁺, Zn²⁺) in their open-framework lattice. They are being developed as low-cost, abundant cathode materials for sodium-ion and potassium-ion batteries, providing a sustainable alternative to lithium-based systems for grid-scale energy storage.

The 18-electron rule governs the stability of organometallic transition metal complexes: the most stable complexes have exactly 18 electrons in the metal's valence shell (including ligand-donated electrons), analogous to the octet rule for main group elements. Ferrocene ([Fe(η⁵-C₅H₅)₂]) is the archetypal 18-electron complex; its discovery in 1951 launched modern organometallic chemistry.

Yttrium barium copper oxide (YBa₂Cu₃O₇, YBCO) was the first superconductor with a transition temperature above 77 K (liquid nitrogen temperature), discovered in 1987. Its ceramic high-temperature superconductivity, while still requiring cryogenic cooling, made practical superconducting power cables, MRI magnets, and particle accelerator windings far more economical.

Photochromic molecules switch reversibly between two structural forms with different optical properties when irradiated with light of different wavelengths. Diarylethene switches, discovered by Masahiro Irie, are thermally stable in both open (colorless) and closed (colored) forms with fatigue resistance over >10,000 switching cycles, making them candidates for rewritable optical data storage and molecular logic gates.

Green chemistry's 12 principles, formulated by Paul Anastas and John Warner in 1998, include atom economy, using renewable feedstocks, designing for energy efficiency, and avoiding hazardous substances. Atom economy — the percentage of reactant atoms incorporated into the product — is calculated as (MW of product / sum of MW of all reactants) × 100 and is a key metric for synthetic efficiency.

The Menshutkin reaction has been used as a benchmark for computational solvation models because its reaction rate changes by over six orders of magnitude between non-polar solvents (hexane) and polar protic solvents (water), making it an ideal probe of solvent effects on reaction rates described by transition state theory.

The Woodward-Hoffmann rules, formulated in 1965, use molecular orbital symmetry to predict the stereochemical outcomes of pericyclic reactions (electrocyclizations, cycloadditions, and sigmatropic rearrangements). They state that thermally allowed pericyclic reactions are photochemically forbidden and vice versa, based on whether the orbital symmetry is preserved in the cyclic transition state.

Combustion chemistry of hydrocarbon fuels involves hundreds of elementary radical chain reactions. The octane rating of a fuel quantifies its resistance to autoignition (knocking) in internal combustion engines; iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) is assigned 100 and heptane is assigned 0. Tetraethyl lead, added to gasoline since 1923 to raise octane rating, was phased out globally due to its neurotoxic effects on children.

Graphene oxide (GO) is produced by Hummers method (treating graphite with KMnO₄ and H₂SO₄), introducing epoxide, hydroxyl, and carboxyl groups on the basal plane and edges. Thermal or chemical reduction yields reduced graphene oxide (rGO), a disordered but electrically conductive material used in composites, supercapacitors, and filtration membranes.

Chiral HPLC separates drug enantiomers using columns packed with chiral stationary phases such as polysaccharide derivatives (amylose/cellulose carbamates) or Pirkle-type phases. The regulatory requirement that racemic drug candidates undergo chiral separation and independent pharmacological testing of each enantiomer has made chiral chromatography indispensable in drug discovery.

Molecular gastronomy applies food chemistry and physics to create novel culinary textures. Sodium alginate, a polysaccharide extracted from brown algae, forms gel spheres instantly when dropped into a calcium chloride bath (ionic crosslinking of alginate chains). This 'spherification' technique invented by chef Ferran Adrià is used to encapsulate liquids in transparent gel spheres that burst in the mouth.

Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) such as MoS₂ and WS₂ form a new class of 2D materials with direct electronic bandgaps when thinned to a monolayer — a property absent in the bulk material. A monolayer MoS₂ transistor was demonstrated in 2011 with an exceptionally high on/off current ratio, and TMDs show promise for next-generation ultra-thin flexible electronics beyond silicon.

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is a prodrug that accumulates as the photosensitizer protoporphyrin IX (PpIX) preferentially in tumor cells due to their dysregulated heme synthesis. ALA-based photodynamic diagnosis uses blue light to make tumors fluoresce bright pink during brain tumor surgery, enabling surgeons to see and remove tumor margins invisible to white light, significantly improving survival rates.

Single-molecule force spectroscopy, performed with atomic force microscopes (AFM) or optical tweezers, measures the mechanical properties and unfolding forces of individual molecules. It has directly measured the 1600 pN rupture force of covalent bonds, the ~100 pN unbinding of biotin-streptavidin, and the refolding dynamics of individual protein domains — information invisible to ensemble biochemical experiments.

The Lobry de Bruyn-Alberda van Ekenstein transformation is a base-catalyzed interconversion of aldoses and ketoses through enediol intermediates; glucose, fructose, and mannose are interconverted at equilibrium under alkaline conditions. This reaction is why heating sugars in alkaline solutions (e.g., caramel sauce) produces complex brown mixtures: the Maillard reaction can then proceed with multiple sugar isomers.

Electrochemical nitrogen reduction (eNRR) aims to synthesize ammonia directly from N₂ and water at ambient conditions using renewable electricity, bypassing the energy-intensive Haber-Bosch process. While many reports claimed eNRR, rigorous isotope-labeling controls with ¹⁵N₂ revealed that most measured ammonia in early experiments came from contamination rather than the reaction — a cautionary tale about the importance of controls in electrochemistry.

The Born-Oppenheimer approximation, the cornerstone of computational molecular chemistry, assumes nuclei are stationary on the timescale of electronic motion because electrons (mass 9×10⁻³¹ kg) adjust instantaneously to nuclear positions. This allows separate computation of electronic wavefunctions and nuclear dynamics, reducing an intractable many-body quantum problem to manageable calculations.

Biodiesel is produced by transesterification of vegetable oils or animal fats with methanol (or ethanol) in the presence of a base catalyst, yielding fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) and glycerol. It is miscible with petroleum diesel in all proportions, biodegradable, and produces 80% fewer lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions per unit energy; soybeans, rapeseed, and palm oil are the main feedstocks.

Photochemical [2+2] cycloadditions, driven by UV light, form cyclobutane rings by coupling two alkene molecules. Unlike the thermally forbidden [2+2] process, the photoreaction is orbital symmetry-allowed according to Woodward-Hoffmann rules. The DNA-damaging thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers) formed by UV radiation in sunlight are [2+2] photocycloaddition products that cause most UV-induced skin cancers.

The Arrhenius equation (k = A·e^(−Ea/RT)) quantitatively relates reaction rate constants to temperature and activation energy. A practical rule of thumb derived from it is that reaction rates approximately double for every 10°C increase in temperature around room temperature — a useful estimate for chemical processes, biological metabolism, and food spoilage rates.

Mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) such as MCM-41 have uniform cylindrical pores of 2–50 nm diameter, enabling high drug loading (up to 30 wt%) and controlled release. Capping the pores with stimuli-responsive gatekeepers (pH-sensitive valves, enzyme-responsive lids) creates 'nanoimpellers' that release drugs only at tumor pH or in response to intracellular signals.

Chemical oscillators in the atmosphere include the ozone-NOₓ cycle in the lower stratosphere, where ozone photolysis creates O(¹D) radicals that react with N₂O to regenerate NO, which catalytically destroys ozone. The hydroxyl radical (·OH) is the key oxidant of the troposphere — sometimes called the 'detergent of the atmosphere' — reacting with methane, CO, and thousands of VOCs to initiate their removal.

Chitosan, produced by deacetylation of chitin from shrimp and crab shells, is the second most abundant natural polysaccharide. Its positive charge at physiological pH enables mucoadhesion, electrostatic binding to negatively charged DNA and RNA, and formation of nanoparticles for oral drug delivery. It is also used in wound dressings because it promotes blood clotting and has antimicrobial activity.

The synthesis of vitamin B12 by Robert Woodward and Albert Eschenmoser, completed in 1973 after 11 years of work by over 100 chemists, remains the most complex total synthesis ever achieved. The vitamin has 9 stereocenters and a corrin macrocycle; the project applied Woodward-Hoffmann orbital symmetry rules, which were discovered during the synthesis itself.

Electrodeposition (electroplating) coats a conductive substrate with a metal layer by reducing metal ions from solution onto the cathode surface. It is used to deposit decorative and protective coatings (nickel, chrome, gold) on jewelry and automotive parts, to form the copper interconnects in semiconductor chips (copper damascene process), and to electroform precision optical mirrors and molds.

The Woodward synthesis of chlorophyll (1960) and then vitamin B12 established the era of modern total synthesis. Chlorophyll's porphyrin macrocycle contains magnesium (not iron like heme), and its light-harvesting properties depend on the extended π-system. The phytol tail is a diterpene alcohol that anchors the molecule in the thylakoid membrane.

Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), invented by Binnig and Rohrer (1986 Nobel Prize in Physics), exploits quantum tunneling of electrons between a sharp metal tip and a conducting surface to image individual atoms and molecules. It can also manipulate individual atoms; IBM famously spelled 'IBM' in xenon atoms on a nickel surface in 1989, demonstrating atomic-scale surface chemistry.

Retinal (vitamin A aldehyde) is the chromophore in all visual pigments. In rhodopsin, 11-cis-retinal is covalently bound as a Schiff base to a lysine residue; photon absorption isomerizes it to all-trans-retinal in ~200 femtoseconds, triggering a conformational change that initiates the visual signal cascade — the fastest photochemical reaction known in biology.

The blood coagulation cascade is a series of sequential proteolytic activations of zymogens (inactive enzyme precursors) culminating in the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin by thrombin. Anticoagulant drugs such as warfarin inhibit vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of clotting factors, while heparin activates antithrombin III to directly inhibit thrombin — two complementary chemical strategies to prevent clotting.

Cerium(IV) ammonium nitrate (CAN) is a mild, single-electron oxidant widely used in organic chemistry for oxidative removal of para-methoxybenzyl (PMB) protecting groups. Its ability to oxidize PMB ethers to labile oxocarbenium ions without affecting other functional groups makes it indispensable in carbohydrate synthesis and natural product chemistry.

Corrosion inhibitors for steel pipelines and offshore structures include organic amines and imidazolines that adsorb as protective monolayers on the metal surface, blocking contact between corrosive species (Cl⁻, H₂S, CO₂) and the metal. They are added at part-per-million concentrations to oil and gas pipelines, where even partial corrosion protection saves hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

Liquid-liquid extraction (solvent extraction) separates compounds based on their differential solubility in two immiscible phases (typically an organic solvent and water). The distribution ratio D = [solute]_organic/[solute]_aqueous quantifies partition; it is the basis for refining uranium with tributyl phosphate in the PUREX process and for industrial production of many pharmaceuticals and natural products.

Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction; it is synthesized from choline and acetyl-CoA by choline acetyltransferase, released into the synapse, and rapidly hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase back to choline and acetate. Nerve agents like sarin and VX irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing continuous muscle stimulation, seizures, and asphyxiation.

The Tammann temperature (approximately half the melting point in Kelvin) is the threshold above which bulk diffusion in solids becomes significant, enabling sintering, grain growth, and solid-state reactions. Knowing Tammann temperatures guides the design of solid-state catalysts and battery materials — for instance, lithium compounds with low Tammann temperatures can be processed at mild temperatures.

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy exploits the fact that nuclei with non-zero spin (¹H, ¹³C, ³¹P, ¹⁹F) precess in a magnetic field at frequencies proportional to the field strength and the nucleus's chemical environment. NMR is the most powerful tool for determining molecular structure in solution, and the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Bloch and Purcell for its discovery.

Silica aerogel's record-low thermal conductivity (~0.015 W/m·K, compared to 0.026 for air) is achieved because its nanoporous structure (pore size ~20 nm) is smaller than the mean free path of air molecules (~70 nm at atmospheric pressure), effectively suppressing gaseous conduction. It is used as insulation in NASA's Mars rovers and in some Arctic expedition clothing.

Polymer brush coatings — dense layers of polymer chains end-grafted to a surface — provide excellent antifouling properties by sterically repelling proteins and bacteria. PEGylation of nanoparticles with polyethylene glycol (PEG) brushes creates a 'stealth' coating that evades immune recognition, dramatically extending circulation time in the blood and is used in liposomal drug formulations like Doxil.

The Maillard reaction and enzymatic browning are distinct processes. Enzymatic browning (responsible for cut apple browning) is catalyzed by polyphenol oxidase (PPO) enzymes that oxidize phenolic compounds in the presence of oxygen, producing brown ortho-quinone pigments. Lemon juice (citric acid and ascorbic acid) prevents enzymatic browning by lowering pH (inhibiting PPO) and acting as an antioxidant.

The electro-Fenton process generates hydrogen peroxide in situ at a cathode (O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O₂) and combines it with catalytic Fe²⁺ to generate hydroxyl radicals for advanced oxidation treatment of wastewater. It degrades persistent organic pollutants like pharmaceuticals, dyes, and pesticides that resist conventional biological treatment.

Fluorite (CaF₂) has the fluorite crystal structure — one of the most common AB₂ structure types — in which calcium occupies a face-centered cubic lattice and fluoride ions fill all tetrahedral holes. Doped ceria (Ce₀.₈Gd₀.₂O₁.₉, CGO) adopts the same structure and is one of the best oxide-ion conductors, used as the electrolyte in solid oxide fuel cells.

Nucleotide analogs form the backbone of antiviral therapy: acyclovir (Zovirax) is an acyclic nucleoside that is selectively phosphorylated by herpes virus thymidine kinase and then incorporated into viral DNA, terminating chain elongation. Tenofovir, lamivudine, and emtricitabine use analogous mechanisms to inhibit HIV reverse transcriptase, and remdesivir inhibits SARS-CoV-2 RNA polymerase.

Stainless steel owes its corrosion resistance to a passivating surface layer of chromium oxide (Cr₂O₃) only 1–3 nm thick that forms spontaneously in air. When scratched, the passive layer self-repairs within seconds in oxygen-containing environments. Adding nickel stabilizes the austenitic crystal structure of 304-grade stainless, while adding molybdenum in 316-grade further resists pitting by chloride ions.

The Simmons-Smith reaction is a stereospecific cyclopropanation of alkenes using diiodomethane and a zinc-copper couple. The carbenoid reagent delivered by zinc adds syn to the alkene (iodomethylzinc iodide), allowing complete stereocontrol and making it a key reaction for synthesizing cyclopropane rings in terpene and pharmaceutical synthesis.

Phosphorescence differs from fluorescence in that emission involves a formally forbidden triplet-to-singlet transition, giving emission lifetimes of milliseconds to seconds rather than nanoseconds. Phosphorescent 'glow in the dark' materials commonly use strontium aluminate doped with europium, which store UV energy and release it slowly as a yellow-green glow for hours.

Colloidal gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) exhibit a size-dependent localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) that gives them brilliant colors: ~20 nm particles appear wine-red, larger particles shift to blue. The LSPR arises from collective oscillation of conduction electrons driven by incident light; it is exploited in rapid lateral flow immunoassays (including COVID-19 antigen tests) for visible colorimetric detection.

Spin-crossover (SCO) complexes switch between high-spin and low-spin electronic configurations in response to temperature, pressure, or light, producing dramatic changes in color and magnetic properties. Iron(II) SCO complexes like [Fe(ptz)₆](BF₄)₂ change from colorless (low-spin) to purple (high-spin) above a sharp transition temperature, making them candidates for displays and sensors.

The chemistry of hair dyeing involves two stages: an alkaline hydrogen peroxide oxidant lightens existing hair pigment (melanin) by oxidizing it, while permanent dye intermediates (p-phenylenediamine and couplers) penetrate the hair cortex and are oxidatively coupled in situ to form large, chromophoric azo and indamine dye molecules too large to diffuse back out.

Thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries occurs when internal cell temperature rises and triggers exothermic reactions between the electrolyte, cathode, and anode materials in a self-accelerating cascade; above ~80°C for some cathode chemistries, oxygen release from the cathode reacts violently with organic electrolyte, potentially causing fire or explosion. Thermal management systems in EVs are designed to prevent any single-cell failure from propagating.

Terpineol is a monoterpene alcohol present in pine, lime, and cajuput oils, used widely in soaps, cosmetics, and household cleaning products for its fresh, floral scent. It is biosynthesized from geranyl pyrophosphate via terpinyl cation intermediate; industrially it is produced by acid-catalyzed hydration of alpha-pinene.

The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation (pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])) describes the relationship between the pH of a buffer and the ratio of deprotonated to protonated species. It is used extensively in biochemistry to formulate physiological buffers (phosphate buffer, HEPES), to predict the ionization state of drug molecules at different pH values, and in protein biochemistry to maintain enzyme activity.

Solid-state synthesis using mechanochemical ball-milling has enabled greener manufacturing of complex materials including pharmaceutical co-crystals, metal-organic frameworks, and battery materials. Milling can access metastable polymorphs, reduce particle size, and create intimate mixtures of reactants — all without solvents, reducing waste and energy consumption versus traditional solution-phase routes.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations propagate Newton's equations of motion for thousands to millions of atoms using empirical force fields or ab initio potentials, allowing chemists to watch protein folding, lipid membrane behavior, and materials phase transitions at atomic resolution over nanosecond-to-microsecond timescales. Anton, a specialized supercomputer by D.E. Shaw Research, can simulate millisecond protein dynamics.

The Reformatsky reaction with chiral auxiliaries or asymmetric catalysts can produce beta-hydroxy esters with high enantioselectivity, which are versatile building blocks for natural product synthesis. Evans' oxazolidinone chiral auxiliaries and Corey's CBS catalyst are commonly combined with the Reformatsky reaction for stereocontrolled aldol-type additions.

Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) are rod-shaped nanoparticles 5–50 nm wide and 100–500 nm long isolated from wood pulp, cotton, or bacterial cellulose by acid hydrolysis of amorphous regions. Their extraordinary stiffness (~150 GPa along the crystal axis), high aspect ratio, renewable origin, and reactive hydroxyl-rich surface make CNCs promising reinforcing fillers in polymer composites and in photonic materials.

The Marcus theory of electron transfer (1992 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, Rudolph Marcus) quantifies electron transfer rates using two parameters: the reorganization energy (λ) — the energy required to rearrange solvent and molecular geometry — and the driving force (ΔG°). The remarkable prediction of the 'inverted region' — where rates decrease with increasing driving force beyond a threshold — was confirmed experimentally in biological photosynthesis.

Nanocellulose aerogels (wood sponges) produced by freeze-drying cellulose nanofiber suspensions have densities as low as 1.5 mg/cm³ and can absorb up to 100 times their weight in oil. They are being developed for oil spill cleanup because the absorbed oil can be squeezed out and recovered, making the aerogel reusable, unlike conventional absorbent materials.

The concentration of hydroxide ions in pure water at 25°C is 10⁻⁷ M (Kw = 10⁻¹⁴), giving pH 7. Kw increases with temperature (to ~10⁻¹³ at 60°C), meaning pH 7 at 60°C is actually slightly acidic. This has practical implications: body temperature (37°C) gives physiological pH = 6.81 for neutral water, and 'pH 7' is only strictly neutral at 25°C.

Terbium and europium are the rare earth luminophores in tri-phosphor white fluorescent lamps and compact fluorescent bulbs: europium provides the red and blue emission while terbium provides the green, and their combined emission appears white. The high color rendering index (CRI >80) of these lamps compared to the older cool-white lamps is due to the narrowband nature of rare-earth emission lines.

Polypyrrole and polyaniline can be electrochemically polymerized as conducting thin films directly onto electrode surfaces. Polyaniline's conductivity depends on both oxidation state (four distinct forms from fully reduced leucoemeraldine to fully oxidized pernigraniline) and protonation; only the half-oxidized emeraldine salt form is highly conductive, making it useful in corrosion protection and electrochromic devices.

Stille-Kelly reaction uses fluoride ion to generate an aryl tin reagent in situ from an aryl trifluorosilane for palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling without handling toxic organotin reagents. This modification exemplifies the broader trend in 'transition metal catalysis for social good' — designing reactions that achieve the same bond-forming goals while replacing hazardous reagents with more benign alternatives.

Nanotopography — surface features at the 10–1000 nm scale — dramatically alters the behavior of cells adhering to surfaces. Titanium implants with nano-rough surfaces promote faster osseointegration (bone-implant bonding) because the nanoscale features enhance adsorption of fibronectin and vitronectin, which present RGD sequences that integrins on osteoblast cells recognize.

Ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE, MW > 3 million g/mol) is the most wear-resistant bulk polymer known. Its very long chains entangle extensively, giving extraordinarily high impact strength and low friction coefficient. It is used for hip and knee implant bearing surfaces, body armor (Dyneema/Spectra fiber), and as a lining for hoppers and chutes in mining.

Chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) is the process that allows stacking of multiple transistor layers in modern semiconductor chips by abrasively polishing each layer flat to within angstrom-scale tolerances. The polishing slurry contains both abrasive nanoparticles (silica or ceria) and a chemical oxidant (H₂O₂) that softens the surface layer to enable removal at controlled rates.

The Dakin oxidation uses hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions to oxidize aromatic aldehydes and methyl ketones to phenols via a Baeyer-Villiger-type mechanism. It is a mild, regioselective reaction notable for its use in the synthesis of the food flavoring vanillin from guaiacol (a lignan-derived phenol) and in the first industrial synthesis of catechol.

Pressure-sensitive adhesives (PSAs), used in masking tape, Post-it notes, and medical dressings, are viscoelastic polymers that can adhere to surfaces under light pressure without chemical bonding or solvent. The optimal PSA must be tacky (low viscosity) to wet the surface rapidly, yet cohesively strong (high modulus) to resist peel — properties tuned by polymer molecular weight, crosslink density, and tackifier resins.

Liquid metal batteries use a low-density metal (lithium or sodium) as the anode, a liquid salt electrolyte, and a dense high-density liquid metal alloy (antimony, bismuth) as the cathode — all three layers self-segregate by density at operating temperature (~450°C). Developed by Donald Sadoway at MIT, they have high power density and potentially very long calendar life for grid storage applications.

Electrospinning produces polymer nanofibers 100 nm–10 µm in diameter by applying a high voltage (~10–30 kV) to a polymer solution droplet on a needle tip, causing the charged jet to whip and stretch into ultrafine fibers that deposit on a collector. Electrospun nonwovens have very high surface area-to-volume ratios and are used in filtration membranes, wound dressings, and tissue engineering scaffolds.

The nucleophilic addition of water to carbon dioxide (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃) is catalyzed 10 million-fold by carbonic anhydrase, one of the fastest known enzymes (kcat ~10⁶ s⁻¹). The zinc-containing active site facilitates water deprotonation, creating a metal-bound hydroxide that attacks CO₂; this reaction is essential for CO₂ transport in blood and pH regulation in cells.

Thin-film optical coatings exploit constructive and destructive interference between light reflected from multiple dielectric layers to create antireflective coatings (camera lenses), highly reflective mirrors (laser cavities), and wavelength-selective filters. A quarter-wave layer of MgF₂ on glass reduces reflectance from 4% to near 0% for a specific wavelength — the principle behind anti-glare eyeglasses.

The concept of Lewis acids and bases, proposed by G.N. Lewis in 1923, extends acid-base chemistry beyond proton transfer: a Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor. BF₃ and AlCl₃ are classical Lewis acids used as catalysts in Friedel-Crafts alkylations; LUMO-HOMO interactions between Lewis acids and bases form the theoretical framework for understanding coordination and organometallic chemistry.

Sodium chloride (common salt) melts at 801°C but dissolves readily in water at room temperature because the hydration energy of the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions exceeds the lattice energy of the crystal — a classic demonstration that ionic crystals dissolve in polar solvents when hydration offsets lattice energy. The solubility of ~357 g/L makes saline solutions critical in physiology, food preservation, and chemical industry.

Chemical space — the estimated number of drug-like organic molecules with molecular weight <500 Da — is often cited as approximately 10⁶⁰ compounds. The actual explored chemical space (all synthesized and tested compounds) numbers only ~10⁸. This vast unexplored territory motivates generative AI models that design novel drug candidates within chemical space in silico before synthesis.

Formic acid (HCOOH) is the simplest carboxylic acid and the primary component of ant sting venom, where it causes the burning sensation. It is also the thermodynamic product of CO₂ reduction by two electrons and two protons, making it a target for electrochemical CO₂ valorization; formic acid can in turn be used as a hydrogen carrier for fuel cells.

Iodine-131 (¹³¹I), a fission product with an 8-day half-life, is used in nuclear medicine to treat thyroid cancer and hyperthyroidism; the thyroid selectively concentrates iodine, so systemically administered ¹³¹I delivers a local radiation dose to thyroid tissue. It is also the radioisotope most dangerous in nuclear fallout, which is why stable potassium iodide tablets are distributed near nuclear plants.

Ring-closing metathesis (RCM), enabled by Grubbs ruthenium catalysts, forms macrocyclic rings from diene precursors by releasing ethylene. The 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognized metathesis broadly; RCM has become invaluable in synthesizing macrolide natural products like epothilone anticancer agents and natural musks in fragrance chemistry at scales and yields impossible with older cyclization methods.

Phosphagenesis — the prebiotic synthesis of organophosphate molecules — is a key unsolved problem in the origin of life. Schreibersite (Fe₂NiP), a mineral abundant in meteorites, can phosphorylate organic molecules under aqueous conditions, offering a plausible abiotic route to ATP precursors and nucleotides in early Earth chemistry without requiring biological enzymes.

The Nernst equation relates electrode potential to concentration: E = E° − (RT/nF)·ln(Q). At 25°C this simplifies to E = E° − (0.0592/n)·log(Q). It is used to determine concentrations of ions from measured electrode potentials (potentiometry) — the working principle of pH electrodes, ion-selective electrodes, and continuous glucose monitors.

Magnetite (Fe₃O₄) nanoparticles are superparamagnetic below a critical size (~25 nm), meaning they are strongly magnetized in a field but have zero remanent magnetization when the field is removed. This prevents particle aggregation during storage while enabling rapid separation by magnet. They are used to separate proteins (functionalized with antibodies) from complex mixtures and in magnetic hyperthermia cancer therapy.

The Tishchenko reaction disproportionates two equivalents of an aldehyde (usually with an aluminum alkoxide catalyst) into an ester. Inorganic titanium oxide catalysts also mediate this reaction and ethyl acetate — the world's most widely used ester solvent — is produced industrially on hundreds of thousands of tons per year by Tishchenko reaction of acetaldehyde.

Sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) is a mild, selective hydride reducing agent that reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols but does not reduce esters or carboxylic acids at room temperature. First synthesized by H.I. Schlesinger in 1942, it is produced in thousands of tonnes per year for pharmaceutical synthesis, paper bleaching, and as a hydrogen-storage material for fuel cell applications.

Aerobic granular sludge (AGS) reactors harness the colloidal chemistry of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) secreted by bacteria to form dense millimeter-scale granules that settle rapidly, allowing much smaller reactor footprints than conventional activated sludge. The EPS matrix acts as a colloidal network of polysaccharides, proteins, and humic substances that holds granule structure.

The photoreduction of CO₂ to formate and other products by semiconductor photocatalysts is inspired by the Calvin cycle's 'dark reactions' of photosynthesis. Bismuth vanadate (BiVO₄) is a visible-light-active photocatalyst whose bandgap of 2.4 eV matches the solar spectrum well, but improving selectivity and efficiency toward specific multi-carbon products like ethanol remains an active area of research.

Protein crystallography resolution depends on the diffraction-limit set by the X-ray wavelength (~1.5 Å for CuKα radiation). Synchrotron X-ray sources produce beams 10¹⁰ times brighter than lab X-ray tubes, enabling rapid data collection from tiny crystals and time-resolved crystallography that captures enzyme intermediates with millisecond resolution.

The chemical oxygen demand (COD) test measures the total amount of oxygen needed to chemically oxidize all organic compounds in a water sample to CO₂ and H₂O using potassium dichromate under acidic conditions at 150°C. It is a standard regulatory metric for wastewater treatment plant performance because it is faster and more comprehensive than the biological oxygen demand (BOD) test.

Yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) is the electrolyte in solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs).
