The human body synthesizes about 400 mg of bile acids daily; after absorption of dietary lipids, ~95% are reabsorbed in the ileum and recycled through enterohepatic circulation.

The Buchwald-Hartwig amination uses palladium catalysts with bulky phosphine ligands to form carbon-nitrogen bonds by coupling aryl halides or triflates with amines. Developed in the mid-1990s by Stephen Buchwald and John Hartwig, it dramatically simplified the synthesis of aryl amines — key structural motifs in more than 80% of FDA-approved pharmaceuticals — replacing lengthy classical multi-step sequences.

Capillary electrophoresis (CE) separates charged analytes in a narrow-bore capillary (25–75 μm internal diameter) by applying a high electric field (200–400 V/cm), which drives ions at speeds proportional to their charge-to-hydrodynamic-radius ratio. CE is capable of separating DNA fragments differing by a single base pair and is one of the core analytical methods used in DNA sequencing and forensic DNA profiling.

Boron forms compounds with unusual electron-deficient bonding: diborane (B₂H₆) is a colorless flammable gas in which two bridging hydrogen atoms form three-center two-electron bonds because there are insufficient electrons for conventional two-center two-electron bonds. The study of electron-deficient boron hydride chemistry, pioneered by William Lipscomb, earned him the 1976 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Polylactic acid (PLA) is a biodegradable thermoplastic polyester derived from fermented corn starch or sugarcane, making it one of the most widely used bio-based polymers. Its life-cycle CO₂ emissions are 60–80% lower than petroleum-based plastics, and it is used in 3D printing filament, food packaging, sutures, and drug-delivery implants that slowly hydrolyze in the body over weeks to months.

Raman spectroscopy is a form of vibrational spectroscopy in which a photon inelastically scatters off a molecule, losing (Stokes) or gaining (anti-Stokes) energy equal to the vibrational quantum of the molecule. Unlike infrared spectroscopy, which requires a change in dipole moment, Raman spectroscopy is sensitive to changes in polarizability and is therefore particularly useful for symmetric stretches and non-polar bonds; surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) on gold or silver nanoparticles can detect single molecules.

Carboxypeptidase A is a zinc-containing exopeptidase that cleaves a single amino acid from the C-terminus of polypeptide chains, with zinc activating the substrate carbonyl for nucleophilic attack by a water molecule. Its mechanism was one of the first enzyme mechanisms fully elucidated by X-ray crystallography in the 1960s by William Lipscomb, and the enzyme's activity depends on the single Zn²⁺ ion — removing it with EDTA renders the enzyme completely inactive.

Chlorophyll fluorescence is the red-orange light (680–740 nm) re-emitted by excited chlorophyll molecules when they return to the ground state without transferring their energy to photochemistry. Measuring chlorophyll fluorescence yield — which decreases when photosynthesis is active and increases when it is inhibited — is a fast, non-invasive way to assess plant photosynthetic efficiency and stress responses in both laboratory and agricultural settings.

Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is a cyclic ether widely used as a polar aprotic solvent in organic synthesis because it dissolves both polar and nonpolar compounds, has a boiling point of 66 °C convenient for reflux, and complexes lithium ions to stabilize organolithium reagents. THF is miscible with water but will separate into two phases upon addition of sufficient salt (salting-out effect), a useful property for aqueous workup in synthesis.

The Birch reduction uses dissolved metal (sodium or lithium in liquid ammonia with an alcohol proton source) to reduce aromatic rings to 1,4-cyclohexadienes via a sequence of electron addition and protonation steps. The selectivity of reduction — electron-donating substituents leave the double bonds adjacent to the substituent, while electron-withdrawing groups leave the double bonds away — makes it a key step in the synthesis of prostaglandins, steroids, and terpene natural products.

Sulfuric acid is the industrial chemical produced in the largest quantity worldwide (~250 million metric tonnes per year), primarily manufactured by the contact process: combustion of sulfur to SO₂, catalytic oxidation over V₂O₅ to SO₃, then absorption in oleum before dilution. About 60% of global production goes to making phosphate fertilizers by reacting sulfuric acid with phosphate rock.

Aqua regia (Latin: 'royal water') is a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and hydrochloric acid in a 1:3 molar ratio that dissolves noble metals such as gold and platinum, which resist individual acids. The dissolution occurs because HCl provides chloride ions that complex with gold to form stable [AuCl₄]⁻ (tetrachloroaurate) or [PtCl₆]²⁻ (hexachloroplatinate) anions, shifting the equilibrium and allowing HNO₃ to oxidize the metal.

Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are crystalline, porous 2D or 3D organic solids built entirely from light elements (C, H, N, O, B) via strong, reversible covalent bonds such as imine, boronate ester, or triazine linkages. Their precisely defined nano-sized pores, tunable functionality, low density (~0.5 g/cm³), and high surface area (up to 4000 m²/g) are being explored for gas storage, heterogeneous catalysis, and ion-transport membranes.

Beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) kill bacteria by covalently acylating the active-site serine of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), the enzymes that cross-link the bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan. Beta-lactamase enzymes, which bacteria evolved to hydrolyze the four-membered beta-lactam ring, are the most common mechanism of antibiotic resistance; beta-lactamase inhibitors such as clavulanic acid are co-administered with penicillins to restore their activity.

Starch is a polysaccharide consisting of two polymers of α-D-glucose: amylose (linear, α-1,4 linkages, 20–30% of starch) and amylopectin (highly branched with both α-1,4 and α-1,6 branch-point linkages, 70–80%). When starch granules are heated in water (gelatinization), hydrogen bonds break and granules absorb water and swell, creating a viscous gel that is the basis for thickening sauces, custards, and gravies.

Photodynamic therapy (PDT) uses photosensitizer molecules that, upon light activation, transfer energy to ground-state molecular oxygen to generate singlet oxygen (¹O₂) — a reactive oxygen species that destroys nearby cancer cells, bacteria, or fungi within a few nanometers. FDA-approved photosensitizers include porfimer sodium (Photofrin) and 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA, a precursor to protoporphyrin IX), which selectively accumulate in rapidly dividing tumor cells.

The ideal gas constant R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ appears in the ideal gas law (PV = nRT), the Arrhenius equation, the Nernst equation, the Van't Hoff equation, and the Boltzmann entropy equation S = R·ln W (in molar form). It is equal to the Boltzmann constant k_B multiplied by Avogadro's number N_A, and since 2019 its exact value is fixed by the SI definition, making it a cornerstone linking mechanical energy, temperature, and chemical amount.

Ziegler-Natta catalysts, developed independently by Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta in the early 1950s (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1963), are heterogeneous transition-metal catalysts (typically TiCl₄ on MgCl₂ with an AlEt₃ cocatalyst) that polymerize alkenes in a stereoregular fashion. They enabled industrial production of isotactic polypropylene and high-density polyethylene, transforming plastics manufacturing; modern metallocene catalysts provide even greater stereocontrol.

Copper has the highest electrical conductivity of any element except silver (~5.96 × 10⁷ S/m at 20 °C), which is why it is the universal choice for electrical wiring. Its conductivity results from the single 4s¹ electron being loosely bound and highly mobile; silver is slightly better conductor but 80× more expensive, so copper carries the vast majority of the world's electrical infrastructure.

The Friedel-Crafts acylation uses an acyl halide and a Lewis acid catalyst (usually AlCl₃) to introduce an acyl group onto an aromatic ring via electrophilic aromatic substitution. Unlike Friedel-Crafts alkylation, acylation does not give polyalkylation products because the electron-withdrawing acyl group deactivates the ring toward further substitution — making it the method of choice for introducing ketone functionality onto aromatic rings in industrial synthesis.

Solvent extraction (liquid-liquid extraction) separates compounds between two immiscible liquid phases based on their relative solubility in each phase, quantified by the distribution coefficient D = [solute]_organic/[solute]_aqueous. In the nuclear fuel cycle, tributyl phosphate (TBP) in kerosene is used to selectively extract uranium and plutonium from spent fuel dissolved in nitric acid, enabling the purex process to recycle fissile material.

Titanium has a high strength-to-weight ratio, biocompatibility, and excellent corrosion resistance (owing to its spontaneous TiO₂ passive layer), making it the material of choice for orthopedic implants (hip/knee replacements), dental implants, and aerospace structural components. Titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V (6% aluminum, 4% vanadium) accounts for over 50% of all titanium used, offering tensile strength ~1000 MPa at half the density of steel.

Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other, meaning they have at least two stereocenters in which at least one has the same absolute configuration. Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers have different physical properties (melting point, boiling point, solubility) and different biological activities, which allows them to be separated by standard chromatographic or recrystallization techniques.

Polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) separates proteins or nucleic acids through a cross-linked polyacrylamide matrix by size: smaller molecules migrate faster under an electric field. SDS-PAGE uses sodium dodecyl sulfate detergent to unfold proteins and coat them with negative charge proportional to mass, so migration rate reflects only molecular weight; the technique is a standard tool for estimating protein size and purity.

Sodium azide (NaN₃) is an ionic solid that decomposes explosively to sodium metal and nitrogen gas when heated above ~300 °C or triggered by shock. This rapid gas generation (1 gram NaN₃ produces 0.85 L of N₂) is exploited in automotive airbags, which inflate within 30 ms of a crash sensor triggering electrical ignition of the azide charge — the chemical reaction filling the bag before the driver contacts it.

The electron transport chain (ETC) in the inner mitochondrial membrane uses the electrons from NADH and FADH₂ to pump protons across the membrane through complexes I–IV, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase to phosphorylate ADP. The overall process (oxidative phosphorylation) generates ~34 ATP per glucose compared to only 2 ATP from glycolysis alone, explaining why aerobic organisms can extract ~20× more energy from glucose than anaerobes.

Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) is the industrial catalyst for the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ in the contact process for sulfuric acid manufacture, operating at 450–600 °C where it cycles between V⁵⁺ and V⁴⁺ oxidation states. Vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) exploit the four accessible vanadium oxidation states (V²⁺/V³⁺ on the negative side, VO²⁺/VO₂⁺ on the positive) in an aqueous sulfuric acid electrolyte to store large amounts of electrical energy for grid-scale energy storage.

The de Broglie wavelength (λ = h/mv) of a particle decreases as mass and velocity increase, which is why quantum mechanical behavior (wave-particle duality, tunneling, interference) is observable for electrons and small molecules but not for macroscopic objects. In hydrogen transfer reactions catalyzed by enzymes, quantum mechanical proton tunneling can contribute significantly to the reaction rate even at physiological temperatures, explaining kinetic isotope effects larger than predicted classically.

Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a cancer treatment in which boron-10 (²⁰B)-containing compounds are delivered selectively to tumor cells, then irradiated with low-energy thermal neutrons. The ¹⁰B nucleus captures a neutron and undergoes fission into ⁷Li and ⁴He nuclei with path lengths of ~5–9 μm — approximately one cell diameter — depositing lethal doses of radiation only in boron-rich tumor cells while sparing adjacent healthy tissue.

Osmotic pressure is the pressure required to stop osmotic flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one. The van't Hoff equation π = iMRT (where i is the van't Hoff factor, M is molarity, R is the gas constant, T is temperature) shows that a 0.154 M NaCl solution (physiological saline, i ≈ 2) has an osmotic pressure of ~7.7 atm at 37 °C, which must be maintained for intravenous solutions to avoid lysing (bursting) red blood cells.

Astatine (At, Z=85) is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, with an estimated total abundance of less than 30 grams at any given time. All its isotopes are radioactive; astatine-211 (t₁/₂ = 7.2 h) is the most studied medically because it decays by alpha emission with range of ~60 μm in tissue, making it ideal for targeted alpha therapy of cancer with At-labeled antibodies.

The retrosynthetic analysis approach, developed by E.J. Corey (1990 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), involves mentally disconnecting a target molecule into simpler precursors by identifying strategic bond disconnections ('retrosynthons'), then working backward until commercially available starting materials are reached. This systematic approach transformed complex natural product synthesis from an art into a logical discipline and is now taught universally in advanced organic chemistry courses.

Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is a silicone elastomer used in soft lithography to fabricate microfluidic chips because it can be easily molded, is optically transparent, gas-permeable, biocompatible, and bonds reversibly to glass and itself by surface activation with oxygen plasma. The 'lab-on-a-chip' devices made from PDMS enable miniaturized chemical and biological analyses requiring nanoliter volumes of fluid in channels as narrow as 1 μm.

Keto-enol tautomerism is a rapid, reversible equilibrium between a carbonyl compound (keto form) and its enol isomer (hydroxyl on the double bond), catalyzed by acid or base. For acetone, the keto form predominates at equilibrium (enol content ~0.0001%), but for 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds such as acetylacetone, the enol content reaches 80% in the liquid phase because the conjugated enol is stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding and extended conjugation.

Neodymium-iron-boron (Nd₂Fe₁₄B) permanent magnets are the strongest type of permanent magnet, with maximum energy products up to 64 MGOe — 20 times that of ferrite magnets. Developed in 1982 by Sagawa (Sumitomo Special Metals) and independently by Croat (General Motors), they are now in nearly every electric motor, generator, hard disk drive, and loudspeaker because of their compactness, making them critical to electric vehicle motors and wind turbines.

Sonochemistry uses high-intensity ultrasound (20 kHz to 1 MHz) to accelerate or initiate chemical reactions through acoustic cavitation — the formation, growth, and violent collapse of microscopic bubbles that generate transient local temperatures exceeding 5000 K and pressures above 1000 atm. These extreme conditions drive reactions that are otherwise difficult or impossible, including metal powder activation, polymer degradation, and synthesis of nanoparticles.

Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is a water-soluble polymer of repeating −(CH₂CH₂O)− units used in pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and biotechnology. PEGylation — covalent attachment of PEG chains to protein drugs — dramatically increases their half-life in the bloodstream (from minutes to days) by reducing kidney filtration (hydrodynamic radius increase) and decreasing immune recognition, without significantly compromising therapeutic activity.

Cerium (Ce) is the most abundant rare-earth element and is unique among the lanthanides in having accessible Ce³⁺/Ce⁴⁺ redox chemistry under mild conditions, because both oxidation states have stable electron configurations ([Xe]4f¹ and [Xe]4f⁰). Cerium oxide (ceria, CeO₂) is the active component of automotive three-way catalytic converters' oxygen-storage material, cycling rapidly between Ce⁴⁺ and Ce³⁺ to buffer oxygen during rich and lean engine conditions.

Metallocenes are sandwich compounds in which a metal atom is coordinated between two cyclopentadienyl (Cp, η⁵-C₅H₅⁻) rings through delocalized π-bonding. Ferrocene (Fe(η⁵-Cp)₂), the first metallocene discovered in 1951, has 18 valence electrons, is highly stable, and undergoes reversible Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ oxidation at 0.40 V vs. NHE, making it the universal internal reference for electrochemical measurements in non-aqueous solvents.

Lactose intolerance results from insufficient production of lactase (β-galactosidase) in the small intestine, so the disaccharide lactose (glucose–β-1,4–galactose) passes undigested to the colon, where bacteria ferment it to gas (H₂, CO₂, CH₄) and organic acids, causing bloating, cramps, and diarrhea. About 68% of the global adult population is lactase non-persistent; the mutation enabling adult lactase persistence arose independently multiple times in dairy-farming populations in Europe and Africa.

Photocatalytic water splitting uses semiconductor photocatalysts (TiO₂, GaN:ZnO solid solutions, or BiVO₄) to absorb solar light and drive the thermodynamically uphill reaction 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (ΔG = +237 kJ/mol). Overall solar-to-hydrogen efficiency for the best photocatalytic systems is currently 1–5%, but research into Z-scheme photocatalysts that mimic the two-photon process of natural photosynthesis aims to exceed 10%.

Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) occurs when a donor fluorophore in an excited state transfers energy non-radiatively to an acceptor fluorophore through dipole-dipole coupling, with efficiency strongly dependent on the inverse sixth power of distance (E ∝ 1/r⁶). This distance sensitivity makes FRET a 'molecular ruler' accurate between 2 and 10 nm, enabling real-time measurement of protein conformational changes and molecular interactions inside living cells.

Nitrous oxide (N₂O, 'laughing gas') is a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential 265 times that of CO₂ over 100 years and is currently the dominant ozone-depleting substance emitted from human activities after the phaseout of CFCs. Agricultural soil is the largest N₂O source (~70% of anthropogenic emissions) due to microbial nitrification and denitrification of nitrogen fertilizers; it is also used as an anesthetic and as a propellant in whipped cream canisters.

Crystal field theory explains the colors and magnetic properties of transition metal complexes by considering the effect of ligand electron repulsion on the energy levels of the metal d-orbitals, splitting them into sets of different energy (Δ). Strong-field ligands (CN⁻, CO) cause large Δ and low-spin configurations with fewer unpaired electrons, while weak-field ligands (F⁻, H₂O) cause small Δ and high-spin configurations with more unpaired electrons, which can be distinguished by magnetic susceptibility measurements.

Self-healing polymers can autonomously repair cracks and damage by releasing encapsulated healing agents or through reversible covalent bonds (Diels-Alder adducts, disulfides) or non-covalent interactions that re-form after damage. Inspired by biological self-repair (bone, skin), these materials are being developed for coatings, flexible electronics, and structural composites where mechanical failure is costly or dangerous.

Methanol fuel cells (direct methanol fuel cells, DMFCs) oxidize liquid methanol electrochemically to CO₂ and water at the anode, generating electricity. They are attractive for portable electronics because methanol can be stored compactly as a liquid; the key challenge is methanol crossover through the Nafion proton-exchange membrane to the cathode, which wastes fuel and poisons the platinum catalyst, limiting current DMFC efficiencies to ~20–30%.

Isotope dilution mass spectrometry (IDMS) is the most accurate quantitative analytical technique, involving the addition of a known amount of an isotopically enriched form of the analyte (the 'spike') to the sample before sample preparation. By measuring the isotope ratio of the mixed spike-sample by mass spectrometry and knowing the spike's isotopic composition and amount added, the original analyte concentration can be calculated with uncertainties below 0.1%; IDMS is the primary method for certifying reference materials for clinical chemistry and environmental monitoring.

Propylene oxide (methyloxirane) is one of the most important industrial epoxides, produced in multi-million tonne quantities annually by the chlorohydrin process or by catalytic oxidation with hydrogen peroxide (HPPO process). It is the precursor to polyether polyols used in polyurethane foams for mattresses, insulation, and automotive seats, and to propylene glycol used as a food additive, antifreeze component, and pharmaceutical excipient.

Tin has the largest number of stable isotopes of any element — ten isotopes with atomic masses from 112 to 124. It also displays two allotropes: white tin (β-Sn, tetragonal metal stable above 13.2 °C) and gray tin (α-Sn, cubic semiconductor stable below 13.2 °C); the transition between them ('tin pest') causes tin objects to crumble to gray powder at cold temperatures, reportedly ruining organ pipes in European cathedrals during severe winters.

Free radical chain reactions proceed in three stages: initiation (generation of a radical, e.g., by heat or light), propagation (radical reacts with substrate to regenerate a new radical, continuing the chain), and termination (two radicals combine to form a stable molecule). In the atmosphere, hydroxyl radicals (•OH) initiate the oxidation of methane and other volatile organic compounds, and a single •OH radical can oxidize thousands of molecules before combining with another radical.

Olefin metathesis is a metal-catalyzed reaction in which carbon-carbon double bonds are redistributed: two alkenes exchange their carbene fragments to form two new alkenes. Developed into a powerful synthetic tool by Chauvin (mechanism), Grubbs (stable ruthenium catalysts), and Schrock (molybdenum catalysts), the reaction earned them the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; ring-closing metathesis is used industrially to produce insect pheromones, polymer precursors, and pharmaceutical intermediates.

Malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) are reactive aldehydes produced by lipid peroxidation — the oxidative degradation of polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes by reactive oxygen species. These products form covalent adducts with proteins and DNA, contributing to aging, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration; the thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) assay measuring MDA is a widely used biomarker of oxidative stress.

Heterogeneous catalysis occurs at the interface between a solid catalyst and a gaseous or liquid reactant, involving adsorption of reactants onto the catalyst surface, bond rearrangement, and desorption of products. The Sabatier principle states that an ideal catalyst should bind adsorbates neither too strongly (blocking active sites) nor too weakly (insufficient activation); this 'Goldilocks' principle is encoded in volcano plots relating catalytic activity to adsorption energy, guiding rational design of new catalysts.

Curium (Cm, Z=96) is the heaviest element named after a person (jointly named after Marie and Pierre Curie), synthesized in 1944 by Seaborg, James, and Ghiorso by bombarding plutonium-239 with helium-4 ions. The most stable isotope, ²⁴⁴Cm (t₁/₂ = 18.1 years), is used as an alpha particle source in the Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) instruments aboard Mars rovers, allowing soil and rock composition to be determined remotely.

Chromatographic separation efficiency is measured by the height equivalent to a theoretical plate (HETP or H), with smaller H indicating a more efficient column. The van Deemter equation H = A + B/u + Cu relates H to linear flow velocity u through three terms: A (Eddy diffusion from multiple flow paths), B (longitudinal diffusion), and C (mass transfer resistance); it predicts an optimal flow velocity at the minimum of H that balances these competing processes.

Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺/NADH) is the most important biological redox cofactor, functioning as a hydride acceptor (forming NADH) in catabolic reactions (glycolysis, Krebs cycle) and as a hydride donor in anabolic reactions. Beyond its redox role, NAD⁺ is the substrate for sirtuins (deacylases that regulate metabolism and longevity) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs, involved in DNA repair), linking cellular energy status to gene regulation and genome maintenance.

Chlorine gas (Cl₂) was the first chemical weapon used in large-scale warfare, deployed by German forces at the Second Battle of Ypres in April 1915. It reacts with water in the lungs to form hydrochloric acid (HCl) and hypochlorous acid (HOCl), destroying tissue. Its characteristic yellow-green color and smell of bleach give brief warning, which is why it was later superseded by colorless, odorless agents such as phosgene (COCl₂).

Rotaxanes and catenanes are mechanically interlocked molecules in which components are held together not by covalent bonds but by physical entanglement — a wheel threaded onto an axle (rotaxane) or two interlocked rings (catenane). Fraser Stoddart and Jean-Pierre Sauvage independently developed synthetic routes to these molecular machines and, together with Ben Feringa, shared the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the design and synthesis of molecular machines.

Cryogenics involves the production and study of materials at very low temperatures, typically below −150 °C (123 K). Liquid helium (boiling point 4.2 K at 1 atm) is the coldest readily available coolant and is essential for maintaining the superconducting magnets in MRI machines (−269 °C), particle accelerators, and quantum computers; helium-3, a rare isotope, allows temperatures as low as 300 mK in dilution refrigerators.

Polycarbonates are tough, transparent thermoplastics made by condensation polymerization of bisphenol A (BPA) and phosgene (or diphenyl carbonate), with carbonate linkages (−OC(O)O−) providing high impact resistance and optical clarity. Polycarbonate is used in eyeglass lenses, bulletproof glass, compact discs, and safety helmets; concern over leaching of BPA (an endocrine disruptor) from polycarbonate food containers has driven development of BPA-free alternatives.

Cis-trans isomerism in alkenes arises because free rotation around a C=C double bond is restricted; substituents on the same side are cis (or Z), and on opposite sides are trans (or E). The photoisomerization of 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal — triggered by a single absorbed photon — is the primary photochemical event of vision in the human eye; this isomerization takes only ~200 femtoseconds, making it one of the fastest biological reactions known.

Potassium superoxide (KO₂) reacts with water and CO₂ in exhaled air to regenerate oxygen, making it useful as a portable breathing medium in submarines and emergency breathing apparatus: 4KO₂ + 2H₂O → 4KOH + 3O₂; 4KOH + 4CO₂ → 4KHCO₃. This unusual O₂⁻ (superoxide) anion, stabilized by the large K⁺ cation, is also a key reactive oxygen species in biological signaling and defense.

Friedel-Crafts alkylation uses an alkyl halide and a Lewis acid (AlCl₃) to introduce an alkyl group onto an aromatic ring. Unlike acylation, it suffers from polyalkylation (the product is more reactive than the starting material) and carbocation rearrangements, which limit its synthetic utility for primary substrates. Nevertheless, it is used on an industrial scale to make ethylbenzene (precursor to styrene for polystyrene) from benzene and ethylene over zeolite catalysts.

Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) from vehicle exhaust react with volatile organic compounds (VOCs) under sunlight to generate ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), the primary irritants in smog. The Los Angeles Basin's geography (mountains trapping air) and car-dependent culture made it the archetypal photochemical smog city; the first identification of the chemistry was made by Haagen-Smit at Caltech in the early 1950s.

Thiols (R−SH) are sulfur analogs of alcohols that form disulfide bonds (R−S−S−R) on oxidation, a process critical in protein biochemistry. The formation and breaking of disulfide bonds between cysteine residues in proteins (catalyzed in the endoplasmic reticulum by protein disulfide isomerase) is essential for the correct folding and stability of secreted proteins such as antibodies, hormones, and extracellular matrix components.

The thermite-like aluminothermic reduction of metal oxides demonstrates the competition between heats of formation of metal oxides: any metal with a more negative standard free energy of formation of its oxide per mole O₂ (lower on the Ellingham diagram) will reduce the oxide of a less reactive metal above it. Aluminum reduces iron, chromium, and manganese oxides; silicon reduces aluminum oxide only above ~1800 °C; and calcium reduces nearly all metal oxides including aluminum oxide.

The Heck reaction (palladium-catalyzed coupling of aryl halides with alkenes in the presence of base) was the first practical palladium-catalyzed C−C bond forming reaction, reported by Richard Heck in 1972. Its mechanism involves oxidative addition of the aryl halide to Pd(0), migratory insertion of the alkene, β-hydride elimination to form the new alkene, and base-assisted regeneration of the Pd(0) catalyst.

Biopolymer CRISPR-Cas9 works by using a guide RNA (gRNA) to direct the Cas9 endonuclease protein to a specific 20-nucleotide DNA sequence matching the gRNA, then making a double-strand break adjacent to a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM). Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this programmable genome editing tool, which is now used in gene therapy, crop improvement, and basic research worldwide.

Silicone rubber (polysiloxane elastomer) has a service temperature range from −60 °C to +230 °C, far superior to organic rubbers, because the Si−O bond (452 kJ/mol) is much stronger than C−C (346 kJ/mol) and the flexible Si−O−Si backbone angle allows very low glass transition temperatures. Medical-grade silicone rubber is used in implants, catheters, sealants, and baby bottle nipples because of its biocompatibility, chemical inertness, and sterilizability.

The Cannizzaro reaction is a disproportionation of non-enolizable aldehydes (lacking α-hydrogens) in strong base, where one molecule is oxidized to a carboxylate salt and another is reduced to an alcohol. Formaldehyde undergoes a crossed Cannizzaro reaction with other aldehydes to give exclusively methanol and the other aldehyde's carboxylate salt; this selectivity is exploited in the industrial synthesis of pentaerythritol from acetaldehyde and excess formaldehyde.

Chloroform (trichloromethane, CHCl₃) was one of the first inhalational anesthetics, introduced into surgical practice by James Young Simpson in 1847. Its anesthetic action is believed to involve potentiation of inhibitory GABA_A receptors in the brain. Chloroform slowly oxidizes in air and light to phosgene (COCl₂), a highly toxic gas, which is why it is stored with 0.5–1% ethanol as a stabilizer and must be tested for phosgene contamination before use.

Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) is a monoamine neurotransmitter synthesized from the amino acid tryptophan via 5-hydroxytryptophan by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase. About 95% of the body's serotonin is found in enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal tract, where it regulates gut motility; only ~5% is in the brain, where it modulates mood, appetite, and sleep — making it the target of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) used to treat depression.

Inorganic polymers include polyphosphazenes (−N=P(R₂)−), polysiloxanes (Si−O backbone), and polycarbosilanes (Si−C backbone), which offer thermal, chemical, and oxidative stability that purely organic polymers cannot match. Polyphosphazenes are of particular interest because the N=P bonds are highly susceptible to nucleophilic substitution by a wide range of organic groups, allowing fine-tuning of properties from hydrophilic biomedical applications to flame-retardant coatings.

Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy detects unpaired electrons in paramagnetic species such as free radicals, transition metal ions, and triplet-state molecules by monitoring the resonant absorption of microwave radiation in an applied magnetic field. EPR is uniquely sensitive to radical intermediates in enzyme mechanisms, oxidative stress in biological tissues, and defects in semiconductor materials, often providing structural information through hyperfine coupling to nearby nuclei.

Galvanic corrosion accelerates the corrosion of a less noble metal when it is in electrical contact with a more noble metal in the presence of an electrolyte, because the less noble metal acts as the anode of a galvanic cell. In marine environments, zinc sacrificial anodes are attached to steel ship hulls and propellers; zinc (standard reduction potential −0.76 V) corrodes preferentially instead of iron (−0.44 V), protecting the structural metal.

Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) lose their magnetization as soon as an external magnetic field is removed (no hysteresis), because thermal energy is sufficient to randomize the magnetic moment of sub-~20 nm iron oxide particles. They are used as MRI contrast agents (shortening T₂ relaxation times), in targeted drug delivery (guided by external magnets to tumor sites), and in magnetic hyperthermia cancer treatment (oscillating magnetic fields heat the particles to destroy tumor cells).

Fumaric acid (trans-butenedioic acid) is a Krebs cycle intermediate produced in the succinic dehydrogenase-catalyzed oxidation of succinate and hydrated by fumarase to form malate. It is also used as a food acidulant (E297), and its esters (fumarates) are employed as fumonisin-free preservatives in animal feed and as pharmaceuticals — dimethyl fumarate (Tecfidera) is an approved multiple sclerosis drug that activates the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway.

Room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) is the emission of light from a triplet excited state at ambient temperature, normally forbidden and quenched by oxygen in solution but achievable in rigid solid-state matrices that slow molecular motion and limit oxygen diffusion. Organic RTP materials with afterglow lasting seconds to minutes are being developed for anti-counterfeiting marks, bioimaging, and optical sensors that are distinct from conventional short-lived fluorescence.

Nitrogen mustards were developed as chemical weapons in World War II by structural analogy to sulfur mustard gas; bis(2-chloroethyl)methylamine was later found to suppress lymphoma growth, becoming mechlorethamine — the first chemotherapy drug approved by the FDA in 1949. These alkylating agents form cross-links between guanine bases in opposing DNA strands, preventing DNA replication in rapidly dividing cancer cells.

Glycine is the simplest and only achiral amino acid, with two hydrogen substituents on the α-carbon, and is the most abundant amino acid in collagen (~35 mol%) where its small size allows it to fit at the inner position of the collagen triple helix. It is also an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem, acting through glycine-gated chloride channels (GlyR) — blocked by the neurotoxin strychnine — to modulate motor and sensory processing.

The Fukuyama coupling uses nickel or palladium catalysis to form C−S bonds between thioesters and organozinc reagents (Reformatsky-type), providing a route to ketones via a thioester intermediate. The Fukuyama disconnection strategy — in which a C−CO bond is retrosynthetically replaced by a C−S (thioester) bond — has been extensively used in the total synthesis of macrolide antibiotics, polyketide natural products, and other complex molecules.

Acid rain forms when sulfur dioxide (SO₂) and nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) from fossil fuel combustion dissolve in atmospheric water droplets to form sulfuric and nitric acids, lowering precipitation pH to 4–5 (vs. natural rain pH ~5.6). Effects include acidification of lakes and rivers (killing aquatic life), leaching of soil nutrients and release of toxic aluminum ions, and corrosion of limestone buildings and marble statues such as the Parthenon.

Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences (TTAGGG in humans) capping chromosomes that shorten with each cell division because DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the 3' end of a linear chromosome. Telomerase, a ribonucleoprotein that uses an RNA template to extend telomeres, is active in germline, stem cells, and most cancers (>85%) but inactive in most somatic cells — Elizabeth Blackburn, Carol Greider, and Jack Szostak discovered telomeres and telomerase, earning the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Superconductors exhibit zero electrical resistance below a critical temperature (Tc) due to the formation of Cooper pairs — pairs of electrons coupled by phonon-mediated lattice vibrations that condense into a macroscopic quantum state described by the BCS theory (Bardeen, Cooper, Schrieffer, 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics). High-temperature superconductors such as yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO, Tc = 93 K) are used in MRI magnets, SQUID magnetometers, and maglev trains.

Ethylene (ethene, C₂H₄) is the most produced organic chemical in the world, with global production exceeding 200 million tonnes per year. It is manufactured by steam cracking of hydrocarbons and is the feedstock for polyethylene, ethylene oxide (for antifreeze and polyesters), vinyl chloride (for PVC), styrene, and ethanol, making it arguably the most economically important organic molecule.

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is the only vitamin that contains a metal atom — cobalt in oxidation state +3, coordinated by a corrin ring (similar to a porphyrin but with one methine bridge absent). Its biosynthesis is the most complex known for a small organic molecule, requiring over 30 enzymatic steps; the total chemical synthesis of vitamin B12 by R.B. Woodward and Albert Eschenmoser in 1972 remains one of the greatest achievements of synthetic organic chemistry.

Boronic acids (R−B(OH)₂) form reversible covalent bonds with 1,2- and 1,3-diols through boronate ester formation, a dynamic covalent reaction that can sense glucose and other polyols selectively. This chemistry is exploited in glucose sensors for diabetics, affinity chromatography resins that capture glycoproteins, and drug delivery systems that release drugs in response to elevated glucose concentrations such as found in tumor environments.

Deuterium (²H or D) is the stable heavy isotope of hydrogen, with one proton and one neutron in the nucleus. Heavy water (D₂O, deuterium oxide) freezes at 3.81 °C (vs. 0 °C for H₂O) and boils at 101.42 °C (vs. 100 °C) due to stronger deuterium bonds; it is used as a neutron moderator in CANDU nuclear reactors and as a solvent in NMR spectroscopy because its NMR signal does not overlap with most common organic solvents.

Capsaicin (8-methyl-N-vanillyl-6-nonenamide) is the compound in chili peppers responsible for the burning sensation, activating the TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1) ion channel that normally responds to heat above ~43 °C and acid. The Scoville scale measures capsaicin concentration in heat units; pure capsaicin scores 16,000,000 SHU, while the Carolina Reaper chili scores over 2,000,000 SHU — about 200× hotter than a jalapeño.

Metal hydrides such as NaH and KH are ionic compounds in which the hydride anion (H⁻) acts as a strong base (but not a strong nucleophile) in organic synthesis, deprotonating acidic C−H bonds (pKa < ~35) to generate carbanions or enolates. Lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) is a more reactive reagent in which four H⁻ ions are coordinated to aluminium; it reduces carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acid derivatives, and even C=N and C=S bonds.

The Lindlar catalyst is a heterogeneous catalyst of palladium deposited on calcium carbonate and poisoned with lead acetate and quinoline, which partially deactivates it so it reduces alkynes to cis-alkenes (but does not further reduce the alkene to an alkane). This selectivity arises because the poisoned surface binds the alkyne strongly enough to reduce it but not the product alkene, making Lindlar catalyst the method of choice for the cis-selective hydrogenation needed in natural product synthesis.

Oxidation state formalism assigns electrons to the more electronegative atom in each bond, giving each atom a formal charge that tracks electron bookkeeping in redox reactions. Carbon's oxidation state ranges from −4 in methane (CH₄, fully reduced) to +4 in carbon dioxide (CO₂, fully oxidized); in biological glucose oxidation, the average carbon oxidation state goes from 0 in glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) to +4 in CO₂, releasing the chemical energy captured originally from sunlight.

Polystyrene-block-poly(ethylene oxide) (PS-b-PEO) block copolymers self-assemble in water into core-shell micelles with a hydrophobic PS core and a hydrophilic PEO corona, or into vesicles (polymersomes) with a PS bilayer membrane enclosing an aqueous lumen. These nanostructures can encapsulate hydrophobic drugs in the core or aqueous cargo in the lumen and are being developed as drug delivery vehicles with improved circulation times over small-molecule drugs.

Selenium is an essential micronutrient that is the twenty-first amino acid (selenocysteine) incorporated into proteins at UGA codons via a specialized translation machinery. The selenoproteins include glutathione peroxidases (antioxidants protecting against oxidative damage), thioredoxin reductases, and iodothyronine deiodinases (activating thyroid hormones); the recommended daily intake is 55 μg/day, but the margin between deficiency and toxicity is narrow (~400 μg/day is the tolerable upper limit).

Perchlorate (ClO₄⁻) is an oxidant so kinetically stable in solution that it is routinely used as a non-coordinating counter-ion in electrochemistry and inorganic synthesis. Ammonium perchlorate (NH₄ClO₄) is the solid oxidizer in solid rocket propellants — mixed with aluminum fuel powder and a polymeric binder, it powers the Space Shuttle solid rocket boosters and many military missiles, releasing HCl, N₂, H₂O, and Al₂O₃ upon combustion.

Gas hydrates (clathrate hydrates) form when small guest molecules such as methane, ethane, CO₂, or H₂S are trapped inside a lattice of hydrogen-bonded water cages at low temperatures and moderate to high pressures. Their formation in deep-sea natural gas pipelines causes blockages that are costly to remove; conversely, CO₂ hydrates are being studied as a way to sequester carbon dioxide permanently in deep ocean sediments by displacing methane from naturally occurring methane hydrate deposits.

The Kolbe electrolysis (1848) is one of the earliest electroorganic reactions: carboxylate anions are oxidized at the anode to carboxyl radicals that rapidly decarboxylate and combine, forming a new C−C bond between two alkyl groups. It was the first synthesis of an organic compound (ethane from acetate) using electricity, and modern variants use platinum electrodes in methanol as solvent to prepare symmetrical and unsymmetrical alkanes, long-chain alkenes, and natural product fragments.

Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a biodegradable semi-crystalline polyester with a melting point of ~60 °C and a glass transition temperature of −60 °C, which is slowly degraded in vivo by hydrolysis of its ester linkages (complete degradation requires 2–4 years). Its very low Tg makes it flexible at body temperature; combined with its biocompatibility, this makes PCL the material of choice for long-term controlled-release drug implants and absorbable sutures.

Mössbauer spectroscopy measures the recoil-free absorption and emission of gamma rays by atomic nuclei in solids, providing information on oxidation state, spin state, and local symmetry of atoms. The ⁵⁷Fe isotope is the most widely used probe (14.4 keV gamma ray), allowing chemists to determine the iron oxidation state and coordination environment in iron-sulfur proteins, cytochromes, iron catalysts, and mineral phases with high sensitivity and precision.

Testosterone is a steroid hormone biosynthesized from cholesterol via pregnenolone, progesterone, androstenediol, and androstenedione. It binds the androgen receptor, a nuclear receptor that dimerizes and acts as a transcription factor upon hormone binding, activating genes for muscle protein synthesis, bone density, and secondary sexual characteristics. Synthetic anabolic steroids structurally related to testosterone are doping agents in sports because they promote skeletal muscle growth.

Zeolite catalysts used in fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) of petroleum are aluminosilicate molecular sieves with acidic Brønsted and Lewis acid sites that protonates and cleaves long hydrocarbon chains into shorter molecules for gasoline and diesel. The Y-zeolite catalyst (FAU topology) dominates FCC; its pore diameter of ~7.4 Å is ideal for cracking the C₂₀–C₄₀ vacuum gas oil molecules while excluding larger asphaltenes that would coke the catalyst.

Photosystem II (PSII) is the membrane protein complex in plants and cyanobacteria that oxidizes two water molecules to molecular oxygen, four protons, and four electrons using the energy of four absorbed photons. The oxygen-evolving complex at the heart of PSII contains a Mn₄CaO₅ cluster that accumulates four oxidizing equivalents through the S-state cycle (Kok cycle, S₀–S₄), releasing O₂ only at the S₄→S₀ transition — the only biological reaction that produces atmospheric oxygen.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) contain five or more principal elements in near-equimolar concentrations, forming a single solid solution phase rather than intermetallic compounds, due to the high configurational entropy stabilizing the solid solution. The Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi) has excellent fracture toughness even at cryogenic temperatures, and some HEAs have corrosion resistances superior to stainless steel; they represent a paradigm shift from traditional alloy design around one principal element.

Thymol (2-isopropyl-5-methylphenol) is a naturally occurring monoterpenoid phenol found in thyme (Thymus vulgaris) that inhibits bacteria by disrupting cell membrane integrity and inhibiting membrane enzymes. It is used as a preservative in mouthwash (Listerine), as an antiseptic in dental care, and as a fungicide in certified organic food production; its biosynthesis in the plant proceeds via the shikimate pathway through p-cymene.

Aniline (C₆H₅NH₂) is the simplest primary aromatic amine and the parent compound of the aniline dye industry that began in 1856 when William Perkin accidentally synthesized the purple dye mauveine while attempting to make quinine. The aniline industry launched the synthetic dye, pharmaceutical, and explosive chemical industries, and the first synthetic drug derived from aniline was acetanilide (1886), the ancestor of paracetamol (acetaminophen).

Reversible addition-fragmentation chain-transfer (RAFT) polymerization is a controlled/living radical polymerization technique that uses a thiocarbonylthio chain-transfer agent (CTA) to give narrow molar mass distributions (dispersity Đ = Mw/Mn < 1.1) and precise control over molecular weight by balancing rapid chain equilibration between active and dormant radical species. RAFT is highly versatile — compatible with most monomers and aqueous conditions — and is used to make complex polymer architectures for drug delivery, coatings, and adhesives.

Ferroelectric materials have a spontaneous electric polarization that can be reversed by an applied electric field, analogous to ferromagnetism. Barium titanate (BaTiO₃) is the archetypal ferroelectric; below its Curie temperature (120 °C) the Ti⁴⁺ ion shifts off-center in its oxygen octahedron, creating a permanent dipole. Ferroelectric materials are used in piezoelectric transducers, capacitors, non-volatile ferroelectric RAM (FeRAM), and medical ultrasound transducers.

The Ugi reaction is a four-component reaction (4-CR) that condenses an amine, a carbonyl compound, an isocyanide, and a carboxylic acid in a single pot to form an α-acylaminoamide product. It is one of the most powerful reactions in combinatorial chemistry, allowing the parallel synthesis of vast libraries of structurally diverse drug-like compounds; combined with post-Ugi transformations, it can deliver complex heterocyclic scaffolds in two or three steps from simple starting materials.

Proton NMR chemical shifts (δ, in ppm) reflect the electronic environment of hydrogen nuclei: protons on sp³ carbons resonate at 0.5–3 ppm, allylic/benzylic protons at 1.5–3.5 ppm, aromatic protons at 6.5–8.5 ppm due to ring current deshielding, and aldehyde protons at 9–10 ppm due to the electron-withdrawing carbonyl. Carboxylic acid OH protons resonate at 10–13 ppm, the most downfield of all common proton types.

Dopamine is a catecholamine neurotransmitter synthesized from tyrosine via DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase (the rate-limiting enzyme). It plays central roles in reward, motivation, and motor control: nigrostriatal dopamine pathways degenerate in Parkinson's disease (causing rigidity and tremor), and mesolimbic dopamine pathways mediate the rewarding effects of food, sex, and addictive drugs. L-DOPA, the immediate precursor to dopamine, crosses the blood-brain barrier and is the primary treatment for Parkinson's disease.

Zwitterionic surfactants carry both a positive charge (quaternary ammonium or amine oxide) and a negative charge (carboxylate, sulfonate, or phosphate) simultaneously, so their net charge is zero but they are highly polar. They are exceptionally mild to skin and eyes compared to anionic surfactants, which is why cocamidopropyl betaine (derived from coconut oil and betaine) is the main surfactant in most baby shampoos and sensitive-skin cleansers.

Anode and cathode designations follow the direction of conventional current: the anode is the electrode at which oxidation occurs, and the cathode is where reduction occurs — regardless of whether the cell is galvanic or electrolytic. In a galvanic cell (battery), the anode is negative; in an electrolytic cell, the anode is the positive electrode connected to the external power supply's positive terminal, which is why the sign convention appears to reverse.

Sickle cell disease is caused by a single nucleotide mutation in the HBB gene that substitutes valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta-globin chain, changing the surface of deoxygenated hemoglobin to expose a hydrophobic patch that promotes intermolecular polymerization into rigid fibers that distort red blood cells into a sickle shape. This is the first 'molecular disease' characterized (Linus Pauling, 1949) and a paradigmatic example of how a single amino acid change in a protein's primary structure can cause profound chemical and physiological consequences.

The trans influence is the thermodynamic weakening of the bond trans to a strongly σ-donating or π-accepting ligand in square-planar and octahedral metal complexes. In Pt(II) square-planar complexes, a hydride (H⁻) trans to a chloride weakens the Pt−Cl bond significantly more than the cis configuration, affecting substitution rates and observed in longer Pt−Cl bond lengths; this effect is distinct from the kinetic trans effect (which describes substitution rate differences).

Caprolactam is the cyclic amide (lactam) monomer for nylon-6, produced industrially from cyclohexanone oxime by the Beckmann rearrangement over sulfuric acid catalyst, which converts the oxime's N−O bond into a C−N amide bond with migration of the anti-carbon. Nylon-6 differs from nylon-6,6 in polymer microstructure and has slightly lower melting point (~220 °C vs. ~265 °C) but higher impact resistance and easier dyeability.

Cholesterol is a sterol that is an essential component of animal cell membranes, where it modulates fluidity by inserting between phospholipid tails to prevent excessive ordering at low temperature and excessive disorder at high temperature. It is the biosynthetic precursor to all steroid hormones (glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, sex hormones), vitamin D₃, and bile acids; despite its bad reputation, every cell in the human body requires cholesterol and synthesizes it via the mevalonate pathway.

Nitrocellulose (guncotton) is produced by nitrating cellulose with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids, introducing up to three nitrate ester groups per glucose unit. Highly nitrated (>12.5% N) nitrocellulose is a powerful propellant used in smokeless powder; less nitrated forms (11–12% N, 'collodion') are used in lacquers, nail polish, and explosives detonators, while low-nitrogen forms are used as waterproof coatings for paper and metal.

Anodizing is an electrolytic passivation process that thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminum alloys from ~4 nm to 5–25 μm (standard) or 25–150 μm (hard anodize) by making the aluminum the anode in a sulfuric or chromic acid bath. The porous anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) layer formed in phosphoric or oxalic acid has precisely controlled nanopore diameters (10–200 nm) that are used as templates for growing carbon nanotubes, nanowires, and nanodots.

Pinacol rearrangement is an acid-catalyzed 1,2-shift in which a 1,2-diol is dehydrated to a carbocation that undergoes migration of an adjacent carbon or hydride to give a carbonyl compound. Named after pinacol (2,3-dimethyl-2,3-butanediol), the reaction provides access to sterically hindered ketones such as pinacolone (3,3-dimethyl-2-butanone) and is a classic example of a 1,2-alkyl shift in organic chemistry.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless toxic gas that binds hemoglobin with an affinity 210 times greater than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen. CO toxicity causes tissue hypoxia; treatment involves breathing 100% oxygen, which displaces CO from hemoglobin due to the mass action effect (t₁/₂ for CO elimination drops from ~5 hours on room air to ~60 minutes on 100% O₂). CO is also an industrially important feedstock for the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis of hydrocarbons from syngas (CO + H₂).

The Hunsdiecker reaction (also known as the Borodin reaction) converts silver carboxylate salts to alkyl bromides one carbon shorter by reaction with elemental bromine via a radical chain mechanism. The reaction involves formation of a silver acylhypobromite intermediate, which homolyzes to a carboxyl radical that decarboxylates to give an alkyl radical, then abstracts bromine from the brominating agent. It is one of the classic methods for chain shortening in organic synthesis.

Acrolein (propenal, CH₂=CHCHO) is the simplest α,β-unsaturated aldehyde and one of the most reactive small molecules in chemistry; it is a Michael acceptor that reacts readily with biological nucleophiles (thiols, amines) in DNA and proteins. It is produced by combustion of wood, tobacco, and cooking oils (especially when overheated), and is a major contributor to the cytotoxicity of cigarette smoke; industrially it is an important precursor to acrylic acid.

Nicotinic acid (niacin, vitamin B₃) is a precursor to NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ and an essential human micronutrient. Pellagra — characterized by the '4 Ds': dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death — results from severe niacin deficiency and was epidemic in the American South in the early 20th century among populations subsisting on corn (maize), in which niacin is bound to hemicellulose and unavailable unless the corn is treated with alkali (nixtamalization), a process traditional in Mesoamerican cultures.

The Wolff-Kishner reduction reduces carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones) to alkanes using hydrazine and strong base (KOH) at high temperature. The mechanism proceeds through a hydrazone intermediate that undergoes base-catalyzed tautomerization and loss of N₂ to give the alkane; together with the Clemmensen reduction (Zn(Hg)/HCl), it is one of the two classical methods for removing the carbonyl oxygen from ketones — Wolff-Kishner uses base, Clemmensen uses acid.

White phosphorus (P₄) consists of four phosphorus atoms arranged in a tetrahedron with P−P−P bond angles of only 60°, far below the preferred ~90° for p-orbital overlap, causing extreme ring strain and making P₄ extremely reactive toward air and oxygen. It ignites spontaneously in air above ~34 °C, glows in the dark (phosphorescence caused by slow gas-phase oxidation), and was used in incendiary weapons until banned by international convention.

Cyclodextrins are cyclic oligomers of α-D-glucopyranose connected by α-1,4 bonds, forming a truncated cone with a hydrophobic cavity and hydrophilic exterior. Alpha-cyclodextrin (6 units, cavity ~5 Å), beta-cyclodextrin (7 units, ~6.5 Å), and gamma-cyclodextrin (8 units, ~8.3 Å) selectively encapsulate guest molecules by size; beta-cyclodextrin is used to encapsulate drugs, flavors, and pesticides to improve solubility, stability, and bioavailability.

Sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆) is a colorless, odorless, non-toxic gas with an octahedral structure and extraordinary chemical and thermal stability due to the strength and steric protection of the six S−F bonds. It is the best electrical insulator known, used in high-voltage circuit breakers and transformers at ~6× atmospheric pressure; however, it is an extremely potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential 23,500 times that of CO₂ over 100 years and an atmospheric lifetime of over 3,000 years.

Glutathione (γ-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinyl-glycine, GSH) is the most abundant intracellular antioxidant, present at 1–10 mM in most cells. Its thiol group (−SH) donates electrons to reduce reactive oxygen species, forming oxidized glutathione (GSSG), which is regenerated by glutathione reductase using NADPH; the GSH/GSSG ratio is a key indicator of cellular redox status and oxidative stress, and depletion of glutathione occurs in cancer, Parkinson's disease, and aging.

Liquid crystals are states of matter that flow like liquids but possess orientational order like crystals; in nematic liquid crystals the rod-like molecules align along a common director axis but lack positional order. Twisted nematic (TN) liquid crystal displays (LCDs) exploit the realignment of the liquid crystal director by an electric field to modulate polarized light and create images; this technology won Sharp and Hoffmann-La Roche engineers the 2019 European Inventor Award and has enabled the flat screen revolution.

Carboplatin and oxaliplatin are second- and third-generation platinum-based anticancer drugs designed to overcome the nephrotoxicity and the acquired resistance of cisplatin. They all work by forming 1,2-intrastrand d(GpG) crosslinks on DNA through bifunctional reaction of the two labile ligands with adjacent guanines, blocking replication; oxaliplatin (with a 1,2-diaminocyclohexane carrier ligand) is active against cisplatin-resistant colorectal tumors because its bulkier adducts evade mismatch repair.

Photosensitive silver halide emulsions (AgCl, AgBr, AgI) form the basis of traditional photographic film: photons excite electrons in the silver halide crystal that are captured at surface defects to create a latent image of a few silver atoms; chemical development with hydroquinone or other reducing agents amplifies each latent site up to 10⁹ times by reducing all nearby Ag⁺ to Ag⁰, while fixer (sodium thiosulfate) dissolves unexposed silver halide to stabilize the image.

Menthol is a cyclic monoterpene alcohol found in peppermint and other Mentha oils that activates the TRPM8 cold receptor in sensory neurons at temperatures below ~25 °C, creating a cooling sensation even at room temperature without actual temperature change. This same receptor activation explains why menthol cigarettes feel smoother — the cooling effect masks irritation — yet the biological effects of nicotine and carcinogens are unchanged or enhanced.

Hydrogels are three-dimensional cross-linked polymer networks that can absorb and retain up to 1000× their dry weight in water, while remaining insoluble due to the cross-links. Polyacrylamide hydrogels are used in gel electrophoresis and contact lenses; polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels are used in tissue engineering scaffolds; and superabsorbent polyacrylate hydrogels (SAP) absorb 300–800× their weight in water and are the active material in baby diapers, capable of absorbing ~30 g of liquid per gram of polymer.

Tetrahedral intermediates form during nucleophilic acyl substitution reactions when a nucleophile attacks a planar sp²-hybridized carbonyl carbon, temporarily converting it to a tetrahedral sp³ center. The subsequent collapse of this intermediate — expelling the leaving group — accounts for the relative reactivity order of acyl derivatives: acid chlorides react fastest, followed by anhydrides, then esters and carboxylic acids, and amides react slowest because the nitrogen lone pair stabilizes the carbonyl through resonance.

Sodium lauryl sulfate (SDS, sodium dodecyl sulfate) is an anionic surfactant that is the most widely used detergent in personal care products (shampoos, toothpastes, body washes). Its 12-carbon alkyl chain and charged head group give it excellent foaming properties; at concentrations above its critical micelle concentration (~8 mM), SDS forms micelles that solubilize oily residues from hair and skin. SDS is also the denaturant used in SDS-PAGE gel electrophoresis.

The Menshutkin reaction is the quaternization of a tertiary amine with an alkyl halide to form a quaternary ammonium salt — a formally SN2 reaction at carbon — named after Nikolai Menshutkin who in 1890 performed systematic studies showing reaction rate depends strongly on solvent polarity. It is one of the first reactions shown to be profoundly affected by solvent, initiating the field of solvent effects in organic chemistry.

Oxytocin is a cyclic nonapeptide hormone and neurotransmitter — the first polypeptide hormone to be sequenced and synthesized (Vincent du Vigneaud, 1953 Nobel Prize in Chemistry). It is released by the posterior pituitary gland during childbirth to stimulate uterine contractions and during breastfeeding to trigger milk letdown, and also acts in the brain to promote social bonding, trust, and pair bonding, giving it the popular name 'the love hormone.'

Photocatalytic degradation of organic pollutants uses semiconductor photocatalysts (most commonly TiO₂ under UV irradiation) to generate hydroxyl radicals (•OH) and superoxide radical anions (O₂•⁻) that attack and mineralize organic contaminants to CO₂, H₂O, and inorganic ions. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) based on TiO₂ photocatalysis can degrade pharmaceutical residues, pesticides, and industrial dyes that resist conventional wastewater treatment, with no residual byproducts.

Chromatin is the complex of DNA and histone proteins in the cell nucleus; DNA wraps ~1.65 times around an octamer of histone proteins (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4) to form a nucleosome — the fundamental packaging unit. Epigenetic modifications — acetylation of lysine residues on histone tails (opens chromatin, activates transcription) and methylation of lysine residues (can activate or repress, depending on position) — constitute a 'histone code' that regulates gene expression without altering DNA sequence.

The Baylis-Hillman reaction forms C−C bonds between the α-carbon of an activated alkene (acrylate, acrylonitrile) and an aldehyde in the presence of a tertiary amine catalyst (DABCO or DMAP). It is a green reaction (atom-economical, no metal required, often performed in water) and the product β-hydroxy-α-methylene carbonyl compound contains multiple functional groups for further diversification, making it a powerful tool in the synthesis of densely functionalized molecules.

Germanium was predicted by Mendeleev in 1871 as 'eka-silicon' (one place below silicon in the periodic table) before its discovery in 1886 by Clemens Winkler, providing one of the strongest validations of the periodic table. Today germanium's semiconductor properties (band gap 0.67 eV, vs. Si's 1.12 eV) are used in infrared optics (transparent to 1.8–12 μm), fiber optic waveguide cores (germanium-doped silica), and high-efficiency triple-junction solar cells for satellites.

Methylmercury (CH₃Hg⁺) is a highly toxic organomercury compound formed by microbial methylation of inorganic mercury in aquatic sediments and bioaccumulated through aquatic food chains, reaching concentrations up to 10⁷ times that of the surrounding water in large predatory fish. It crosses the blood-brain barrier and the placenta via neutral amino acid transporters (mimicking methionine), causing devastating neurological damage; the mass poisoning in Minamata, Japan (1956) — caused by industrial mercury discharge — was the seminal environmental chemistry disaster.

Quantum chemistry calculations using density functional theory (DFT) approximate the many-body electron correlation energy as a functional of the electron density, dramatically reducing computational cost compared to wavefunction-based methods (HF, MP2, CCSD). The B3LYP functional (Becke three-parameter exchange + Lee-Yang-Parr correlation) became the most widely cited DFT method after the mid-1990s; Walter Kohn (who developed DFT) and John Pople (who implemented DFT computationally) shared the 1998 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Acetaldehyde (ethanal, CH₃CHO) is produced in the body from ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase and is primarily responsible for the symptoms of a hangover — flushing, nausea, and headache — because it accumulates when aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2) is overwhelmed or genetically slow. About 36% of East Asians carry a dominant-negative ALDH2*2 allele that renders ALDH2 nearly inactive, causing the 'alcohol flush reaction' and increased risk of esophageal cancer with alcohol consumption.

Electroplating deposits a thin metal layer onto a substrate by making the substrate the cathode in an electrolytic cell containing a soluble salt of the plating metal. Nickel plating requires ~60% current efficiency; chromium plating (decorative or hard chrome) uses Cr(VI) in sulfuric acid at current densities of 150–5000 A/m², but Cr(VI) is a carcinogen, driving replacement by Cr(III) trivalent chrome plating processes and physical vapor deposition for decorative coatings.

The Fischer indole synthesis is the most widely used method to prepare indoles — the core scaffold of the neurotransmitter serotonin, the amino acid tryptophan, and hundreds of alkaloids. It involves acid-catalyzed [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of an arylhydrazone intermediate followed by elimination of ammonia; the reaction is highly reliable and can be performed with a wide variety of arylhydrazines and carbonyl compounds to access diverse indole substitution patterns.

Ruthenium(II) polypyridyl complexes, particularly [Ru(bpy)₃]²⁺ (where bpy = 2,2'-bipyridine), are the quintessential photoredox catalysts because they absorb visible light strongly (ε ~14,000 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ at 452 nm), have long-lived triplet excited states (~600 ns in degassed solution), and can act as either single-electron donors or acceptors from their excited state. This versatility has driven an explosion of visible-light-mediated synthetic transformations — C−H functionalization, radical cyclizations, and dehalogenation reactions — that are impossible under purely thermal conditions.

Poloxamers (e.g., Pluronic F127) are ABA-type block copolymers of poly(propylene oxide) (PPO) flanked by two poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) blocks that exhibit reverse thermal gelation: they are liquid at low temperatures and form a gel at body temperature because PPO blocks become hydrophobic above ~15 °C and drive micelle packing into a cubic lattice. This property makes poloxamer gels useful as injectable, temperature-responsive drug delivery depots.

Bromine is the only non-metallic element that is liquid at room temperature and pressure (melting point −7.3 °C, boiling point 58.8 °C). It is extracted from seawater (which contains ~65 mg/L) by oxidizing bromide ions with chlorine, then steam-stripping the bromine vapor; Israel and Jordan, which have access to the highly bromide-rich Dead Sea brine (~12 g/L), produce a large fraction of the world's bromine.

The transmetalation step in palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions transfers the organic group from a main-group metal (boron in Suzuki, tin in Stille, zinc in Negishi) to the palladium center, forming a diorganopalladium species that undergoes reductive elimination to give the cross-coupled product and regenerate Pd(0). The choice of transmetalating metal dictates functional-group tolerance, reactivity, and environmental impact — boronic acids (Suzuki) are the least toxic and most stable option.

Photosynthetic antenna systems harvest photons over a broad spectral range and funnel excitation energy with near-unity efficiency to the reaction center through coherent excitation energy transfer among tightly packed pigment molecules. The FMO (Fenna-Matthews-Olson) complex in green sulfur bacteria, containing 7–8 bacteriochlorophyll molecules, was the first antenna complex whose structure was solved by X-ray crystallography (1975) and is a model system for studying quantum coherence in biology.

Mauveine, the first synthetic dye, was accidentally made by William Henry Perkin in 1856 at age 18 while attempting to synthesize quinine from aniline by oxidation with potassium dichromate. The purple residue stained silk brilliantly and was color-fast — launching the synthetic dye industry and establishing organic chemistry as a commercially important science. Perkin patented the process and became a wealthy manufacturer before returning to academic research.

Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) subjects ions to two stages of mass analysis: the first stage selects a precursor ion of interest, a collision cell fragments it with inert gas (helium or argon), and the second stage analyses the product ions. The fragmentation pattern allows sequencing of peptides (reading off b-ions from N-terminus and y-ions from C-terminus), identifying metabolites, and confirming the identity of drugs and environmental contaminants with high specificity.

The Sharpless 'click chemistry' concept (2001) defined a set of reactions that are modular, wide in scope, high yielding, near-stereospecific, and can be conducted under mild conditions. The CuI-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC, the 'gold standard' click reaction) forms a 1,4-disubstituted 1,2,3-triazole from an azide and a terminal alkyne with complete regioselectivity; K. Barry Sharpless, Morten Meldal, and Carolyn Bertozzi received the 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing click chemistry.

Manganese dioxide (MnO₂) is the active positive electrode material in the common alkaline battery, reduced to MnOOH (then Mn(OH)₂) as zinc is oxidized at the anode. Natural MnO₂ (pyrolusite) was historically used as an oxidant in glass making to decolorize glass tinted green by iron impurities, and the reaction of MnO₂ with HCl to produce Cl₂ gas was Scheele's original method of discovering chlorine in 1774.

Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) hydrolyze the 3',5'-cyclic phosphodiester bond in cyclic AMP (cAMP) and cyclic GMP (cGMP), terminating second messenger signaling. Sildenafil (Viagra) inhibits PDE5 specifically in smooth muscle of the penis and pulmonary vasculature, preventing cGMP degradation; elevated cGMP activates protein kinase G, which phosphorylates and relaxes smooth muscle, increasing blood flow.

Sodium alginate, extracted from brown algae cell walls, is a polysaccharide of β-D-mannuronic acid and α-L-guluronic acid residues that gels instantaneously when exposed to divalent calcium ions (Ca²⁺), which cross-link adjacent guluronate-rich blocks. This property is used in molecular gastronomy 'spherification' to create liquid-filled spheres; in tissue engineering as a cell-encapsulation hydrogel; and industrially as a food thickener (E401) in ice cream and yogurt.

The Reformatsky-type reactions and related organometallic additions demonstrate the Cram-Felkin-Anh model for stereochemical prediction of nucleophilic addition to α-chiral carbonyl compounds: the nucleophile attacks anti to the largest group (L) on the α-carbon, giving a preferred diastereomer. This model, superseding Cram's simpler rule, correctly predicts facial selectivity for a wide range of nucleophiles and substrates and is a cornerstone of predictive stereochemistry.

Gas-phase infrared spectroscopy identifies molecules by the pattern of vibrational modes (stretching and bending of bonds) that absorb specific infrared wavelengths. The IR spectrum is often called a molecular 'fingerprint' because the complex combination of all vibrational modes below 1500 cm⁻¹ (the fingerprint region) is unique to each molecule; characteristic group frequencies (e.g., C=O stretch at 1700–1750 cm⁻¹, O−H stretch at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹) allow rapid identification of functional groups.

Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is a metalloenzyme that catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide radical anion (O₂•⁻) to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen: 2 O₂•⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O₂ + O₂. Eukaryotic SOD1 (Cu,Zn-SOD) operates in the cytoplasm and intermembrane space; SOD2 (Mn-SOD) in mitochondria; and SOD3 (Cu,Zn-SOD) is secreted. Mutations in SOD1 cause about 20% of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), implicating oxidative stress in the disease.

Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) is the monomer of natural rubber (polyisoprene), emitted in massive quantities by many tree species as a volatile secondary metabolite — an estimated 600 million tonnes per year globally, exceeding all anthropogenic hydrocarbon emissions. In the atmosphere, isoprene is oxidized by •OH radicals and contributes to the formation of secondary organic aerosols and ground-level ozone in forested regions.

Nuclear fission releases energy when a heavy nucleus (U-235, Pu-239) absorbs a neutron and splits into two lighter fission products plus 2–3 new neutrons and ~200 MeV of energy, mostly as kinetic energy of the fission fragments. The energy density of uranium fission (~80 million MJ/kg) exceeds that of chemical combustion of coal by a factor of ~2.5 million — which is why a single uranium fuel pellet the size of a fingertip contains as much energy as 3 barrels of oil.

The Ramberg–Bäcklund rearrangement converts α-halo sulfones to alkenes by an intramolecular SN2-type displacement forming a three-membered episulfone intermediate, which spontaneously loses SO₂ to yield the olefin. The reaction is notable for introducing a C=C bond at the position previously occupied by two C−S bonds, making it a valuable chain-shortening and alkene-forming strategy in natural product synthesis.

Lanthanide luminescence uses the sharp, 4f–4f forbidden electronic transitions of Eu³⁺, Tb³⁺, Nd³⁺, and other lanthanide ions to produce intensely narrow emission lines with long luminescence lifetimes (microseconds to milliseconds). Time-gated detection after direct excitation or sensitization through an organic 'antenna' chromophore eliminates background autofluorescence, making lanthanide chelates ideal labels for time-resolved fluoroimmunoassays (TRFIA) in diagnostics and biological imaging.

The Born equation estimates the Gibbs free energy of solvation of an ion of charge z and radius r in a medium of dielectric constant ε: ΔG_solv = −(z²e²)/(8πε₀r)(1 − 1/ε). It predicts that smaller, more highly charged ions have larger (more negative) solvation energies, which is why F⁻ is more strongly hydrated than I⁻ (despite being less polarizable) and why Li⁺ is more strongly hydrated than Cs⁺.

Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is a hormone synthesized from serotonin by the pineal gland exclusively during darkness, signaling the sleep-wake cycle to the brain and peripheral tissues through MT1 and MT2 G-protein-coupled receptors. Its synthesis requires acetylation of serotonin by arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT, the rate-limiting step), then methylation by acetylserotonin methyltransferase; light suppresses AANAT expression via the suprachiasmatic nucleus within minutes.

Carbonyl sulfide (OCS) is the most abundant sulfur-containing gas in the atmosphere (about 500 ppt by volume), released by ocean biology, volcanoes, and biomass burning. It reaches the stratosphere largely unchanged (unlike SO₂, which is removed in the troposphere) and is oxidized by OH there to SO₂ and ultimately to H₂SO₄, contributing to the stratospheric sulfate aerosol layer (Junge layer) that reflects incoming solar radiation and affects climate.

Trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (triflic acid, CF₃SO₃H) is one of the strongest Brønsted acids known (pKa ~ −14 in water, Hammett H₀ ~ −14), stronger than sulfuric acid, due to the strong electron-withdrawing effect of the CF₃ group stabilizing the triflate anion. The triflate anion (TfO⁻) is also one of the weakest coordinating anions, making it an excellent counter-ion for generating highly reactive cationic metal catalysts and reactive electrophiles in synthesis.

The nucleobase pairing rules (Watson-Crick base pairs) in DNA — adenine pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, guanine pairs with cytosine via three — arise from the complementary pattern of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors on each base in the anti conformation. The three G−C hydrogen bonds make G−C-rich regions of DNA more thermally stable (higher Tm) than A−T-rich regions, which is why the denaturation temperature of a DNA duplex increases approximately 4 °C per %G+C.

Infrared atmospheric window refers to the wavelength region (~8–13 μm) where Earth's atmosphere is largely transparent to outgoing longwave radiation, allowing the planet to cool. Carbon dioxide absorbs at 15 μm and water vapor absorbs at other wavelengths, but the 8–13 μm window is partially open; N₂O, CH₄, and man-made gases like SF₆ and HFCs absorb precisely in this window region, making them potent greenhouse gases despite low atmospheric concentrations.

Copper(I) iodide (CuI) in combination with a diamine ligand is the Buchwald copper catalyst system for C−N, C−O, and C−S bond formation, providing a much cheaper alternative to palladium for coupling reactions involving amines, alcohols, and thiols with aryl iodides. Copper-catalyzed Ullmann-type couplings were first reported in 1903, predating palladium catalysis by 70 years, but poor scope and harsh conditions limited their use until mild ligands were developed in the 2000s.
