Acetyl-CoA is the pivotal metabolic intermediate that connects carbohydrate, fat, and amino acid catabolism to energy production in the Krebs cycle; it is also the building block for fatty acid and steroid biosynthesis. Its thioester bond (between the acetyl group and coenzyme A) has a high free energy of hydrolysis (~31 kJ/mol), making it a 'high-energy' metabolic intermediate that can drive otherwise unfavorable biosynthetic condensation reactions.

Homogeneous catalysts operate in the same phase as the reactants, offering high selectivity and activity, but require separation from the product at the end. The Wilkinson catalyst [RhCl(PPh₃)₃] was the first highly active homogeneous hydrogenation catalyst for terminal alkenes at room temperature and 1 atm H₂; mechanistic studies of its oxidative addition/migratory insertion/reductive elimination pathway by Geoffrey Wilkinson and John Osborn in 1965 laid the foundation for all of modern homogeneous transition-metal catalysis.

Thalidomide was prescribed as a sedative and antiemetic for morning sickness in Europe from 1957–1961, causing severe birth defects (phocomelia) in ~10,000 children because the (R)-enantiomer is teratogenic while the (S)-enantiomer is the active sedative — and even when (S)-thalidomide is given, it racemizes in vivo at physiological pH. This tragedy led directly to modern stereospecific drug approval regulations and the requirement to test both enantiomers of chiral drugs.

Molecular orbital (MO) theory describes chemical bonding by combining atomic orbitals into linear combinations that belong to the symmetry operations of the molecule. The bonding–antibonding framework explains why O₂ is paramagnetic (two unpaired electrons in degenerate π* antibonding orbitals) while N₂ is diamagnetic, and why the bond order of O₂ is 2 and N₂ is 3; valence bond theory, in contrast, incorrectly predicts O₂ to be diamagnetic.

Palytoxin, isolated from soft coral (Palythoa) and first characterized by Richard Moore in 1981, is one of the most complex and toxic natural products known: it has a molecular formula C₁₂₉H₂₂₃N₃O₅₄, 71 stereocenters (2⁷¹ ≈ 10²¹ possible stereoisomers), and a molecular weight of ~2,678 Da. It acts by locking the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in an open channel conformation, disrupting ion gradients in all cells, and has an LD₅₀ in mice of ~0.15 μg/kg.

Titanocene dichloride (Cp₂TiCl₂) was one of the first metallocene complexes tested as an anticancer agent (1970s) as structural analogs to cisplatin, but failed in clinical trials due to poor water solubility and insufficient activity. It did, however, establish that metals beyond platinum can have anticancer activity, and study of titanocene chemistry opened the field of non-platinum anticancer metallodrugs now including ruthenium, gold, and copper complexes in clinical trials.

Nitrogen fixation by the enzyme nitrogenase converts atmospheric N₂ to ammonia (N₂ + 8H⁺ + 8e⁻ + 16 ATP → 2NH₃ + H₂ + 16 ADP + 16 Pi), a reaction requiring cleavage of the exceptionally strong N≡N triple bond (945 kJ/mol). The iron-molybdenum cofactor (FeMo-co) of nitrogenase — a [Mo:7Fe:9S:C] cluster — is the active site where N₂ binds and is reduced by six sequential proton-coupled electron transfers; understanding its mechanism is a key goal for developing synthetic nitrogen fixation catalysts.

Glucose sensors most commonly use glucose oxidase (GOx), an FAD-containing enzyme that oxidizes glucose to gluconolactone with transfer of two electrons to a mediator or electrode, generating a current proportional to glucose concentration. Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) now used by millions of diabetics measure this electrochemical signal from a glucose oxidase sensor inserted subcutaneously, providing real-time glucose readings every 1–5 minutes without finger-prick blood sampling.

The Reppe reactions are a family of chemical transformations developed by Walter Reppe at BASF in the 1930s-40s that use acetylene under pressure with transition-metal catalysts to produce important industrial chemicals: carbonylation gives acrylic acid from acetylene, CO, and water; cyclotrimerization of acetylene over nickel catalysts gives benzene; and vinylation adds acetylene to alcohols to give vinyl ethers. They enabled large-scale production of these chemicals from acetylene when coal-based chemistry dominated.

Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic produced by Amycolatopsis orientalis that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding tightly (Kd ~10⁻⁶ M) to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, preventing transpeptidation. It was the 'antibiotic of last resort' for decades, but vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) emerged when bacteria acquired genes (vanA) that replace D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac, lowering affinity by 1000-fold.

Coenzyme A (CoA) is a thiol-containing cofactor derived from pantothenate (vitamin B₅), cysteine, and ATP that forms high-energy thioester bonds with acyl groups, activating them for transfer in biosynthesis and degradation. In fatty acid synthesis, malonyl-CoA is the two-carbon extender unit; in fatty acid oxidation, acetyl-CoA units are sequentially released; and in the Krebs cycle, succinyl-CoA is a key intermediate — making CoA a central hub of carbon metabolism.

Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body, with ~1 kg present in an adult (99% in hydroxyapatite in bones and teeth). Calcium ion (Ca²⁺) is also the most versatile intracellular second messenger: transient rises in cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ from nanomolar to micromolar concentrations (released from the endoplasmic reticulum via IP₃ receptors or entered through plasma membrane channels) trigger muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release, fertilization, gene expression, and apoptosis.

Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) operate at 600–1000 °C, using a dense ceramic electrolyte (yttria-stabilized zirconia, YSZ) that conducts oxide ions (O²⁻) from cathode to anode. At the anode, fuel (H₂ or hydrocarbons) is oxidized electrochemically by oxide ions; the high operating temperature allows internal reforming of natural gas, eliminates the need for precious metal catalysts at the anode, and gives electrical efficiencies of 50–65% in combined heat and power applications.

Acetal resin (polyoxymethylene, POM) is an engineering thermoplastic formed by the homopolymerization of formaldehyde or copolymerization with dioxolane, with a molecular structure of alternating −CH₂−O− units that give high crystallinity, rigidity, and excellent dimensional stability. POM (sold as Delrin by DuPont and Celcon by Celanese) is used for precision gears, bearings, fasteners, and knife handles because it has a coefficient of friction similar to lubricated metal-on-metal.

Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is the universal energy currency of cells, storing chemical energy in its two phosphoanhydride bonds (ΔG°' of hydrolysis = −30.5 kJ/mol each). The human body turns over its own body weight in ATP (~40 kg) every day through a combination of oxidative phosphorylation (producing ~34 ATP per glucose), substrate-level phosphorylation (2 ATP per glucose in glycolysis), and the adenylate kinase reaction; at rest, the body's total ATP pool is only ~250 g.

Molybdenum cofactor (Moco) is essential for all kingdoms of life and contains a molybdopterin (MPT) ligand that coordinates the molybdenum through two sulfur atoms. Enzymes using Moco include sulfite oxidase (which converts toxic SO₃²⁻ to sulfate), xanthine oxidase (purine catabolism), and nitrate reductase (plant nitrogen assimilation); humans cannot synthesize Moco without the MOCS1 and MOCS2 genes, and genetic deficiency of Moco biosynthesis causes severe neonatal encephalopathy.

Xenon difluoride (XeF₂) and xenon tetrafluoride (XeF₄) were among the first noble gas compounds synthesized, following Neil Bartlett's 1962 preparation of [O₂⁺][PtF₆⁻], which demonstrated that xenon (with a similar ionization energy to O₂) should also react with PtF₆. These discoveries overturned the prevailing dogma that noble gases are entirely chemically inert and earned Bartlett wide recognition; today over 100 xenon compounds are known.

The Paternò-Büchi reaction is a [2+2] photocycloaddition between a carbonyl compound and an alkene, producing an oxetane ring. The reaction proceeds through the triplet excited state of the carbonyl compound, which adds to the alkene in a stepwise diradical mechanism; the resulting four-membered ring is found in natural products such as penaresidins (antifungal agents from sea sponges) and is used to install oxetane motifs that improve the metabolic stability of pharmaceutical candidates.

The Keeling Curve is the longest continuous record of atmospheric CO₂ concentration, started by Charles David Keeling at Mauna Loa Observatory in 1958. In 1958, the concentration was 316 ppm; by June 2023 it exceeded 424 ppm — a 34% increase driven predominantly by fossil fuel combustion. The annual 6–8 ppm seasonal oscillation superimposed on the rising trend reflects the 'breathing' of the terrestrial biosphere as Northern Hemisphere vegetation fixes CO₂ in summer and releases it in winter.

Electroosmotic flow (EOF) in capillary electrophoresis arises when the silanol groups on the fused silica capillary wall are deprotonated at pH > ~4, creating a negatively charged surface that attracts a diffuse layer of cations; application of the electric field drags this electrical double layer and the bulk solution toward the cathode with a flat (plug) flow profile. EOF allows simultaneous separation of cations, neutrals (separated by size), and even anions (if their electrophoretic mobility is less than EOF velocity) in a single run.

Berberine is a quaternary ammonium isoquinoline alkaloid with a bright yellow color found in barberry, goldenseal, and coptis roots that has been used in traditional medicine for 3000 years. Modern pharmacology has shown it activates AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase), lowering blood glucose and lipids through mechanisms similar to metformin; it also intercalates into DNA, inhibits bacterial topoisomerases, and has antimicrobial activity against MRSA.

Biuret test is a colorimetric assay for proteins that gives a purple color when Cu²⁺ ions in alkaline solution form coordinate bonds with the nitrogen atoms of peptide bonds (–CONH–), producing a flat square-planar Cu²⁺–peptide complex that absorbs at 540–560 nm. The color intensity is directly proportional to the number of peptide bonds (and thus protein concentration), making it a simple protein quantification method; the test gets its name from biuret (H₂N–CO–NH–CO–NH₂), the first compound shown to give this color.

Furans are aromatic five-membered heterocyclic rings containing an oxygen atom; they are less aromatic than benzene (resonance energy ~67 kJ/mol vs. ~150 kJ/mol for benzene) because the oxygen lone pair participates in the π system, making the ring electron-rich and susceptible to electrophilic substitution at C2 and C5. Furfural, derived from the dehydration of agricultural pentose sugars (oat husks, corn cobs), is an important bio-based platform chemical for making solvents, pharmaceuticals, and polymers.

Chiral HPLC stationary phases (e.g., polysaccharide-derived cellulose tris(3,5-dimethylphenylcarbamate) coated on silica, sold as Chiralcel OD) separate enantiomers based on differential formation of transient diastereomeric complexes between the chiral stationary phase and each enantiomer through a combination of hydrogen bonding, π−π stacking, and steric interactions. Preparative chiral HPLC is the dominant method for obtaining kilogram-scale batches of enantiopure drug substances that are too complex to synthesize asymmetrically.

Nuclear fusion releases energy when two light nuclei merge into a heavier nucleus; the D-T reaction (deuterium + tritium → helium-4 + neutron + 17.6 MeV) is the most accessible fusion reaction because it has the highest cross-section at 'only' ~100 million °C. The energy density of fusion fuel is ~40 million MJ/kg of D-T fuel — about 10 million times that of coal — and the primary fuel (deuterium from seawater) is essentially inexhaustible.

Tantalum is a blue-grey refractory metal (melting point 3017 °C) that forms an exceptionally stable, self-repairing Ta₂O₅ oxide layer that resists attack by nearly all acids except hydrofluoric acid and hot concentrated alkali. Because of its biocompatibility (it is biologically inert and not rejected by the body), tantalum is used in implantable devices such as skull plates, surgical clips, and stents; its high atomic number also makes it useful as an X-ray contrast agent in some medical procedures.

Green fluorescent protein (GFP) was isolated from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria by Osamu Shimomura in 1962 and developed as a genetic tag by Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien; all three shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. GFP's chromophore is formed post-translationally from residues Ser65-Tyr66-Gly67 by spontaneous cyclization, dehydration, and oxidation, producing the p-hydroxybenzylideneimidazolinone chromophore that absorbs at 395 nm and emits at 509 nm without any added cofactor.

Polysorbates (Tween series) are polyoxyethylene sorbitan fatty acid esters used as non-ionic emulsifiers in foods, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetics. Polysorbate 80 (Tween 80), with ~20 ethylene oxide units and an oleic acid ester, has an HLB (hydrophilic-lipophilic balance) value of ~15, making it strongly hydrophilic; it is used in ice cream to control fat crystal structure, in vaccines as a solubilizer, and in intravenous formulations of poorly water-soluble drugs such as docetaxel.

The Sanger method (chain-termination sequencing) reads DNA sequences by incorporating dideoxy nucleoside triphosphates (ddNTPs) that terminate chain elongation at each type of base, generating four nested sets of fragments that are separated by size using gel electrophoresis or capillary electrophoresis. Frederick Sanger developed this method in 1977 and used it to sequence the first DNA genome (bacteriophage φX174); he earned his second Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1980) for this work, making him one of only four double Nobel laureates.

Hydrazine (N₂H₄) is a colorless, highly reactive liquid that spontaneously ignites in contact with oxidants such as N₂O₄, making the combination a hypergolic propellant used in spacecraft thrusters (Voyager, Cassini, Mars rovers). In organic chemistry, hydrazine reacts with carbonyl compounds to form hydrazones (R₂C=N-NH₂) and is used in the Wolff-Kishner reduction; industrially it is a precursor to pharmaceutical intermediates, agricultural chemicals, and foaming agents.

The Hammett equation log(k/k₀) = ρσ relates the rate or equilibrium constant of a meta or para substituted benzene reaction to two parameters: the substituent constant σ (a measure of the electron-withdrawing or -donating ability of the substituent) and the reaction constant ρ (the sensitivity of the reaction to electronic effects). A positive ρ indicates the reaction is accelerated by electron-withdrawing groups (negative charge builds in the transition state); a negative ρ indicates acceleration by electron-donating groups.

Anthocyanins are water-soluble flavonoid pigments responsible for the red, purple, and blue colors of many fruits, vegetables, and flowers. Their color depends on pH: cyanidin glucoside is red at pH < 3 (flavylium cation form), purple-violet around pH 6–7 (quinonoidal base form), and blue-green in alkaline conditions (ionized quinonoidal base); the blue color of hydrangeas is due to complexation of anthocyanins with aluminum ions mobilized in acidic soil.

Lead-acid batteries, invented by Gaston Planté in 1859, are the oldest and most widely used rechargeable battery technology; every car starter battery is lead-acid. The discharge reaction (Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O) gives a cell voltage of ~2.1 V per cell; despite their low specific energy (~35 Wh/kg), they are inexpensive, reliable, highly recyclable (~99% in developed countries), and capable of delivering high peak currents.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies a specific DNA sequence millions of times using thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus), two flanking oligonucleotide primers, and temperature cycling between denaturation (~95 °C), annealing (~55–65 °C), and extension (~72 °C). Kary Mullis received the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this invention; PCR is now the foundational tool in forensics, diagnostics (COVID-19 testing), genetic research, and molecular cloning.

Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) are nuclear receptors activated by fatty acid-derived ligands that regulate lipid metabolism, inflammation, and glucose homeostasis. PPARα (activated by fibrate drugs) reduces triglycerides; PPARγ (activated by thiazolidinedione drugs such as rosiglitazone) increases insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes by promoting adipocyte differentiation. Their chemistry illustrates how endogenous lipid metabolites function as hormone-like signaling molecules.

Magnesium is produced industrially by two main routes: electrolysis of molten MgCl₂ (Dow process) at ~700 °C, or thermal reduction of calcined dolomite with silicon or ferrosilicon (Pidgeon process) at ~1200 °C under vacuum. It is the lightest structural metal (density 1.74 g/cm³, 35% lighter than aluminum) and its alloys are used in automobile engine blocks, racing car frames, laptop housings, and aerospace structures where weight reduction is paramount.

The Marcus theory of electron transfer predicts the rate of outer-sphere electron transfer between donor (D) and acceptor (A) from the free energy change (ΔG°) and the reorganization energy (λ), which captures the energy cost of reorganizing nuclear coordinates (bond lengths, solvent orientation) from D to A geometry. The Marcus inverted region — where increasing driving force beyond λ makes the reaction slower — was initially counterintuitive but confirmed experimentally by Miller, Calcaterra, and Closs (1984), validating a key quantum mechanical prediction.

Toluene (methylbenzene) is an aromatic hydrocarbon used as an industrial solvent, a precursor to TNT (2,4,6-trinitrotoluene) and benzaldehyde, and a petrol octane enhancer (octane number 114). Its ring methyl group is activated toward benzylic radical reactions because the benzylic C−H bond dissociation energy (~89 kcal/mol) is lower than that of alkane C−H bonds (~100 kcal/mol), making toluene more flammable than benzene in air and easier to functionalize at the methyl group.

Alpha-synuclein is a 140-amino acid intrinsically disordered protein expressed at high levels in brain neurons where it localizes to presynaptic terminals and is thought to regulate synaptic vesicle trafficking. In Parkinson's disease, α-synuclein misfolds and aggregates into insoluble amyloid fibrils called Lewy bodies; point mutations in α-synuclein gene (A53T, A30P, E46K) cause rare familial Parkinson's, making understanding its aggregation mechanism a major goal of neurochemistry.

Sulfonamide antibiotics were the first synthetic drugs to treat systemic bacterial infections; Gerhard Domagk discovered Prontosil (a prodrug metabolized to sulfanilamide) in 1932 and received the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Sulfonamides act as competitive inhibitors of dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS), which bacteria use to synthesize folate from p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) — humans must obtain folate from diet and lack DHPS, giving sulfonamides selective toxicity.

Hypervalent iodine reagents such as (diacetoxyiodo)benzene (PhI(OAc)₂) and Dess-Martin periodinane (DMP) are mild, selective oxidants that convert primary and secondary alcohols to aldehydes and ketones without overoxidizing or epimerizing sensitive substrates. The Dess-Martin periodinane (DMP), based on an iodine(V) acetate ester of 1-hydroxy-1,2-benziodoxol-3(1H)-one, oxidizes alcohols at room temperature in CHCl₃ within minutes, tolerating a wide range of functional groups incompatible with Cr(VI) or Swern oxidations.

Galactose is an epimer of glucose differing only in the configuration at C4. It is a component of lactose (milk sugar), blood group antigens (glycolipids and glycoproteins on red blood cell surfaces), and many glycoproteins. Galactosemia is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT), leading to accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in liver, brain, and kidney, causing serious developmental damage unless lactose is immediately excluded from the diet.

Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) such as zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC), and tenofovir are the cornerstone of HIV antiretroviral therapy. They are prodrugs that are intracellularly phosphorylated to their triphosphate forms, which compete with natural nucleoside triphosphates for incorporation into HIV reverse transcriptase; once incorporated, the modified nucleoside lacks a 3'-OH group, acting as a chain terminator that halts viral DNA synthesis.

Bioorthogonal copper-free strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) reacts a ring-strained cyclooctyne (such as DIBO or DBCO) with an azide without requiring a copper catalyst, enabling labeling of biomolecules in living organisms where Cu(I) would be cytotoxic. The ring strain in cyclooctyne (estimated at ~18 kcal/mol) provides the activation energy, giving rate constants of ~0.1 M⁻¹s⁻¹ — orders of magnitude faster than uncatalyzed Huisgen cycloaddition and sufficient for cell surface glycan labeling within minutes.

Acetone (propan-2-one) is both the simplest ketone and the smallest molecule with a carbonyl group flanked by two carbon atoms on both sides. It is produced in the body during ketosis (fat breakdown exceeds carbohydrate availability, as in fasting or type 1 diabetes) and can be detected on the breath of diabetic patients in ketoacidosis (a medical emergency). Industrially, 85% of acetone is produced as a co-product of phenol in the cumene hydroperoxide process.

Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) amplifies the normally weak Raman signal by up to 10¹⁰-fold when molecules adsorb onto the surface of metallic nanoparticles (gold or silver) within plasmonic 'hot spots' — nanometer-scale gaps between adjacent nanoparticles where the electromagnetic field is intensified by coupled localized surface plasmon resonances. SERS can detect single molecules and is being developed for ultrasensitive detection of explosives, toxins, biomarkers, and pathogens.

Carbamates (urethanes, R−O−C(O)−NR'R'') are the linkages in polyurethane polymers and are also important functional groups in pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. They are formed by reaction of isocyanates with alcohols; their mild electrophilicity and ability to be cleaved by bases or in specific physiological conditions make them popular as prodrug linkers that slowly release the active amine drug in vivo through hydrolysis.

The Cope rearrangement is a thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of 1,5-dienes that forms a new C−C bond while breaking the old one, proceeding through a chair-like six-membered transition state. The oxy-Cope variant, where one double bond bears a hydroxyl group, is thermodynamically driven to give an enol product that tautomerizes to a thermodynamically stable ketone; treatment of the diol with base (to form the alkoxide) accelerates the reaction 10¹⁰–10¹⁷-fold by stabilizing the transition state electrostatically.

Hyaluronic acid (hyaluronan, HA) is a linear glycosaminoglycan composed of alternating units of D-glucuronic acid and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, with molecular weights ranging from 5 kDa to 20 MDa. It is the major component of synovial fluid (where it provides lubrication and shock absorption in joints) and the extracellular matrix of skin (where it retains water, as each disaccharide can hold up to 1000× its weight in water). Crosslinked HA hydrogels are the active ingredient of dermal fillers (Juvéderm, Restylane).

Nickel-cadmium (NiCd) batteries use cadmium anode, nickel oxyhydroxide cathode, and KOH electrolyte, operating at 1.2 V per cell and exhibiting exceptional cycle life (>1000 cycles) and performance at low temperatures. They suffer from 'memory effect' (capacity loss if repeatedly discharged to only partial depth) and cadmium toxicity restricts their use; they have largely been replaced by nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) and lithium-ion batteries in consumer electronics.

Meso compounds are achiral molecules that contain stereocenters but whose internal mirror plane (or other symmetry element) makes the two halves of the molecule mirror images of each other. Meso-tartaric acid (2R,3S-tartaric acid) has a C2 axis of symmetry and one internal mirror plane, making it optically inactive despite having two stereocenters; it was key to Pasteur's work on chirality because it separated the two enantiomeric forms of sodium ammonium tartrate as distinct crystals.

Molecular imprinting creates synthetic receptors by polymerizing functional monomers around a template molecule; when the template is removed, a complementary cavity remains that can selectively rebind the template. Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) have been developed as robust, stable, low-cost alternatives to antibodies in sensors, solid-phase extraction, and catalysis; their selectivity for the template molecule can rival antibodies, and unlike antibodies they are stable at high temperatures and in organic solvents.

Liquid ammonia (boiling point −33.4 °C at 1 atm) is a useful polar aprotic solvent with high solubility for alkali metals (sodium dissolved in liquid NH₃ gives a vivid blue solution of solvated electrons and Na⁺ cations). These solvated electrons are strong reducing agents used in the Birch reduction and dissolving metal reductions; concentrated sodium-in-ammonia solutions are bronze-colored and electrically conducting, and are metastable on timescales of hours.

The Diels-Alder reaction is stereospecific: substituents that are cis on the dienophile remain cis in the product (syn addition), and the approach geometry is controlled by endo-preference (Alder endo rule) in kinetically controlled reactions, where secondary orbital interactions between diene and dienophile substituents stabilize the endo transition state. This stereospecificity and endo selectivity enable reliable construction of complex cyclohexene rings with multiple stereocenters in a single step.

Folic acid (vitamin B₉) is essential for one-carbon metabolism, serving as a coenzyme for the transfer of single carbon units in the biosynthesis of purines, thymidylate, and the amino acids serine, glycine, and methionine. Methotrexate, a folic acid analog used in cancer chemotherapy and autoimmune disease treatment, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) by binding ~1000-fold more tightly than the natural substrate, blocking folate metabolism and killing rapidly dividing cells.

Radiocarbon dating (¹⁴C dating) measures the ratio of radioactive ¹⁴C (t₁/₂ = 5730 years) to stable ¹²C in organic material to determine how long ago the organism died, since living organisms continually exchange carbon with the atmosphere but dead ones do not. Developed by Willard Libby (1949 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), the technique is accurate to ±30 years for material up to ~50,000 years old and has revolutionized archaeology, paleontology, and art authentication.

Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a semi-crystalline thermoplastic polyester made by condensation polymerization of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, with intrinsic viscosity controlled to give either fiber-grade (for textiles, Dacron) or bottle-grade (Coca-Cola bottles) polymer. PET bottles are recycled (designated resin code #1) more than any other plastic; chemically recycled PET from depolymerization with methanol (methanolysis to dimethyl terephthalate) or ethylene glycol (glycolysis) can regenerate virgin-quality polymer.

Nitinol is a shape-memory alloy of approximately equiatomic nickel and titanium that 'remembers' its trained shape and returns to it when heated above its transformation temperature. The shape memory effect arises from a reversible thermoelastic martensitic transformation between a high-temperature austenite (cubic B2) phase and a low-temperature martensite (monoclinic B19') phase; the superelastic form (at room temperature in the austenite phase) recovers up to 8% strain elastically, making nitinol stents self-expandable when deployed at body temperature.

Protease inhibitor drugs (PI) used in HIV treatment, such as ritonavir, saquinavir, and lopinavir, are designed to fit precisely into the C₂-symmetric active site of HIV protease, a homodimeric aspartyl protease that cleaves viral polyproteins. The inhibitors mimic the tetrahedral intermediate of peptide hydrolysis with a hydroxymethyl or hydroxyethyl isostere; ritonavir also inhibits CYP3A4 strongly, and is co-administered at sub-therapeutic doses as a pharmacokinetic 'booster' to slow the metabolism of other PIs.

Amylase is a digestive enzyme (α-amylase in saliva and pancreatic juice) that hydrolyzes the α-1,4-glycosidic bonds of starch, breaking it into maltose and oligosaccharides. The catalytic mechanism involves two carboxylate residues (one aspartate nucleophile and one glutamate proton donor/acceptor) in a double-displacement retaining mechanism, producing product with the same anomeric configuration as the substrate; measuring salivary amylase activity is a biomarker of pancreatic disease and stress.

Carbohydrate chemistry uses anomeric terminology: in the cyclic (furanose or pyranose) form of monosaccharides, the new stereocenter at C1 (the anomeric carbon, derived from the carbonyl) can be either α (axial OH in glucose) or β (equatorial OH in glucose). The anomeric effect — the preference of electronegative substituents at the anomeric position for the axial orientation, contrary to steric predictions — arises from hyperconjugative electron donation from the ring oxygen lone pair into the σ* of the C1−OX bond, stabilizing the axial conformer.

Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) use a sulfonated fluoropolymer membrane (Nafion) that selectively conducts protons from anode to cathode while blocking electrons, which must travel through an external circuit. Hydrogen is oxidized at the platinum anode (H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻), protons cross the membrane, and oxygen is reduced at the platinum cathode (O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O), producing water as the only byproduct; Toyota's Mirai and Hyundai's Nexo FCEVs use PEMFC stacks of ~100 kW.

The Curtius rearrangement converts an acyl azide (from carboxylic acid + DPPA or azide) to an isocyanate via loss of N₂, which is then hydrolyzed to a primary amine, one carbon shorter. Together with the Hofmann rearrangement (hypobromite oxidation of amide) and the Lossen rearrangement (hydroxamic acid), the Curtius rearrangement forms a family of reactions that degrade carboxylic acids to amines while migrating the nitrogen with inversion (1,2-shift), useful for installing amine groups in complex molecule synthesis.

Benzene's aromaticity satisfies Hückel's rule (4n+2 π electrons, n=1 → 6 electrons) and gives it exceptional thermodynamic stability ~150 kJ/mol relative to a hypothetical cyclohexatriene. Aromatic stabilization can be quantitatively measured by comparing the heat of hydrogenation of benzene (−208 kJ/mol) to three times that of cyclohexene (3 × −120 = −360 kJ/mol); the difference (152 kJ/mol) is the empirical resonance energy, confirming the prediction of molecular orbital theory.

Phthalocyanines are macrocyclic conjugated ligands related to porphyrins that form intensely blue or green metal complexes (copper phthalocyanine, Pigment Blue 15) widely used in inks, paints, plastics, and cosmetics. Beyond pigments, metallophthalocyanines are excellent electrocatalysts for the 4-electron reduction of oxygen to water (relevant to fuel cells), sensors for gases like NO₂, and sensitizers in photodynamic therapy; cobalt phthalocyanine mimics cytochrome P450 and oxidizes hydrocarbons.

Cyclopentadienyl anion (Cp⁻, C₅H₅⁻) is aromatic: it has 6 π electrons (4n+2, n=1) delocalized across five equivalent carbon atoms, giving it remarkable stability compared to the neutral cyclopentadienyl radical and making cyclopentadiene one of the most acidic hydrocarbons (pKa ~16 in DMSO vs. ~43 for most alkenes). The ease of forming Cp⁻ and its strong donor ability toward metals makes it one of the most widely used ligands in organometallic chemistry.

Carvacrol (5-isopropyl-2-methylphenol) is the major phenolic component (~60–80%) of oregano and thyme essential oils, with potent antimicrobial, antifungal, and antioxidant properties. It disrupts bacterial cell membranes similarly to thymol and is used as a natural food preservative; it is GRAS (generally recognized as safe) by the FDA. Its pleasant spicy aroma makes it an approved food flavoring, while its antimicrobial activity is exploited in natural sanitizing sprays.

Wacker oxidation converts terminal alkenes to methyl ketones using PdCl₂ as catalyst and O₂ as the terminal oxidant (with CuCl₂ as a redox mediator) in water: CH₂=CHR + ½O₂ → CH₃C(O)R. The mechanism involves coordination of the alkene to Pd(II), anti-hydroxyl palladation, β-hydride elimination, and Pd(0) reoxidation; it is the most atom-economical catalytic oxidation in organometallics and underpins the industrial production of acetaldehyde from ethylene.

Salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) is a plant hormone (phytohormone) that mediates systemic acquired resistance to pathogens; it is also the active metabolite from aspirin hydrolysis. In its own right, salicylic acid is used in topical products for acne, psoriasis, and dandruff because it exfoliates keratin-rich dead skin cells (keratolytic action) by dissolving the intercellular cement of the stratum corneum at concentrations of 2–10%.

Organohalide pollutants such as dioxins (polychlorinated dibenzodioxins, PCDDs) and furans (PCDFs) are unintentional byproducts of combustion and chemical manufacturing that bind the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) with extraordinarily high affinity, inducing expression of CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 enzymes that activate polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons to carcinogenic epoxides. TCDD (2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin) is the most toxic synthetic chemical known, with an LD₅₀ in guinea pigs of ~1 μg/kg.

Perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS, 'forever chemicals') contain the extremely stable C−F bond (bond energy 544 kJ/mol, the strongest single bond to carbon) and include PFOA (perfluorooctanoic acid) and PFOS (perfluorooctane sulfonate). They persist indefinitely in the environment and accumulate in human blood and liver; regulatory concern focuses on associations with cancer, thyroid disorders, and immune suppression at concentrations in the ppt range in drinking water.

Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) are the key technology that enabled long-haul fiber-optic telecommunications: erbium ions in silica fiber absorb 980 nm pump laser light and emit at 1550 nm (matching the lowest-loss window of silica fiber) through a ⁴I₁₃/₂ → ⁴I₁₅/₂ 4f–4f transition. A single EDFA can amplify hundreds of wavelength channels simultaneously by stimulated emission without any optical-to-electrical conversion, with gains of 20–40 dB over an 80 nm bandwidth.

The isomerization of glucose to fructose — critical for high-fructose corn syrup (HFCS) production — is catalyzed by the enzyme glucose isomerase (xylose isomerase) through a hydride-shift mechanism requiring a metal cofactor (Mg²⁺ or Mn²⁺). Industrial glucose isomerase is immobilized on solid supports at ~60 °C and pH 7–8, converting a ~52:48 glucose:fructose equilibrium mixture; the product stream is further enriched to 42% or 55% fructose by chromatographic separation and blending.

Aromatic C−H activation (CDC, cross-dehydrogenative coupling) uses transition-metal catalysts (often Pd, Rh, or Ru) to functionalize inert aromatic C−H bonds directly, without pre-installing leaving groups (halides or triflates). Directed ortho-metalation uses a coordinating directing group (amide, pyridine, oxazoline) to position the metal near the desired C−H bond; this approach dramatically reduces synthetic steps and waste compared to classical multi-step sequences.

Haemocyanin is an oxygen-transport metalloprotein found in the hemolymph of mollusks and arthropods (crabs, lobsters, spiders) that uses a copper pair (two Cu⁺ ions) rather than iron to bind O₂, giving the blood a blue color when oxygenated. Each Cu₂ active site binds one O₂ molecule as a bridging peroxo-dicopper(II) complex; unlike hemoglobin, haemocyanin is dissolved freely in the hemolymph rather than enclosed in red blood cells, and can account for >98% of the hemolymph protein.

Polymer electrolyte membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) splits water into H₂ and O₂ using proton-conducting Nafion membranes at high current densities (1–3 A/cm²) and produces ultra-pure H₂ (>99.999%) suitable for fuel cells and semiconductor manufacturing. The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) at the anode requires iridium oxide catalyst — iridium's scarcity (annual production ~7 tonnes) is the main bottleneck for large-scale green hydrogen production, driving research into cheaper alternatives.

Retrosynthetic analysis of natural products often reveals 'strategic bonds' — typically C−C bonds adjacent to heteroatoms or at ring junctions — whose disconnection most efficiently simplifies the target. The 1994 Corey synthesis of taxol (paclitaxel), the anticancer drug from Pacific yew bark, required 40 steps and disconnected the complex tricyclic system using a Diels-Alder reaction to build the six-membered A ring; taxol's scarcity drove development of the semi-synthetic route from abundant 10-deacetylbaccatin III.

Rhodopsin is the photoreceptor protein of rod cells in the vertebrate retina, consisting of the protein opsin covalently bound to 11-cis-retinal via a protonated Schiff base linkage to Lys296. Absorption of a photon isomerizes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal within 200 femtoseconds, triggering a conformational change in opsin that activates the G-protein transducin and initiates the visual phototransduction cascade; a single photon absorbed by rhodopsin can be detected by the human eye in absolute darkness.

Microneedle patches are arrays of tiny needles (100–1000 μm tall) typically made of dissolvable polymer (PVA, PVP, or carbohydrates) containing drugs or vaccines embedded in the needle matrix. On skin insertion, the microneedles penetrate the stratum corneum painlessly (nerve endings lie deeper), then dissolve in interstitial fluid to release payload in the viable epidermis — enabling transdermal drug delivery of macromolecules such as insulin that cannot cross intact skin.

Formic acid (methanoic acid, HCOOH) is the simplest carboxylic acid, produced commercially by hydrolysis of methyl formate or by carbonylation of methanol. It is interesting as a hydrogen-storage molecule: it can be catalytically decomposed to H₂ + CO₂ (formic acid as a H₂ carrier), or catalytically produced from H₂ + CO₂, making it a potential liquid energy vector for renewable hydrogen in a carbon-neutral economy.

Arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4, Δ5,8,11,14) is an omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A₂ in response to inflammatory stimuli. It is the substrate for cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) enzymes that produce prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and prostacyclin; and for 5-lipoxygenase that produces leukotrienes. Both pathways drive inflammation, pain, and fever, explaining why COX inhibitors (NSAIDs like ibuprofen) and 5-LOX inhibitors are therapeutic.

Indigo is one of the oldest synthetic dyes, first made by Adolf von Baeyer (who received the 1905 Nobel Prize in Chemistry partly for this work) from aniline derivatives. It dyes cotton by forming hydrogen bonds between its C=O and N−H groups and the OH groups of cellulose; the distinctive fading of denim arises because indigo only surface-dyes the cotton fibers rather than penetrating to the core, so abrasion progressively exposes undyed fiber.

The Staudinger ligation (not to be confused with the Staudinger reaction for phosphine + azide → iminophosphorane) is a bioorthogonal ligation reaction between an azide and a triphenylphosphine modified with a methyl ester that traps the aza-ylide intermediate before hydrolysis, forming a stable amide bond. Developed by the Bertozzi group for cell-surface glycan labeling, it was one of the first truly bioorthogonal reactions performed in living organisms.

Allosteric ribozymes (riboswitches) are RNA molecules in bacterial mRNA 5' UTRs that fold into aptamer domains that bind specific small molecules (coenzyme B₁₂, thiamine pyrophosphate, SAM, lysine, guanine) with high affinity and specificity, and in response change their structure to regulate downstream gene expression by terminating transcription or sequestering the ribosome binding site. They represent an ancient form of gene regulation by metabolite sensing that predates proteins.

Tetracycline antibiotics (tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline) are broad-spectrum antibacterials that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and preventing aminoacyl-tRNA from entering the A-site of the ribosome. They require Mg²⁺ chelation for their biological activity (the Mg-tetracycline complex is the active form that binds the ribosome), and their affinity for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ explains their yellow-brown discoloration of developing teeth when taken by children.

Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) deposits thin films of materials onto heated substrates by thermally decomposing volatile gaseous precursors on the surface; plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) uses plasma to lower deposition temperatures. Silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) passivation layers in microchips are deposited by PECVD of silane (SiH₄) and ammonia (NH₃) at 300–350 °C; graphene sheets can be grown on copper foil by CVD from methane at 1000 °C, enabling wafer-scale production of this material.

Protein Data Bank (PDB) is the global open-access repository for three-dimensional structural data of biological macromolecules, founded in 1971 with 7 structures; by 2024 it contained over 210,000 structures, of which ~85% were solved by X-ray crystallography, ~12% by cryo-electron microscopy, and ~3% by NMR spectroscopy. The explosive growth of cryo-EM structures since 2013 (the 'resolution revolution' triggered by direct electron detectors) has made it possible to determine membrane protein and large complex structures previously inaccessible.

The Favorskii rearrangement converts α-halo ketones to carboxylic acid derivatives under basic conditions via a cyclopropanone intermediate (or, for compounds without α'-hydrogens, via a semibenzilic mechanism involving a 1,2-shift). The ring-opening of the cyclopropanone by the nucleophile (OH⁻, RO⁻, or RNH₂) gives carboxylate, ester, or amide products, respectively; the overall result is migration of a carbonyl group by one carbon, making it useful for ring contraction of cyclic ketones.

Photovoltaic effect was discovered by Edmond Becquerel in 1839 when he observed that an electrolytic cell produced a voltage when illuminated — the first observation of light-to-electricity conversion. Modern first-generation crystalline silicon solar cells rely on a p-n junction: photogenerated electron-hole pairs are separated by the built-in electric field at the junction, driving electrons to the n-type contact and holes to the p-type, producing a direct current without any moving parts.

Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) are neuropeptides that signal through G-protein-coupled receptors (PAC1, VPAC1, VPAC2) to activate adenylate cyclase and elevate cAMP. Their chemistry involves conserved N-terminal histidine residues essential for receptor activation; VIP regulates gastrointestinal motility, vasodilation, and immune function, and VIP neurons in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) coordinate the circadian clock.

Chlorinated solvents such as dichloromethane (DCM), chloroform, and carbon tetrachloride are dense, immiscible-with-water solvents historically used for dry cleaning, metal degreasing, and chemical extraction. Their hepatotoxicity (CCl₄ causes centrilobular liver necrosis via cytochrome P450-generated •CCl₃ radicals) and contribution to the ozone hole (CCl₄) and ground-level ozone (CH₂Cl₂) have driven regulatory restrictions and transitions to less toxic alternatives like dimethyl carbonate and cyclopentyl methyl ether.

The Birch reduction applied to benzoic acid leaves the double bonds adjacent to the carboxylate substituent (electron-withdrawing group, EWG) because reduction occurs preferentially at positions of highest electron density (para and meta to EWG), giving 1,4-dihydrobenzoic acid with the C=C bonds at C2,3 and C5,6 positions. This regioselectivity rule (EDG → double bonds adjacent to substituent; EWG → double bonds remote from substituent) follows from orbital coefficient analysis in the relevant LUMO.

Electrocatalytic CO₂ reduction to formate, CO, methanol, ethylene, or ethanol requires catalysts that bind CO₂ preferentially over the competing H₂ evolution reaction. Copper is unique in producing multi-carbon products (C₂+) from CO₂ reduction by electrochemically coupling two CO* adsorbates via a C−C bond-forming step; understanding the oxophilicity and CO-binding energy of copper surfaces guides the design of alloy electrocatalysts (Cu-Ag, Cu-Zn) with improved selectivity toward a single product.

Phospholipase D (PLD) cleaves the phosphodiester bond of glycerophospholipids to release phosphatidic acid and the head group (choline for phosphatidylcholine), generating a lipid second messenger that activates multiple downstream effectors including mTOR. Plant PLD is activated in response to drought, cold, and pathogen attack, generating phosphatidic acid signals that modulate abscisic acid signaling and stomatal closure, linking lipid chemistry to plant drought tolerance.

Aqueous biphasic systems (ABS) consist of two immiscible aqueous phases formed when two incompatible polymers (PEG + dextran) or a polymer and a salt (PEG + K₂HPO₄) exceed critical concentrations. Proteins and organelles partition between the phases based on surface hydrophobicity, charge, and size, making ABS useful for cell separation, enzyme purification, and nanoparticle fractionation without organic solvents; PEG-salt ABS are now used for extractive fermentation, partitioning the product directly from the broth.

Proline is unique among the 20 standard amino acids in that its α-amine is part of a five-membered pyrrolidine ring, making it an imino acid (secondary amine). As a result, proline adopts a restricted φ backbone angle and does not donate an NH hydrogen bond, causing kinks or twists in α-helices when incorporated; it also forms the special Pro-Pro-Gly repeat units in collagen triple helices. Hydroxyproline (4-hydroxy-L-proline), made by prolyl hydroxylase using vitamin C as cofactor, further stabilizes the collagen triple helix.

Thermochemical water splitting uses concentrated solar heat above 1500 °C to drive multi-step redox cycles that produce H₂ and O₂ from water without electricity. The two-step cerium oxide (CeO₂/Ce₂O₃) cycle reduces CeO₂ to Ce₂O₃ at ~1500 °C (solar heat), then re-oxidizes it with water to regenerate CeO₂ and release H₂ at ~800 °C; peak demonstrated solar-to-hydrogen efficiency approaches 5%, with theoretical efficiencies potentially exceeding 30%.

Calixarenes are macrocyclic compounds built from para-substituted phenol units linked by methylene bridges, forming a 'basket' or 'chalice' shape (calyx in Greek). Calix[4]arene has a cavity ~3 Å deep that selectively binds small cations (Cs⁺ > K⁺ > Na⁺) and neutral organic guests; functionalized calixarenes are used as ion-selective electrode sensing membranes, supramolecular hosts for drug delivery, and building blocks for more complex self-assembled capsules.

Organoboron chemistry encompasses a wide range of compounds including boronic acids, boronate esters, and organoboron reagents that are central to Suzuki-Miyaura coupling, hydroboration reactions, and asymmetric synthesis. The ability of boron to undergo facile transmetallation and its compatibility with diverse functional groups makes organoboron reagents the dominant coupling partners in modern pharmaceutical synthesis; the FDA approved more drugs via Suzuki coupling in 2020 than by any other C−C bond-forming method.

Anisole (methoxybenzene, C₆H₅OCH₃) is the simplest aryl ether and a precursor to many pharmaceuticals and fragrances, including para-methoxybenzaldehyde (heliotropin), vanillin precursors, and anise-flavored compounds. Its oxygen lone pair donates electron density into the aromatic ring by resonance, making anisole 1000-fold more reactive than benzene toward electrophilic aromatic substitution and directing substituents predominantly to the ortho and para positions.

Peptide bond isomerism in proline-containing sequences (Xaa-Pro bonds) involves significant cis-trans isomerization (cis population up to 30%), whereas non-proline peptide bonds are >99.95% trans due to partial double-bond character. The enzyme peptidyl-prolyl isomerase (PPIase), including the immunosuppressant-binding proteins cyclophilin and FKBP12, catalyzes interconversion of cis and trans Xaa-Pro peptide bonds, regulating protein folding rates and acting as a key checkpoint in the folding of many signaling proteins.

Solid-state NMR spectroscopy can determine the structures of materials that cannot be studied by solution NMR or X-ray crystallography, including microcrystalline powders, amorphous solids, membrane proteins in lipid bilayers, and polymers. Magic-angle spinning (MAS) at the 'magic angle' of 54.74° with respect to the static magnetic field averages out anisotropic interactions (chemical shift anisotropy, dipolar coupling) to give narrow lines, and cross-polarization from ¹H to ¹³C or ¹⁵N enhances sensitivity dramatically.

Pyrethrin insecticides are naturally occurring esters produced by pyrethrum flowers (Chrysanthemum cinerariifolium) that paralyze insects by holding voltage-gated sodium channels open, preventing repolarization of nerve membranes. Their rapid knockdown of insects and quick photodegradation in sunlight (half-life of hours outdoors) make them among the safest insecticides for non-target species; synthetic pyrethroids (permethrin, cypermethrin) have improved photostability and are widely used in agriculture and mosquito control.

Dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄) exists in equilibrium with nitrogen dioxide (NO₂): N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ (ΔH = +57 kJ/mol). In pure form at room temperature, N₂O₄ is a pale yellow liquid that is ~0.1% dissociated; warming to higher temperatures shifts the equilibrium toward the brown paramagnetic NO₂ radical. The N₂O₄/hydrazine propellant combination (both hypergolic — ignite on contact) powers many spacecraft maneuvering thrusters, including those on the Space Shuttle Orbital Maneuvering System.

The anomeric carbon in pyranose and furanose ring forms of sugars is C1 for aldoses and C2 for ketoses; the hemiacetal or hemiketal bond at this center is in dynamic equilibrium through ring-opening/closing (mutarotation). Freshly dissolved glucose in water shows an initial optical rotation of +113° (pure α-D-glucopyranose) that equilibrates to +52.7° as the mixture reaches the equilibrium ratio of ~36% α and ~64% β forms, a process catalyzed by acid, base, or the enzyme mutarotase.

Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) uses laser-excited fluorescent dyes or antibody-dye conjugates to label specific cell surface markers, then sorts cells individually at rates of up to 70,000 cells/second as they pass single-file through the laser beam. Multicolor FACS using 10–40 fluorescent dyes simultaneously can resolve rare cell populations (1 in 10⁶ cells) and is the primary tool for characterizing and isolating T cells, B cells, stem cells, and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in immunology and oncology research.

Cyclophosphamide is a nitrogen mustard prodrug that is biologically inert until hydroxylated by liver cytochrome P450 enzymes (primarily CYP2B6) to 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide, which decomposes spontaneously to phosphoramide mustard and acrolein. Phosphoramide mustard alkylates DNA at the N7 position of guanine, forming interstrand crosslinks that prevent DNA replication in rapidly dividing cancer cells; acrolein, the co-product, causes hemorrhagic cystitis and is co-administered with mesna (sodium 2-mercaptoethane sulfonate) to inactivate it in the bladder.

The Stork enamine synthesis uses a secondary amine (pyrrolidine, piperidine) to convert a carbonyl compound to a nucleophilic enamine, which then alkylates or acylates at the α-carbon; hydrolysis of the resulting iminium ion gives the α-substituted carbonyl product. This was the first practical method for alkylating ketones at a specific α-carbon without competing dialkylation, predating organocatalytic asymmetric methods by decades and still used for racemic synthesis.

Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) exist as single-walled (SWCNT) or multi-walled (MWCNT) cylinders of graphene with diameters of 1–100 nm. SWCNTs can be either metallic or semiconducting depending on their 'chirality' (roll-up vector), with armchair nanotubes always metallic and zigzag/chiral nanotubes semiconducting if the diameter satisfies a divisibility-by-3 condition; this electronic structure diversity, combined with tensile strengths ~100× that of steel and thermal conductivity exceeding diamond, makes CNTs of intense interest for transistors, sensors, and composites.

Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) bleach solutions slowly degrade on storage because hypochlorite undergoes disproportionation: 2 OCl⁻ → O₂ + 2 Cl⁻ (catalyzed by light and transition metal ions), explaining why bleach should be stored in opaque containers away from heat. When bleach contacts ammonia or urea (from urine), toxic chloramine gases form; when it contacts hydrogen peroxide, rapid disproportionation of peroxide occurs and oxygen gas is evolved — the basis of an 'elephant toothpaste' chemistry demonstration.

Oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid, HOOC-COOH) is the simplest dicarboxylic acid and a natural product found in high concentrations in spinach, rhubarb, and cocoa. It forms very insoluble calcium oxalate monohydrate (Ksp ~2 × 10⁻⁹) that precipitates in the kidneys, composing ~80% of kidney stones. Industrially, oxalic acid is produced by oxidation of carbohydrates or by sodium formate pyrolysis; it is used as a bleaching and cleaning agent, as a precipitant for rare earth elements, and as a wood restorer.

The Mitsunobu reaction inverts the configuration of a secondary alcohol by reacting it with an acidic pronucleophile (pKa < ~13; carboxylic acid, phenol, sulfonamide, phthalimide) in the presence of diethyl azodicarboxylate (DEAD) or diisopropyl azodicarboxylate (DIAD) and triphenylphosphine. The reaction proceeds via a betaine intermediate and an SN2-type displacement with complete inversion, making it an essential tool for stereodivergent synthesis when only one enantiomer of a chiral alcohol is available.

Photoacoustic spectroscopy (PAS) detects absorbed light energy as a pressure (sound) wave: a modulated light source absorbed by a sample heats it periodically, generating thermal expansion and a pressure wave detected by a microphone or piezoelectric transducer. PAS is unique in being able to measure light absorption in highly scattering, opaque, or strongly absorbing media (soils, biological tissues, powders) where transmission and reflection methods fail; it is used for trace gas detection at ppb levels in atmospheric monitoring.

Urea (CO(NH₂)₂) was the first organic compound synthesized from inorganic precursors (Wöhler, 1828), which disproved the vitalist theory that organic compounds required a 'vital force' from living organisms. Today, ~180 million tonnes of urea are produced annually from ammonia and CO₂ at 150–200 atm and 180–190 °C via the Bosch-Meiser process; it is the most widely used nitrogen fertilizer in the world, slowly hydrolyzed by urease to ammonium carbonate in soil.

Dihydroxylation of alkenes produces vicinal diols: osmium tetroxide (OsO₄) gives syn-addition (both OH groups on the same face), while peracid (m-CPBA) epoxidation followed by acid hydrolysis gives anti-addition (OH groups on opposite faces). The Sharpless asymmetric dihydroxylation uses catalytic OsO₄ with chiral cinchona alkaloid ligands (AD-mix-α or AD-mix-β) to give either enantiomeric diol with >90% ee, and the reaction is so reliable that it is taught as a standard undergraduate laboratory reaction.

The ether oxygen in morphine (and related opioids) is not involved in receptor binding; rather, the critical pharmacophore is the protonated tertiary amine (pKa ~8.0), the aromatic ring A, and the 3-hydroxyl group that interact with specific residues in the μ-opioid receptor's orthosteric binding site. Subtle changes in opioid structure produce dramatically different pharmacological profiles: codeine (3-methoxy ether of morphine) is a prodrug requiring O-demethylation by CYP2D6 to active morphine, while heroin (3,6-diacetylmorphine) enters the brain faster due to increased lipophilicity.

Chlorophyll degradation in autumn leaves proceeds through pheophytinization (loss of Mg from chlorophyll) catalyzed by chlorophyllase to give pheophytin, then chlorophyllide, then pheophorbide. These colorless breakdown products unmask the yellow-orange carotenoid pigments that were always present but invisible. In maple trees, additional anthocyanin pigments are synthesized in autumn from sugars trapped by early cold snaps that halt phloem transport, producing the brilliant reds and purples characteristic of autumn foliage.

The chemistry of soap-making (saponification) involves hydrolysis of triglycerides (fats or oils) by strong alkali (NaOH for solid soap, KOH for liquid soap) to give glycerol and three fatty acid salts (soap). Cold-process soap making mixes lye solution with oils without external heat, relying on the exothermic saponification reaction itself; the degree of saponification (SAP value) differs by oil type — olive oil requires 0.134 g NaOH per gram of oil, while coconut oil requires 0.190 g/g, because coconut oil is richer in short-chain fatty acids.

Epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) is the most abundant catechin polyphenol in green tea, comprising up to 50% of the total dry weight of green tea extract. It is a potent antioxidant (reducing capacity ~25× that of vitamin C) and a promiscuous bioactive compound that inhibits numerous enzymes; its anti-cancer, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects in cell culture studies have driven intense research, though clinical trial results have been mixed due to EGCG's poor bioavailability and rapid methylation/glucuronidation in vivo.

Glycoconjugates — glycoproteins, proteoglycans, glycolipids, and glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins — form a dense carbohydrate coat on cell surfaces called the glycocalyx (2–100 nm thick). The glycocalyx mediates cell-cell recognition (ABO blood group antigens on red blood cells are oligosaccharides), pathogen binding (influenza virus hemagglutinin binds sialic acid), and signaling; chemical glycobiology tools (metabolic labeling with unnatural sugars bearing azide or alkyne handles) allow visualization of glycan dynamics in living cells.

The Balz-Schiemann reaction converts aryldiazonium tetrafluoroborates to aryl fluorides by thermal decomposition: ArN₂⁺BF₄⁻ → Ar-F + N₂ + BF₃. Because direct fluorination of aromatics with F₂ is too violent and electrophilic fluorinating agents (NFSI, Selectfluor) typically give other products, the Schiemann reaction and related HF-diazotization (Halex) reactions remain important for introducing fluorine at specific positions in pharmaceutical intermediates.

Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) is one of the most acutely toxic substances known (LC₅₀ in rats ~140 ppm for 1 hour), because the cyanide anion (CN⁻) inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV of the electron transport chain) by binding the ferric iron in the enzyme's heme a₃ center, preventing electron transfer to O₂ and halting aerobic respiration in all cells. The antidotes — hydroxocobalamin (which sequesters CN⁻ as cyanocobalamin) and sodium thiosulfate (which regenerates thiocyanate via rhodanese) — must be administered within minutes.

Synthetic biology uses genetic engineering, metabolic engineering, and systems biology to redesign organisms for biosynthesis of valuable chemicals. Amyris engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae to produce artemisinic acid — the precursor to the antimalarial drug artemisinin — at 25 g/L titer in fermenters by introducing 12 enzymes from the native Artemisia annua biosynthetic pathway; this semi-synthetic artemisinin, approved by WHO in 2013, provides a reliable, affordable supply independent of weather-dependent plant crops.

Phenolphthalein is a pH indicator that is colorless in acid and pink in base (pKa ~9.4), transitioning through a ring-opening of its lactone form to a resonance-stabilized trianion that absorbs at 552 nm. In very strongly alkaline solutions (pH > ~12) the pink color fades to a colorless carbinol form as the central carbon adds hydroxide; this 'alkaline fading' is a complication when using phenolphthalein as an indicator in strongly basic titrations.

Thyroxine (T₄, 3,3',5,5'-tetraiodothyronine) and triiodothyronine (T₃, 3,3',5-triiodothyronine) are iodine-containing thyroid hormones made from the amino acid tyrosine by sequential iodination by thyroid peroxidase and coupling reactions in thyroglobulin. They regulate the basal metabolic rate of virtually every cell by binding nuclear thyroid hormone receptors (TRα, TRβ) that directly regulate gene transcription; hyperthyroidism causes weight loss, tachycardia, and sweating, while hypothyroidism causes fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance.

Organocatalytic asymmetric Michael addition uses chiral secondary amines to activate α,β-unsaturated aldehydes as iminium ions (making the β-carbon more electrophilic) and ketones as enamine intermediates (making the α-carbon nucleophilic). This 'iminium-enamine' catalysis enabled the asymmetric Diels-Alder reaction, Mannich reaction, and direct aldol with simple unmodified carbonyl compounds — the breakthrough that earned List and MacMillan the 2021 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The Biginelli reaction is a three-component condensation of an aldehyde, a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound (typically ethyl acetoacetate), and urea (or thiourea) under acid catalysis to give 3,4-dihydropyrimidin-2(1H)-ones (DHPMs). DHPMs have a wide range of biological activities — the calcium channel blocker monastrol and the antihypertensive SQ 32,547 are DHPMs — and the one-pot, atom-economical Biginelli reaction has become a model multicomponent reaction in medicinal chemistry for rapid library synthesis.

Alpha decay occurs when an unstable nucleus emits a helium-4 nucleus (⁴He, α-particle, ²p + ²n), reducing the atomic number by 2 and mass number by 4. The alpha decay of uranium-238 (t₁/₂ = 4.47 × 10⁹ years) through a 14-step decay chain ultimately produces stable lead-206; measurement of the U-238/Pb-206 ratio is used to date rocks and minerals by uranium-lead geochronology, which has confirmed the age of Earth at ~4.54 billion years.

Zymogen (proenzyme) activation involves proteolytic cleavage of an inactive precursor protein to generate the active enzyme; this irreversible mechanism prevents enzymes from acting prematurely in the wrong cellular compartment. Trypsinogen is activated in the small intestine by enteropeptidase cleaving the N-terminal hexapeptide; pepsinogen is activated at low pH in the stomach by autocatalytic cleavage; and prothrombin is activated to thrombin by factor Xa in the coagulation cascade, ensuring clotting only at sites of injury.

Organotin compounds (organostannanes) are used in agriculture (tributyltin as a biocide in antifouling ship paint), as PVC heat stabilizers (diorganotin carboxylates), and as reagents in Stille coupling reactions. Tributyltin compounds (TBT) were found to cause imposex (masculinization of female marine mollusks) at concentrations as low as 1 ng/Sn/L, leading to severe population declines in dogwhelks and other mollusks near harbors; TBT-based antifouling paint was banned globally by the IMO in 2008.

Molecular motors are molecular machines that convert chemical or light energy into mechanical work: ATP synthase rotates its γ-subunit driven by proton gradient (producing ~100 ATP molecules per second per enzyme), kinesin walks unidirectionally along microtubules consuming ATP to transport cargo, and myosin produces muscle contraction by cyclically binding and releasing actin filaments. Ben Feringa synthesized the first light-powered molecular motor (1999, unidirectional rotation around a C=C bond), earning a share of the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) is an unusual polar aprotic solvent that can penetrate and transport substances through skin because it displaces water in protein and lipid membrane structures; it is used as a carrier for topical medications. DMSO is also a cryoprotectant at 5–10% concentration for freezing cells by penetrating cells and preventing ice crystal formation; concentrated DMSO (>50%) causes vasoconstriction and a characteristic garlic-oyster breath odor arising from exhaled dimethyl sulfide, a metabolism product.

Lewis base/acid FLP (frustrated Lewis pair) chemistry, developed by Douglas Stephan at the University of Toronto after 2006, uses bulky Lewis acid and Lewis base components whose steric bulk prevents them from forming a classical dative Lewis acid-base adduct, leaving the active sites free to cooperatively activate small molecules such as H₂, CO₂, NO, and N₂O. FLP catalysts are being explored as metal-free hydrogenation catalysts that can rival transition-metal catalysts in scope and selectivity.

Polystyrene foam (expanded polystyrene, EPS) consists of ~95–98% air trapped in closed cells of polystyrene walls, giving it a thermal conductivity of only ~0.033 W/m·K (comparable to polyurethane foam) and a density as low as 10 kg/m³ — 100× less dense than water. Its low cost, excellent insulating properties, and shock-absorbing ability make it the dominant packaging material worldwide; it is recycled at only ~15% globally because its very low bulk density makes transport costs prohibitive.

Glycosylation is the most common post-translational modification of proteins: in N-glycosylation, an oligosaccharide is transferred en bloc from dolichol-pyrophosphate to the amide nitrogen of asparagine (Asn) in the Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequon in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen; in O-glycosylation, sugars are added one at a time to the hydroxyl of serine or threonine in the Golgi. These carbohydrate modifications alter protein folding, half-life, solubility, and immune recognition, and are essential for the biological activity of most therapeutic proteins.

Copper-catalyzed aerobic oxidation (CuI/TEMPO systems) oxidizes primary and secondary alcohols to aldehydes and ketones using air as the terminal oxidant — the most 'green' possible oxidant — under mild conditions. The mechanism involves coordination of alcohol to Cu(II) followed by PCET oxidation to ketyl radical, then electron transfer to O₂; these reactions have been adapted to flow chemistry reactors where safe handling of O₂-organic solvent mixtures is possible at scale.

Oximes (R₂C=NOH) are formed by condensation of hydroxylamine (H₂NOH) with aldehydes or ketones and can be used to reactivate organophosphate-inhibited acetylcholinesterase — the mechanism underlying antidotes to nerve agents. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) and obidoxime are oxime antidotes that displace the phosphate ester from the enzyme active-site serine before 'aging' (dealkylation) makes the inhibited enzyme irreversible; they are effective for tabun and sarin poisoning if administered within 30–60 minutes.

The Bucherer-Bergs reaction converts a carbonyl compound (aldehyde or ketone) with ammonium carbonate and potassium cyanide to a hydantoin in a single pot. The mechanism proceeds through a Strecker-like α-aminonitrile intermediate, followed by cyclization and intramolecular rearrangement to the five-membered 2,4-dioxo-imidazolidine (hydantoin) ring; hydrolysis of the product gives racemic α-amino acids, making this reaction historically important for amino acid synthesis.

Chemical ocean acidification occurs as the ocean absorbs CO₂ from the atmosphere: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Ocean pH has decreased by ~0.1 units (from 8.2 to 8.1) since pre-industrial times — a 26% increase in [H⁺] concentration — and threatens organisms that build calcium carbonate shells, because the saturation state of aragonite (CaCO₃ polymorph) decreases as [H⁺] rises, reducing the ability of corals, oysters, and pteropods to calcify.

Polypropylene (PP) is the second most produced thermoplastic after polyethylene, with global annual production exceeding 75 million tonnes. Isotactic PP (iPP) is semi-crystalline with a melting point of ~165 °C and is used for packaging, ropes, textiles, and automotive components; atactic PP is amorphous and used as a sealant and adhesive. Biaxially oriented PP (BOPP) film, stretched in two directions to align crystallites, has improved strength and clarity and is the dominant film for food packaging (chips, candy) and tape.

Photon upconversion is a process in which two or more low-energy photons are absorbed and a higher-energy photon is emitted, the reverse of Stokes fluorescence. Lanthanide-doped upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) containing sensitizer (Yb³⁺) and activator (Er³⁺, Tm³⁺) ions convert near-infrared light (980 nm) to visible or UV emissions through successive energy transfer steps between lanthanide ions; they are used in deep-tissue bioimaging, photodynamic therapy, and anti-counterfeiting inks because NIR light penetrates tissue and is not background-autofluorescent.

Transition metal-catalyzed C−H borylation uses iridium catalysts with bulky bipyridyl or phenanthroline ligands to functionalize aromatic and aliphatic C−H bonds with pinacolborane (HBpin), converting them directly to arylboronate esters. The Ir-catalyzed borylation is highly selective for the sterically least hindered C−H bond regardless of electronics, complementing electrophilic aromatic substitution; boronate products can be directly used in Suzuki coupling, oxidized to phenols, or converted to amines or fluorides.

Acetylcholine (ACh) is the neurotransmitter at neuromuscular junctions and in the autonomic nervous system, formed by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) from choline and acetyl-CoA and hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase (AChE) in the synaptic cleft within ~1 ms of release. AChE is one of the fastest enzymes known (kcat ~14,000 s⁻¹); organophosphate nerve agents (sarin, VX) and pesticides (parathion, malathion) irreversibly inhibit AChE by phosphorylating the active site serine, causing uncontrolled nerve firing.

Inverse electron-demand Diels-Alder (iEDDA) reaction between trans-cyclooctene (TCO) and tetrazine is the fastest bioorthogonal reaction known, with rate constants up to ~4 × 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹ in water — 40,000× faster than CuAAC click chemistry. The reaction releases N₂ and forms a stable dihydropyridazine product; its extraordinary speed allows in vivo pre-targeting strategies where a TCO-labeled antibody localizes to a tumor, then a tetrazine-radioisotope probe reacts with it within minutes for PET imaging without off-target irradiation.

Corundum (α-Al₂O₃) is the second hardest mineral (9 on Mohs scale, just below diamond) due to the exceptional strength of Al−O bonds in its hexagonal close-packed oxide lattice. It occurs as sapphire (blue, from trace Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ and Ti⁴⁺ color centers) and ruby (red, from Cr³⁺ substituting for Al³⁺); synthetic single-crystal Al₂O₃ grown by the Verneuil flame fusion process is used for watch crystals, laser tubes, and semiconductor wafer substrates because of its hardness, chemical inertness, and optical transparency.

Flavorists use the concept of 'flavor release kinetics' to design food products: some flavor compounds must be perceived quickly (high volatility, rapid mass transfer through saliva) while others should linger. The Leffingwell model quantifies the relationship between partition coefficients (air/water and fat/water) and the perceived intensity and timing of flavor notes; encapsulation in cyclodextrins or spray-dried micro-beads controls the release profile so that fruit flavors burst immediately while savory notes persist.

The Lindemann-Hinshelwood mechanism explains unimolecular gas-phase reactions: a molecule A is first energized by collision with another molecule M (bimolecular step), then the energized molecule A* can either lose energy back to M or decompose unimolecularly to products. At high pressures, the rate-determining step is unimolecular decomposition (first-order kinetics); at low pressures, the rate-determining step is bimolecular energization (second-order kinetics); the fall-off from first-order to second-order behavior as pressure decreases is a characteristic signature of this mechanism.

Citric acid (2-hydroxypropane-1,2,3-tricarboxylic acid) is produced industrially at over 2 million tonnes per year by aerobic fermentation of sucrose or glucose by Aspergillus niger under conditions of phosphate and trace metal limitation that impair the TCA cycle and cause citrate to accumulate. It is used as a food acidulant (E330) in soft drinks, confectionery, and fruit juice; as a chelating agent in cleaning products; and as an anticoagulant in blood collection tubes.

Palladium-catalyzed C−H/C−H coupling (oxidative Heck or direct CDC) forms C−C bonds between two unactivated C−H bonds using an oxidant (Cu(OAc)₂, K₂S₂O₈, or Ag₂CO₃) to regenerate the Pd(II) catalyst after each catalytic cycle, without requiring any pre-functionalized starting material. When combined with a directing group for site selectivity and a chiral ligand for enantioselectivity, this approach represents the most atom-economical possible C−C bond-forming strategy.

The Pauli principle applied to atomic ground states follows the Aufbau principle, Hund's rules, and the Madelung energy ordering. Chromium (Z=24) and copper (Z=29) are classic exceptions: chromium has the configuration [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ rather than [Ar]3d⁴4s² because a half-filled 3d shell is particularly stable; copper is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ because a fully filled 3d shell is more stable than [Ar]3d⁹4s², reflecting the comparably close energies of 3d and 4s orbitals.

Fischer-Tropsch synthesis converts syngas (CO + H₂) over iron or cobalt catalysts at 150–350 °C into liquid hydrocarbons including paraffins, olefins, and alcohols through a surface polymerization mechanism starting with CO dissociation and CH₂ insertion. The product distribution follows the Anderson-Schulz-Flory (ASF) distribution governed by a chain-growth parameter α; high α (promoted cobalt catalysts, low temperature) favors waxes for further hydrocracking to diesel, while high temperatures give gasoline and olefins.

Ubiquitin is a small (76 amino acid, 8.6 kDa) protein that is covalently attached to lysine residues of target proteins through a three-enzyme cascade (E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme, E2 conjugating enzyme, E3 ligase) to mark them for degradation by the 26S proteasome. Polyubiquitin chains linked through different lysines (K48 → proteasomal degradation; K63 → DNA repair, autophagy; M1/linear → NF-κB signaling) constitute a complex regulatory code for protein fate; Ciechanover, Hershko, and Rose received the 2004 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering this system.

Polyhedral boranes are a class of boron-hydrogen cage compounds described by Wade's rules: closo clusters (complete cage, 2n+2 skeletal electron pairs, e.g., B₆H₆²⁻), nido (nest-like, 2n+4 pairs, e.g., B₅H₉), and arachno (spider web, 2n+6 pairs). Carboranes (C₂BₙHₙ₊₂) are isoelectronic analogs where two BH units are replaced by CH; 1,2-dicarba-closo-dodecaborane (ortho-carborane, C₂B₁₀H₁₂) is thermally stable to 750 °C and its lipophilicity makes it attractive for boron neutron capture therapy drug design.

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) include superoxide (O₂•⁻), hydroxyl radical (•OH), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and singlet oxygen (¹O₂); at low levels they function as signaling molecules regulating cell proliferation, apoptosis, and immune responses. Excess ROS overwhelms antioxidant defenses (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase) and causes oxidative stress, leading to lipid peroxidation, DNA strand breaks, and protein carbonylation — a molecular signature of aging and many chronic diseases.

Dehalogenation reactions remove halogen atoms from organic molecules through reduction, substitution, or elimination pathways; biologically, reductive dehalogenation (using cobalamin-dependent reductive dehalogenases) allows anaerobic bacteria (Dehalococcoides) to use chlorinated solvents as terminal electron acceptors, converting PCE and TCE to ethylene in contaminated groundwater. This process (bioattenuation) is harnessed in bioremediation strategies that stimulate indigenous Dehalococcoides populations by adding electron donors (whey, molasses) to contaminated sites.

The Meisenheimer complex (sigma complex or Jackson-Meisenheimer complex) is an anionic intermediate formed when a nucleophile attacks the ipso carbon of an electron-poor aromatic ring bearing good leaving groups (halides, nitro groups) in SNAr (nucleophilic aromatic substitution). Unlike EAS which proceeds through a cationic Wheland intermediate, SNAr requires electron-withdrawing groups ortho or para to the leaving group to stabilize the negative charge in the Meisenheimer complex; fluoro groups are the best leaving groups in SNAr despite being poor leaving groups in SN2.

Spectroscopic ellipsometry measures the change in polarization state of light upon reflection from a thin film surface, allowing precise determination of film thickness (1–10,000 nm) and optical constants (refractive index n, extinction coefficient k) without contact. It is used in semiconductor manufacturing to monitor SiO₂ gate oxide thickness during chip fabrication, to characterize multilayer coatings on optical elements, and to study adsorbed biomolecular films on biosensor surfaces.

Photopolymerization uses light-activated photoinitiators to generate radicals or cations that initiate chain-growth polymerization, curing liquid monomers or oligomers into solid polymers in seconds to minutes under UV or visible light. Applications include 3D printing (stereolithography and digital light processing use photopolymer resins), dental composite fillings (blue-light cured methacrylate resins), optical fiber coatings, and inkjet-printable adhesives and coatings that cure without heat.

Cytochrome P450 enzymes are a superfamily of heme-containing monooxygenases that insert one oxygen atom from O₂ into substrates while reducing the other to water using electrons from NAD(P)H. They are responsible for metabolizing ~75% of clinical drugs through phase I oxidative metabolism in the liver; CYP3A4 alone metabolizes ~50% of drugs.
