The 'compound I' high-valent oxo-iron(IV) porphyrin π-cation radical intermediate, [Fe⁴⁺=O P⁺•], is the reactive species that abstracts hydrogen atoms from C−H bonds.

Benzophenone (diphenyl ketone) is the classical photosensitizer used in photochemistry because it has a high intersystem crossing efficiency (~100%) that rapidly produces a long-lived triplet state capable of abstracting hydrogen from C−H bonds of organic substrates. When dissolved in acetone with benzhydrol or isopropanol, UV-irradiated benzophenone produces benzopinacol through radical coupling; this Norrish type II reaction of benzophenone is one of the best-studied photochemical reactions and is a standard undergraduate photochemistry laboratory experiment.

Ion exchange resins are cross-linked polymer beads carrying permanently ionized groups that exchange their counter-ions for ions of the same charge in solution. Strong-acid cation exchange resins (sulfonic acid groups, −SO₃H⁺) and strong-base anion exchange resins (quaternary ammonium groups, −N⁺R₃) are combined in water demineralizers to produce ultra-pure water for semiconductor manufacturing, laboratory use, and boiler feed water; they work by exchanging Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (and all other ions) for H⁺ and OH⁻, which combine to give water.

Electrochemical ammonia synthesis at room temperature and pressure is being pursued as a green alternative to the energy-intensive Haber-Bosch process; however, the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) faces the challenge of selectivity against the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which is thermodynamically more favorable. Lithium-mediated NRR is the most promising approach: lithium deposited on the electrode surface reacts with N₂ to form Li₃N, which is then protonated by an alcohol proton source to release NH₃, with Faradaic efficiencies up to 70% demonstrated.

Phosphorylation of serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues on proteins by protein kinases is the most widespread post-translational modification in signal transduction, with over 500 kinases encoded in the human genome. It reversibly alters protein conformation and function by adding a bulky, negatively charged phosphate group; correspondingly, about 1/3 of cellular proteins are phosphorylated at any given time. Dysregulation of kinase signaling is implicated in >400 human diseases, making protein kinases the largest class of drug targets after GPCRs.

Sulfur mustard (2,2'-dichlorodiethyl sulfide, HD, 'mustard gas') blisters skin, eyes, and airways within 2–24 hours of exposure by alkylating DNA (forming N7-guanine adducts), RNA, and proteins through a sulfonium ion intermediate generated by intramolecular displacement of chloride. Unlike the nitrogen mustards, HD acts despite low water solubility (it penetrates skin before hydrolyzing) and has no known antidote; treatment is purely supportive (anti-inflammatory, analgesic). It was used extensively in World War I and subsequently banned by the Chemical Weapons Convention.

Electrochemical carbon capture and utilization (eCCU) systems use electrochemically generated bases (e.g., OH⁻ from water oxidation) to absorb CO₂ from air or flue gas as carbonate/bicarbonate, then electrochemically regenerate the base while releasing concentrated CO₂ for storage or conversion to fuels and chemicals. Unlike thermal regeneration of monoethanolamine (MEA) scrubbers, which requires ~3.7 GJ/tonne CO₂ at 120 °C, electrochemical regeneration at room temperature using renewable electricity is emerging as a more energy-efficient approach.

Abiotic synthesis of amino acids from inorganic precursors under prebiotic conditions was demonstrated by Stanley Miller and Harold Urey in 1953: sparking a mixture of CH₄, NH₃, H₂, and H₂O with electrical discharges (simulating lightning in a reducing early atmosphere) produced at least 20 amino acids including glycine, alanine, and aspartic acid. Later analysis of the original archived samples found 25 amino acids, and similar synthesis from CO₂/N₂/H₂O mixtures (more realistic for the early Earth) also produces amino acids, supporting their prebiotic availability.

Spin crossover (SCO) materials are coordination compounds (typically iron(II) or iron(III) complexes) that can reversibly switch between low-spin (LS, t₂g⁶ for Fe(II)) and high-spin (HS, t₂g⁴eg², for Fe(II)) electronic states in response to temperature, pressure, or light (LIESST: light-induced excited spin state trapping). The switching is accompanied by large changes in color, volume (~10%), and magnetic susceptibility, making SCO materials candidates for bistable molecular switches in memory devices and sensors.

Chitosan is derived from chitin (the second most abundant biopolymer after cellulose, found in crustacean shells and fungal cell walls) by partial deacetylation under alkaline conditions, producing a polycationic polysaccharide with primary amine groups that can form gels, films, and fibers. Its biodegradability, biocompatibility, and antimicrobial activity (disrupts bacterial membranes) make chitosan valuable in wound dressings, drug delivery, water treatment (flocculation of negatively charged pollutants), and food preservation.

Tandem catalysis cascades multiple catalytic steps in a one-pot reaction to build molecular complexity efficiently. The Sorensen sequential one-pot Suzuki coupling-cyclization-Sonogashira sequence assembles complex heterocyclic natural products in fewer operations than traditional multistep sequences; computationally designed de novo enzymes (e.g., Kemp eliminase designed by David Baker's group) demonstrate that entirely new catalytic functions not found in nature can be engineered into protein scaffolds from first principles.

Atomic layer deposition (ALD) deposits ultra-thin, conformal films one atomic layer at a time by alternating pulses of two reactive precursor gases, each self-limiting to a single monolayer because the surface reaction saturates at full monolayer coverage. Al₂O₃ ALD using trimethylaluminum (TMA) and water is the most studied ALD process: TMA reacts with surface OH groups to deposit one layer of AlMe₂, and subsequent water pulses convert it to Al₂O₃−OH, ready for the next cycle; each cycle deposits ~0.1 nm, allowing angstrom-level thickness control.

Hydrogen bonds in water ice have been studied by neutron diffraction and are 1.97 Å long (O⋯H) in hexagonal ice (Ih), compared to the covalent O−H bond of 0.96 Å. The network topology of ice Ih has each water molecule donating two H-bonds and accepting two, arranged tetrahedrally; this creates open hexagonal rings that make ice 9% less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats — a thermodynamically anomalous property that is critical for aquatic life surviving frozen winters.

Electrostatic potential maps (EPM), computed from quantum chemical wave functions and plotted on an electron density isosurface, visualize where a molecule is nucleophilic (electron-rich, red) and electrophilic (electron-poor, blue). They are invaluable for predicting and rationalizing regioselectivity in chemical reactions, intermolecular interactions (H-bond donor/acceptor sites, π-stacking), and drug-receptor binding, and are standard tools in modern computational drug design and molecular education.

Nanoparticle surface plasmon resonance (SPR) arises when the frequency of incident light matches the collective oscillation frequency of conduction electrons in a metallic nanoparticle, causing strong absorption and scattering. For gold nanospheres (~20 nm), the SPR peak is at ~520 nm (green light), giving them their characteristic wine-red color; as size, shape, and aggregation state change, the SPR red-shifts dramatically — gold nanorods absorb in the near-infrared — enabling colorimetric sensors and SERS substrates.

Lactic acid fermentation by Lactobacillus bacteria converts glucose to lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) via pyruvate reduction by NADH, regenerating NAD⁺ for continued glycolysis. The product, L-lactic acid, acidifies milk to produce yogurt and cheese; in human muscle during intense anaerobic exercise, L-lactate accumulates when O₂ supply cannot meet demand (not lactic acid per se, as the pKa of lactic acid is 3.86 so it is fully dissociated at physiological pH, releasing protons that reduce pH).

Polyaniline (PANI) is a conducting polymer discovered in 1985 by MacDiarmid, Heeger, and others (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2000 shared with Shirakawa for conducting polymers) that exists in multiple oxidation states from leucoemeraldine (fully reduced) through emeraldine (half-oxidized) to pernigraniline (fully oxidized). The emeraldine salt form (protonated with HCl or CSA) is electrically conducting (~10 S/cm) because protonation creates polarons and bipolarons on the conjugated π-system that carry charge; PANI is used in anticorrosion coatings, sensors, and flexible electronics.

The Periodic Table of the Elements, established by Mendeleev in 1869 and refined into its modern form, organizes all 118 confirmed elements by increasing atomic number, with chemical properties repeating periodically across periods. The most recently confirmed element is oganesson (Og, Z=118), a superheavy noble gas synthesized at JINR (Dubna) by bombarding californium-249 with calcium-48 ions, with only a few atoms ever produced; theoretical calculations predict its chemistry may deviate significantly from that of lighter noble gases due to relativistic effects.
